title: Developers’ Reference
text:
This page is the canonical reference for contributing to TimeToAlign!. The conceptual model lives in Concepts and the per-class API lives under API Reference; everything you need to build, test, document, and release the library is here.
The package is named timetoalign for machines (imports, PyPI) and written TimeToAlign! for humans (prose, headings, comments).

title: Developers’ Reference
text:
1. Repository Layout
The git repository is a multi-project workspace; the library itself lives in timetoalign/.
tta/                                 # Repository root
├── timetoalign/                     # The Python library — the focus of this doc
│   ├── timetoalign/                 # Importable package
│   ├── tests/                       # pytest suite (mirrors the package layout)
│   ├── docs/                        # Documentation source
│   │   ├── page/                    # Quarto site (this site)
│   │   ├── tuto-notebooks/          # Tutorial notebooks (jupytext .py + paired .ipynb)
│   │   └── howto-notebooks/         # How-to notebooks (jupytext .py + paired .ipynb)
│   ├── pyproject.toml               # PEP 621 project metadata + ruff/coverage/pytest config
│   ├── tox.ini                      # Build/test/lint/publish orchestrator
│   ├── .pre-commit-config.yaml      # Pinned formatter/linter versions
│   ├── .github/workflows/           # CI (release-please)
│   └── CHANGELOG.md                 # Auto-generated by release-please — DO NOT edit by hand
├── tta_article/                     # TISMIR article (LaTeX, published 2026) — out of scope here
├── pyMeasureMap/                    # Sibling project; standalone
└── dashboard/                       # Sibling project; standalone
Sibling projects (tta_article/, pyMeasureMap/, dashboard/) have their own build infrastructure and are not governed by the rules below.

title: Developers’ Reference
text:
2. Architecture Overview

2.1 Subpackages
The importable package timetoalign/ is organised into focused subpackages, each with a single responsibility:







Subpackage
Responsibility




core/
Foundational types: enums (Domain, TimeUnit, …), Coordinate / IdCoordinate, TimeStamp and the id minter of core/ids.py; core/fields.py contains the SemanticField bases plus the Arrow translator/builder.


display/
ASCII rendering helpers for timelines, groups, bundles, flows.


maps/
ConversionMap family (LinearMap, TableMap, ChainMap, PiecewiseMap, …).


timelines/
Timeline classes for all six domain × modality combinations, TimelineGroup, regions, flow control, beat grids.


alignment/
MatchClaim, AlignmentAnchor, AlignmentBundle, MatchGraph, MatchLine, WarpMap.


storage/
PyArrow-backed EventData / EventStore storage primitives.


loader/
File-format-specific ingestion.





2.2 Import Direction (MANDATORY)
Subpackages are arranged in strict layers. Imports may only flow downward, from a higher-numbered layer to a lower-numbered one. This is a hard rule: violations create circular-import landmines and are refused at review.
                    ┌──────────────────────────────┐
       Layer 5 ──▶  │            loader            │
                    └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                   │ may import from layers 0–4
                    ┌──────────────▼───────────────┐
       Layer 4 ──▶  │          alignment           │
                    └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                   │ may import from layers 0–3
                    ┌──────────────▼───────────────┐
       Layer 3 ──▶  │          timelines           │
                    └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                   │ may import from layers 0–2
                    ┌──────────────▼───────────────┐
       Layer 2 ──▶  │           storage            │
                    └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                   │ may import from layers 0–1
                    ┌──────────────▼───────────────┐
       Layer 1 ──▶  │             maps             │
                    └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                   │ may import from layer 0
                    ┌──────────────▼───────────────┐
       Layer 0 ──▶  │       core       display      │
                    └──────────────────────────────┘
                       (no internal dependencies)
Equivalently:







Subpackage
May import from




core/
nothing internal


display/
nothing internal at runtime (TYPE_CHECKING only)


maps/
core


storage/
lower layers as needed; owns EventData and EventStore


timelines/
core, maps, storage


alignment/
lower layers, including timelines


loader/
all lower layers




Storage ownership and timeline dependencies
storage/ is a first-class layer that owns EventData and EventStore, the PyArrow-backed event storage used by timelines and loaders. Timeline instances therefore import storage types at runtime as part of the normal layering:
from timetoalign.storage import EventData
There is no timelines–loader import cycle: loader/ is the upper layer and imports downward to construct storage-backed timelines. Runtime imports from timelines/ to storage/ are legitimate dependencies; keep all imports flowing from a higher layer to a lower one.



2.3 Stable Architectural Invariants
These invariants are tested at the unit level and enforced at review. If you find yourself wanting to break one, raise it as a discussion before coding.

Coordinate resolution returns a shared stamp type. TimeStamp and MatchStamp implement the common Stamp interface; each exposes raw and unit-bearing coordinate access consistently.
Coordinate and IdCoordinate are the canonical input types for every method that takes a coordinate value. Raw numbers are accepted for ergonomics; raw numbers are not acceptable as return types — every getter returns a Coordinate.
ConversionMap properties belong to a single Timeline. They are not graph edges between timelines.
MatchGraph is on-demand and analytical. It is built from claims when needed, not maintained as a system-wide structure.
Loaders use a strict two-phase contract. loader.load(*sources) ingests files; loader.create_*() produces domain objects and never takes file paths. The from_file() classmethod is sugar for the common case.
All enums live in core/enums.py and subclass FancyStrEnum. Member names are lowercase. The single documented exception is NumberType, whose values are Python type objects.
Minted IDs are random and seeded: a type prefix (clt/dlt/cpt/ dpt/cgt/dgt for the six domain × modality combinations of a timeline), _ and 13 random base-36 characters, led by an optional role (score:clt_…). An ID is minted when its object is constructed and never renamed; an ID held twice is refused at a join. Loaders seed from the bytes they read, objects built in code from their content, and seed= gives exact IDs: a test asserts minted IDs only where it is about minting, and otherwise gives speaking IDs or reads them through the object (timeline.id).

For the full conceptual rationale see Concepts and the Glossary.


2.4 Architectural decision log
The invariants below are load-bearing design rules. They are not auto-discoverable from any single docstring; new code is expected to respect them, and breaking changes are expected to be discussed and recorded here.
Pydantic-derived schemas + value projectors. Every scalar (Coordinate, Duration, SpecificPitch, Note, Measure, the pitch / harmony hierarchies, …) is a pydantic BaseModel subclass with model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True). The corresponding PyArrow pa.StructType is derived once at class-definition time via derive_arrow_struct(model_cls) (see timetoalign/core/fields.py). Computed pydantic fields are deliberately excluded from the derived struct. Individual fields may be denormalised or dropped via register_value_projector(model_cls, field_name, projector): for example, Coordinate.value projects to {value, numerator, denominator} so rationals survive Parquet, and Note.pitch is dropped entirely so pitch lives in its own field (midi_pitch / specific_pitch) rather than as a sub-field of Note.
Union-of-BaseModel rejected. Distinct scalar types live in distinct PyArrow fields. The translator deliberately raises on BaseModel | BaseModel unions: storing them as PyArrow dense_union is forbidden because consumers (DuckDB, polars, pandas) cannot project the union arms cleanly. The required pattern is columnar separation — drop the polymorphic field with register_value_projector(..., lambda *_: []) and expose each scalar type in its own field.
Bulk construction path. The canonical bulk constructor is StructArrayBuilder.from_model(model_cls).build(objects), with build_struct_array(model_cls, objects) as the public facade and build_coordinate_struct_array as the specialised facade for the rational denormalisation of Coordinate / Duration. The builder traverses each scalar once and accumulates per-field arrays. Never model_dump row-wise in production paths. The microbenchmark gate requires the store-builder to be ≥ 2× faster than row-wise model_dump; on Coordinate the observed ratio is ~5×, and the underlying load-bearing claim — vectorised pa.compute operations on a 1M-element field being ~150–210× faster than the equivalent per-object Python loop — is the justification for the columnar architecture as a whole.
Paired scalar + field convention. Every scalar X is followed in the same source file by its paired XField(SemanticField[X]). core/time.py cohabits the time scalars (DenominateNumber, Coordinate, Duration, IdCoordinate, IdDuration, Interval) and their paired fields under a single TimeScalarField parent that consolidates from_field / from_table / metadata plumbing; core/events.py cohabits pitch, harmony, Note, and Measure with their paired fields. Object + ObjectField is the unit of code organisation and must never be split across files. DenominateNumber is the unit-bearing number every time scalar is built on, and Interval is the half-open span two Coordinates make; both follow the same rule, so DenominateNumberField and IntervalField sit immediately after them.
Raw vs semantic DataField branch. DataField is the abstract base for field wrappers. Raw subclasses (NumericField, StringField, StructField, MapField, plus the struct-shaped numeric branch NumberField → RedundantNumberField → DenominateNumberField) wrap PyArrow data with type checks and accessors. SemanticField[T] is the strictly-typed bridge between a pydantic scalar T and a struct-shaped raw field; it pins the inner raw type via the _raw_cls ClassVar (default StructField, refined to DenominateNumberField by TimeScalarField).
Unified TimeStamp architecture. TimeStamp is the canonical result of coordinate resolution for timelines and groups, MatchStamp for bundles. They share the same Stamp interface for timeline presence, raw coordinates, and unit-bearing coordinate access. MatchGraph remains on-demand (see §2.3).

title: Developers’ Reference
text:
3. Environment & Installation

3.1 Python

Supported: Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 (CI matrix).
Required: >=3.11 per pyproject.toml.



3.2 Install
From the timetoalign/ directory:
pip install -e ".[dev]"
dev is the convenience extra that pulls in everything: all loaders, plotting, the tutorial Jupyter stack, the docs build chain, the test stack, and the formatter/linter tooling. See pyproject.toml for the full extras hierarchy (midi, partitura, music21, ms3, audio, graphical, plot, scores, loaders, tutorial, docs, testing, all, dev).
timetoshare, the TimeToShare package (the manifest schema and its validator, which checks every manifest the library reads and writes), is a runtime dependency listed in [project] dependencies, so every install above brings it. Until a release of TimeToShare carries the schema version the library writes, it is a git reference to TimeToShare’s main branch. PyPI refuses a direct reference in a published package’s requirements, so a release of the library needs the registry range in its place.
The conformance tests also need a test oracle that no extra installs: pymeasuremap, the Measure Map reference implementation, the oracle for compressed measure-map rows. It is installed from a git reference to a fixed commit, so it lives in the conformance dependency group (PEP 735), which is not part of the published distribution metadata. Install it beside the extras (pip 25.1 or later):
pip install --group conformance
tox installs the group in every test environment by itself. From a checkout with the sibling repositories, pip install -e ../TimeToShare/python -e ../pyMeasureMap installs both packages from source instead.


3.3 Pre-commit Hook
After installing, register the git hook once per clone:
pre-commit install
The pinned hook versions in .pre-commit-config.yaml are:








Hook
Version
Settings




black
26.1.0
language_version: python3.11


isort
7.0.0
--profile black --filter-files


flake8
7.3.0
max-line-length=120, __init__.py:F401 ignored, docs/howto-notebooks/*.py:E402 ignored


seed-isort-config
2.2.0



pre-commit-hooks
6.0.0
trailing-whitespace, check-ast/json/xml/yaml, end-of-file-fixer, mixed-line-ending (auto), debug-statements, requirements-txt-fixer



These are pinned deliberately — bump them in a dedicated chore: commit so the diff is isolated.

title: Developers’ Reference
text:
4. Build, Test, Publish (tox)
tox is the canonical entry point for everything CI-relevant. It uses tox-uv for fast environment creation. All commands run from timetoalign/.







Command
Effect




tox
Runs the full pytest suite under py311, py312, py313 (skips missing interpreters).


tox -e lint
pre-commit run --all-files --show-diff-on-failure.


tox -e build
PEP 517 sdist + wheel into ./dist/ via python -m build.


tox -e clean
Removes ./build/ and ./dist/.


tox -e publish
twine check dist/* then twine upload dist/* (testpypi by default).



To publish to production PyPI explicitly:
tox -e publish -- --repository pypi
The publish env passes TWINE_USERNAME / TWINE_PASSWORD / TWINE_REPOSITORY / TWINE_REPOSITORY_URL through from the environment.
There is no tox -e docs env; documentation is built directly with quartodoc + quarto (see §6).

4.1 Direct pytest for Iteration
Inside the active venv, plain pytest is faster than tox for tight edit-test loops:
pytest                              # full suite, parallel via pytest-xdist (-n auto)
pytest -n 0                         # serial — debugging only
pytest tests/timelines              # one subtree
pytest tests/timelines/test_base.py::test_lock
Coverage is on by default (configured in pyproject.toml [tool.pytest.ini_options]).


4.2 Test Discipline (MANDATORY)

Parallel-safe. No global mutable state, no inter-test ordering, use tmp_path not hardcoded /tmp/ paths, no port collisions.
Exact assertions. Use exact gold-standard counts, never >=, never “approximate”. If floating-point tolerance is required, document the mathematical reason in the test and the test data README.
Cover happy path + edge cases. Boundaries, empty inputs, type mismatches.
Property tests for math. ConversionMap-style code uses hypothesis to verify invariants such as inverse(forward(x)) == x.
Test data needs a README. Every directory under tests/data/ documents provenance, validation logic, and known discrepancies between loaders.

title: Developers’ Reference
text:
5. Coding Standards

5.1 Style and Formatting

Line length 120 (enforced by black + flake8).
from __future__ import annotations is the first non-comment line.
Imports grouped: standard library, third-party, local — handled by isort with the black profile.
Module logger: module_logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) immediately after imports.
Use # region <name> / # endregion <name> to group related class / function definitions inside a module.



5.2 Class Member Order
Inside a class, declare members in this order:

Class variables.
@classmethod @property accessors.
@classmethod factories / helpers.
Nested classes (especially Schema).
__init__.
Magic methods (__eq__, __hash__, __repr__, __str__).
@property accessors.
Public and private methods.



5.3 Typing

Every public function signature and class attribute is type-hinted.
Use modern generics (list[str], dict[str, int], X | None) — the __future__ annotations import makes these free at runtime on 3.11+.
Use typing_extensions.Self for methods returning the instance type.
Break circular dependencies with if TYPE_CHECKING: blocks and string annotations, not by collapsing modules.



5.4 Docstrings (Google Style)
Every public module, class, function, and method needs a Google-style docstring. Quartodoc renders them into the API reference site.
def lookup(self, coord: CoordinateSpec) -> TimeStamp:
    """Return the timestamp at ``coord``.

    Args:
        coord: A raw value, ``Coordinate``, or ``IdCoordinate``.

    Returns:
        A `timetoalign.TimeStamp` populated with all synchronous child
        coordinates and conversion-map results.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``coord`` is outside the timeline length.
    """

Cross-linking

In docstrings: wrap fully-qualified names in backticks (`timetoalign.ConversionMap`); the interlinks filter resolves them.
In .qmd pages and notebook markdown: every model term goes through the glossary shortcode: . Bare uses without the shortcode are documentation bugs.
When you add a new concept: update glossary.yml and glossary.qmd in the same commit as the implementation.




5.5 Error Handling

Never use assert for runtime validation — it disappears under -O.
ValueError for invalid arguments.
TypeError for unit / type mismatches.
RuntimeError (or a custom subclass) for invalid state, e.g. mutating a locked timeline.



5.6 Pitch Spelling
Normalise all input to canonical Unicode characters:

Sharp: ♯ (U+266F)
Flat: ♭ (U+266D)

#, b, -, etc. are converted at the boundary.

title: Developers’ Reference
text:
6. Documentation Site
The docs site is built with Quarto + quartodoc and lives at https://timetoalign.github.io/.

6.1 Building Locally
cd docs/page
quarto render             # build the full site into _site/ (not tracked)
The committed API reference pages (reference/*.qmd) are regenerated with quartodoc build only when the public API or its docstrings change, because it is slow. The site is published per version (X.Y.Z/, dev/ from main, stable/ for the newest release) on the gh-pages branch by the docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml).
The Quarto pre-render hook automatically runs sync_notebooks.py (see §6.3) to refresh tutorial and how-to notebooks before rendering.


6.2 Site Structure (Diátaxis)
The site follows the Diátaxis framework:

Tutorials (tutorials.qmd + tutorials/): learning-oriented, step-by-step.
How-to Guides (howto.qmd + howto/): task-oriented, focused recipes.
Explanation (concepts.qmd, glossary.qmd): understanding-oriented.
API Reference (reference.qmd + auto-generated reference/): information-oriented; this Developers’ Reference lives here too.

The navigation (top navbar + per-section sidebar) is configured in _quarto.yml.


6.3 Notebook Integration Pipeline
Tutorial and how-to notebooks live as jupytext py:percent files in docs/tuto-notebooks/ and docs/howto-notebooks/. The paired .ipynb files are regenerated mechanically; the .py is the source of truth in git.
The pipeline is driven by docs/page/notebooks.csv, with one row per notebook:







Column
Meaning




section
Either tutorials or howto. Selects the source directory and target subdirectory of the rendered site.


source
Filename of the .py jupytext source.


slug
Stem used for the rendered .ipynb (without extension).


title
Title injected as Quarto YAML front matter.


description
Short description used in listing pages.



docs/page/sync_notebooks.py (run as the Quarto pre-render step) does three things per row:

Runs jupytext --sync --execute on the .py source, regenerating the paired .ipynb with fresh outputs.
Copies the resulting .ipynb into docs/page/{tutorials,howto}/<slug>.ipynb.
Replaces the notebook metadata with a Quarto-friendly YAML cell built from the CSV row.

A SHA-256 cache (docs/page/.sync_state.json) skips notebooks whose .py source has not changed.

Adding a new how-to / tutorial notebook

Drop the new .py (jupytext py:percent) into docs/tuto-notebooks/ or docs/howto-notebooks/.
Add a row to docs/page/notebooks.csv.
Add a sidebar entry under the appropriate section in docs/page/_quarto.yml.
If the notebook introduces a new model term, also update glossary.yml and glossary.qmd.
Run cd docs/page && python sync_notebooks.py --verbose once locally to confirm it executes cleanly.
Run quartodoc build && quarto render to confirm it renders.



Notebook style rules

Markdown cells use the  shortcode for every model term. A bare “Timeline” / “ConversionMap” / etc. is a documentation bug.
Use Loader.from_file() rather than the two-phase load() + create_*() pattern in tutorials. The two-phase form is library-internal.
Coordinate conversion is demonstrated through a TimeStamp or MatchStamp, which expose the resolved coordinates directly.




6.4 Jupytext and Quarto: Upgrade-Only
Jupytext and Quarto versions may only ever be upgraded, never downgraded.
Both tools rewrite notebook structure on save; downgrading silently introduces incompatible changes that break the diff history and may corrupt outputs across the entire notebook corpus. If a contributor’s local install is older than the version that last touched the notebooks, they must upgrade before running sync_notebooks.py.
This rule applies equally to CI environments — pin versions upward only.


6.5 quartodoc API Reference
The API reference under docs/page/reference/ is fully generated from the live docstrings. Do not hand-edit those files; they are overwritten by quartodoc build. To add a class to the reference:

Make sure the class is exported from timetoalign/__init__.py (or list it with an explicit name: / package: entry).
Add it to the appropriate contents: list under quartodoc: in docs/page/_quarto.yml.
quartodoc build regenerates the page.

title: Developers’ Reference
text:
7. Conventional Commits & Releases
The library is released by release-please, configured in .github/workflows/release-please.yml with release-type: python and package-name: timetoalign. The action runs on every push to main and:

Reads commit messages since the last release tag.
Computes the next semantic version from those messages.
Opens (or updates) a release PR that bumps pyproject.toml’s version and rewrites CHANGELOG.md.
When the release PR is merged, tags the commit and creates a GitHub release.

Because the version bump is computed from commit messages, every commit that lands on main must follow Conventional Commits.

7.1 Commit Types








Prefix
Effect on version
Use for




feat:
minor bump
New user-facing capability.


fix:
patch bump
Bug fix.


perf:
patch bump
Performance improvement (no behaviour change).


docs:
none
Documentation only.


style:
none
Formatting / whitespace.


refactor:
none
Restructuring with no behaviour change.


test:
none
Adding or correcting tests.


build:
none
Build system or dependency changes.


ci:
none
CI configuration changes.


chore:
none
Repo housekeeping with no src/test impact.


revert:
depends on reverted
Revert of a previous commit.



Optional scopes are encouraged for clarity: feat(loader): …, fix(maps): ….


7.2 Breaking Changes (MAJOR Bump)
A breaking change triggers a major version bump. Mark it both ways:

Add ! after the type, e.g. refactor!:, feat!:.
Include a BREAKING CHANGE: footer describing the migration.

refactor!: make every TimelineGroup member span the whole group

BREAKING CHANGE: TimelineGroup.add_timeline no longer takes start, end or
allow_extension. To let only part of a timeline take part, add the child
timeline covering that part.
The ! is what release-please reads to compute the bump; the BREAKING CHANGE: footer is what readers of the changelog rely on. Use both.


7.3 Manual Edits Are Forbidden

Do not edit pyproject.toml’s version by hand.
Do not edit CHANGELOG.md by hand.

Both are owned by release-please. Manual edits will be overwritten or, worse, will fight the next release PR.

title: Developers’ Reference
text:
8. Branching and Pull Requests

main is the release branch; release-please runs against it.
Feature work happens on topic branches; squash-merge into main with a Conventional Commit message that becomes the merge commit.
The PR title also follows Conventional Commits — release-please reads the merge commit, but a consistent title makes the PR list scannable.
Run tox -e lint and tox (or at least targeted pytest) locally before opening a PR.

title: Developers’ Reference
text:
9. IDE
PyCharm is the preferred IDE. The repo is set up to work cleanly with it out of the box:

Import the timetoalign/ directory as a PyCharm project (not the repo root — sibling projects have their own settings).
Configure the project interpreter to a venv with pip install -e ".[dev]" applied.
Enable the Black and isort integrations and point them at the project tools (PyCharm reads .pre-commit-config.yaml for the pinned versions; mirror them in Settings → Tools → Black and Settings → Editor → Code Style → Python → Imports).
Enable Settings → Editor → Inspections → Python → Type checker with strict mode if you want the same level of typing the codebase already enforces.
The flake8 line length is 120; set Settings → Editor → Code Style → Python → Hard wrap at to 120 to match.

VS Code, Neovim, and other editors all work — the formatters and linters are externally driven by pre-commit and tox, so editor choice is not load-bearing — but PyCharm is what the maintainers use day-to-day.

title: How to Build Beat Grids
text:
You have a recording, you know its tempo, and you know the second at which a beat sounds. You want the beat and measure times, and you want them in a file an annotation program can open.
A BeatGrid is the arithmetic for that. It stores only what a source states — where an anchor beat sits, how fast the music runs, how beats group into bars, and which beat of a bar the anchor is — and generates every beat from those facts. It is not a Timeline: nothing is stored per beat, so a grid can cover a whole DJ set as cheaply as a bar.

from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from timetoalign import BeatGrid, BeatGridSegment, BeatPolicy



BeatGrid.from_tempo() states a tempo in beats per minute, the meter as the source spells it, the second at which the anchor beat sounds, and which beat of the bar that anchor is. extent bounds the grid — for a recording, its duration.
Positions are read exactly. A decimal string spells the decimal it looks like; a float contributes the exact binary value it holds, which is a different and much longer rational. Pass a string or a Fraction wherever the decimal is the fact.

grid = BeatGrid.from_tempo(160, metro="4/4", start="0.092", extent="212.48")
grid

BeatGrid(1 segment, extent=5312/25, 142 measures)


The grid holds one segment: the four stated facts, plus the end the grid gave it from extent.

segment = grid.segments[0]
segment

BeatGridSegment(start=23/250, end=5312/25, bpm=160, policy=4/4, battito=1)


Beat length, bar length and the first downbeat are derived from those facts rather than stored beside them, so they cannot fall out of step with the tempo. metro="4/4" reads as four beats of one quarter each; the grid’s lattice ticks once per counted value, so "6/8" would be six beats of an eighth, not two dotted ones.
The derived values come back as exact rationals — 23/250 is 0.092, and 3/8 of a second is one beat at 160 BPM.

{
    "beat length (s)": segment.beat_seconds,
    "bar length (s)": segment.bar_seconds,
    "quarters per second": segment.quarters_per_second,
    "first downbeat (s)": segment.first_downbeat,
    "measures in the grid": grid.n_measures,
}

{'beat length (s)': Fraction(3, 8),
 'bar length (s)': Fraction(3, 2),
 'quarters per second': Fraction(8, 3),
 'first downbeat (s)': Fraction(23, 250),
 'measures in the grid': 142}

A grid does not have to be written by hand. Where a loader reads tempo statements out of a file, it builds the grid for you: RekordboxLoader.create_beatgrid() returns the grid of the loaded track (and create_beatgrids() one per track of a collection), a BeatGrid with the same surface as everything above.

title: How to Build Beat Grids
text:
BeatGrid.from_tempo() states a tempo in beats per minute, the meter as the source spells it, the second at which the anchor beat sounds, and which beat of the bar that anchor is. extent bounds the grid — for a recording, its duration.
Positions are read exactly. A decimal string spells the decimal it looks like; a float contributes the exact binary value it holds, which is a different and much longer rational. Pass a string or a Fraction wherever the decimal is the fact.

grid = BeatGrid.from_tempo(160, metro="4/4", start="0.092", extent="212.48")
grid

BeatGrid(1 segment, extent=5312/25, 142 measures)


The grid holds one segment: the four stated facts, plus the end the grid gave it from extent.

segment = grid.segments[0]
segment

BeatGridSegment(start=23/250, end=5312/25, bpm=160, policy=4/4, battito=1)


Beat length, bar length and the first downbeat are derived from those facts rather than stored beside them, so they cannot fall out of step with the tempo. metro="4/4" reads as four beats of one quarter each; the grid’s lattice ticks once per counted value, so "6/8" would be six beats of an eighth, not two dotted ones.
The derived values come back as exact rationals — 23/250 is 0.092, and 3/8 of a second is one beat at 160 BPM.

    "bar length (s)": segment.bar_seconds,
    "quarters per second": segment.quarters_per_second,
    "first downbeat (s)": segment.first_downbeat,
    "measures in the grid": grid.n_measures,
}

title: How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes
text:
A measure on a scanned page, a zone of an MEI facsimile and a rectangle drawn on an analytical diagram are all areas of an image. An image has no time axis of its own: neither its width nor its height is one. It has one only along a time path, the line a reader follows through it. On a page of a score the path runs along the first accolade (a system, one line of the page) from left to right, then along the second, and so on. A page is therefore built of its accolades, laid end to end, and a volume of its pages. Along one accolade each area is an interval: it starts where the area starts in x, counted from the accolade’s left end, and lasts as long as the area is wide.
The library holds both views in one event, the Box. A Box keeps the area as the source states it, its shape, in the image’s own pixels: either a BoundingBox (x, y, width, height, the IIIF and Media Fragments xywh) or a Quadrilateral (four corners, for the skewed measures of a scan). Its start and duration are the interval on the timeline. The two always agree, and the library refuses a Box in which they do not.
This guide builds shapes and writes them in the forms other formats use, makes the time path of a page from the areas drawn on it, builds the page from its accolades and puts Boxes on them, shows the rectangles of a graphical analysis as Boxes on its image crops, reads pages from a DMOS page layout and from an MEI facsimile, lays the pages of an IIIF volume along their paths, and writes a bundle holding Boxes as a package and reads it back.


Install the library with pip install timetoalign. Every source file this guide reads, except the annotation table of the graphical analysis, is written by the guide into a temporary directory. A timeline’s Boxes come back as the events of any type do: get_events(event_type="Box") selects them and get_field(Box) reads them as Box objects, each with its ID, interval and shape. The helpers: box_table shows them one per row with the x extent of each shape beside the interval, segment_table lists the timelines a page or a volume is built of, refusal runs a call the library refuses and prints its message, write writes a source file into the temporary directory, and show prints one key of a manifest file.

import json
import tempfile
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from timetoshare import dumps, loads

from timetoalign import (
    AlignmentBundle,
    BoundingBox,
    Box,
    ContinuousLogicalTimeline,
    DiscreteGraphicalTimeline,
    DmosLoader,
    IIIFManifestLoader,
    MeiFacsimileLoader,
    Quadrilateral,
)
from timetoalign.loader.graphical import TimeAxisPath
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data
from timetoalign.timelines import SegmentLine

FILES = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())


def box_table(timeline):
    """One row per Box: its interval on the timeline and its shape's x extent."""
    return pd.DataFrame(
        [
            {
                "id": box.id,
                "start": box.start.value,
                "duration": box.duration.value,
                "shape": type(box.shape).__name__,
                "x_min": box.shape.x_min.value,
                "x_max": box.shape.x_max.value,
            }
            for box in timeline.get_events(event_type="Box").get_field(Box)
        ]
    )


def segment_table(line):
    """One row per timeline a page or a volume is built of, in reading order."""
    return pd.DataFrame(
        [
            {
                "id": child_id,
                "name": line.get_child(child_id).name,
                "offset": line.get_child_offset(child_id).value,
                "length": line.get_child(child_id).length.value,
            }
            for child_id in line.list_children()
        ]
    )


def write(name, text):
    """Write a source file into the temporary directory."""
    (FILES / name).write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")


def refusal(call):
    """Run a call the library refuses and print its message."""
    try:
        call()
    except ValueError as error:
        print(error)


def show(manifest_path, key):
    """Print one key of a manifest file as canonical YAML."""
    print(dumps({key: loads(manifest_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))[key]}), end="")




A shape is an area of an image in image space: the origin is the image’s top-left corner, x runs right and y down, and every number is in one unit and one number type. On pixels the numbers are integers.
A BoundingBox is built from its top-left corner and its extent with from_xywh(). This one is a rectangle of the graphical analysis used below: x 385, y 46, 139 pixels wide, 20 high.

rect = BoundingBox.from_xywh(385, 46, 139, 20, unit="pixels")
rect

BoundingBox(x=Coordinate(385, pixels), y=Coordinate(46, pixels), width=Duration(139, pixels), height=Duration(20, pixels))


A shape writes itself in the forms other formats use: its dict form (as a manifest holds it), a Media Fragments and IIIF selector, the points of an SVG polygon (corners in the order top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left), and the attributes of an MEI zone, whose lrx and lry are the lower-right corner (x + width, y + height).

{
    "dict form": rect.to_dict(),
    "media fragment": rect.as_media_fragment(),
    "SVG points": rect.as_svg_points(),
    "MEI zone": rect.as_mei_zone(),
}

{'dict form': {'x': 385, 'y': 46, 'width': 139, 'height': 20},
 'media fragment': 'xywh=385,46,139,20',
 'SVG points': '385,46 524,46 524,66 385,66',
 'MEI zone': {'ulx': '385', 'uly': '46', 'lrx': '524', 'lry': '66'}}


Each form reads back into the same box: from_media_fragment() reads the selector, from_corners() the corners an MEI zone states.

(
    BoundingBox.from_media_fragment("xywh=385,46,139,20", unit="pixels") == rect,
    BoundingBox.from_corners(385, 46, 524, 66, unit="pixels") == rect,
)

(True, True)


A Quadrilateral holds four corners, so it can follow a measure whose sides are not upright. from_points() takes the points in any order the source writes them, with order= naming the corner each one is; the optical music recognition tool DMOS writes a measure top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right. These are the corners of the first measure of the first system on page 2 of a printed score in Gallica (ark:/12148/bpt6k11620688), as DMOS states them; measure 2 follows it on that system, and measure 3 is the first of the second system. The quadrilateral keeps the corners in the canonical order.

DMOS_MEASURE_ORDER = ("top_left", "top_right", "bottom_left", "bottom_right")
MEASURE_1 = [[1221, 1589], [2151, 1589], [1221, 2266], [2161, 2266]]
MEASURE_2 = [[2151, 1589], [2766, 1589], [2161, 2266], [2775, 2266]]
MEASURE_3 = [[971, 2493], [1935, 2493], [971, 3192], [1945, 3192]]

measure_1, measure_2, measure_3 = (
    Quadrilateral.from_points(corners, order=DMOS_MEASURE_ORDER, unit="pixels")
    for corners in (MEASURE_1, MEASURE_2, MEASURE_3)
)
measure_1

Quadrilateral(top_left=(1221, 1589), top_right=(2151, 1589), bottom_right=(2161, 2266), bottom_left=(1221, 2266), unit=pixels)


Its top edge is 930 pixels long and its bottom edge 940: the scan is slightly skewed. The quadrilateral’s bounding box is the smallest upright box holding it, and its MEI zone carries both, the box as ulx to lry and the corners as points.

measure_1.bounding_box

BoundingBox(x=Coordinate(1221, pixels), y=Coordinate(1589, pixels), width=Duration(940, pixels), height=Duration(677, pixels))



{"SVG points": measure_1.as_svg_points(), "MEI zone": measure_1.as_mei_zone()}

{'SVG points': '1221,1589 2151,1589 2161,2266 1221,2266',
 'MEI zone': {'ulx': '1221',
  'uly': '1589',
  'lrx': '2161',
  'lry': '2266',
  'points': '1221,1589 2151,1589 2161,2266 1221,2266'}}


SVG and MEI points may start at any corner and run in either direction. from_svg_points() reads such a list and brings it into the canonical order; here the list starts at the bottom-right corner and runs anticlockwise.

Quadrilateral.from_svg_points(
    "2161,2266 2151,1589 1221,1589 1221,2266", unit="pixels"
) == (measure_1)

True


A shape’s numbers are never rounded. A whole number given as a float is taken (385.0 is 385); a pixel position of 385.5 cannot be held on an integer axis and is refused.

BoundingBox.from_xywh(385.0, 46, 139, 20, unit="pixels") == rect

True



refusal(lambda: BoundingBox.from_xywh(385.5, 46, 139, 20, unit="pixels"))

A shape's x is 385.5, which pixels as int cannot hold exactly: geometry is never rounded.





No image has a time axis until its path through the image is defined. A set of boxes makes one: TimeAxisPath.from_boxes() takes the areas of one page in reading order and returns a PiecewisePath, one horizontal piece per accolade.
DMOS states the systems of the page as areas too (corners top-left, bottom-left, top-right, bottom-right). Each system is one accolade, so accolades= gives every box its own label.

PAGE_URL = "https://gallica.bnf.fr/iiif/ark:/12148/bpt6k11620688/f2"
DMOS_SYSTEM_ORDER = ("top_left", "bottom_left", "top_right", "bottom_right")
SYSTEM_1 = [[1221, 1589], [1221, 2266], [4097, 1589], [4101, 2266]]
SYSTEM_2 = [[971, 2493], [971, 3192], [4104, 2493], [4112, 3192]]
system_areas = [
    Quadrilateral.from_points(corners, order=DMOS_SYSTEM_ORDER, unit="pixels")
    for corners in (SYSTEM_1, SYSTEM_2)
]

path = TimeAxisPath.from_boxes(system_areas, accolades=[1, 2])
path.pieces

(HorizontalLinePath(x0=1221, x1=4101, y=Fraction(3855, 2), tolerance=Fraction(677, 2)),
 HorizontalLinePath(x0=971, x1=4112, y=Fraction(5685, 2), tolerance=Fraction(699, 2)))


A piece spans its boxes exactly: x0 is their least x and x1 their greatest, y is the middle of their y extent and tolerance half of it, so the strip y ± tolerance is the accolade’s height. Nothing is rounded: the first system spans y 1589 to 2266, whose middle is 3855/2.
The path’s length is the sum of its pieces, 2880 + 3141 pixels, and each piece starts on the path where the ones before it end.

(path.offsets, path.length)

((0, 2880), 6021)


The path converts between its own coordinate and the image’s (x, y). Coordinate 2880 is the left end of the second accolade, x 971; the point (2151, 1900) lies in the first accolade’s strip, 930 pixels from its left end; a point between the two strips is on no piece.

(path.to_2d(2880), path.from_2d(2151, 1900), path.from_2d(2151, 2400))

((971, Fraction(5685, 2)), 930, None)


Where a source states no accolades, accolades= is left out and from_boxes() finds them: reading on, the left edges of the boxes grow within an accolade and fall back at the start of the next, so a box begins a new accolade when its left edge lies left of the previous box’s by more than half the span of all left edges. Of the three measures, the third falls back from x 2151 to 971 and begins the second piece; each piece spans the measures given, not the whole system.

TimeAxisPath.from_boxes([measure_1, measure_2, measure_3]).pieces

(HorizontalLinePath(x0=1221, x1=2775, y=Fraction(3855, 2), tolerance=Fraction(677, 2)),
 HorizontalLinePath(x0=971, x1=1945, y=Fraction(5685, 2), tolerance=Fraction(699, 2)))





The timelines mirror the path. An accolade is a timeline as long as its piece, and it says which area of which image it stands for in its meta: meta["box"] is that area as a shape’s dict form, in the image’s space, and meta["image"] names the image. Identifiers are given at creation: uid= for a timeline, id= for a Box.
Box.from_shape() makes the Box of a shape on a timeline. Its origin is the x at which the timeline stands in the image, here the accolade’s x_min. The Box’s interval follows from the shape:

start = the shape’s x_min − the timeline’s origin,
duration = the shape’s x_max − x_min.


system_1, system_2 = (
    DiscreteGraphicalTimeline(
        length=(area.x_max - area.x_min).value,
        unit="pixels",
        uid=f"system_{number}",
        name=f"System {number}",
        meta={"box": area.to_dict(), "image": PAGE_URL},
    )
    for number, area in enumerate(system_areas, start=1)
)
system_1.add_events(
    [
        Box.from_shape(measure_1, origin=system_areas[0].x_min, id="m1"),
        Box.from_shape(measure_2, origin=system_areas[0].x_min, id="m2"),
    ]
)
system_2.add_events([Box.from_shape(measure_3, origin=system_areas[1].x_min, id="m3")])

Measure 1 starts at x 1221 of the image and the accolade stands at x 1221, so the measure starts at 0 on the accolade; measure 2 starts at 2151, which is 930 on the accolade.
The page is the segment line of its accolades, in reading order. It names its image and states no meta["box"]: its axis is the accolades laid end to end, which is no area of the image.

page = SegmentLine[DiscreteGraphicalTimeline](
    length=0, unit="pixels", uid="page", name="Page 2", meta={"image": PAGE_URL}
)
page.append_segment(system_1, name="System 1")

The page is as long as the path, 6021 pixels, and its accolades start at the path’s offsets. A coordinate on the page is therefore a position along the path, not an x of the image: measure 3 starts at x 971 of the image, at 0 on its accolade, and at 2880 on the page.

A Box whose interval contradicts its shape is refused, on every path that adds events. Forgetting the origin is the common case: the Box below starts at 1221, the shape’s x in the image, but on an accolade standing at x 1221 of its image the shape starts at 0.

refusal(lambda: system_1.add_events([Box.from_shape(measure_1, id="m1_again")]))

How to Transfer Annotations Between Graphical Analyses places eleven rectangles, drawn on five image crops of an analytical diagram, on a segment line of those crops. The diagram is read along one horizontal line per crop, one crop after the other, so the crops are to the analysis what accolades are to a page. Each rectangle is stated in its image’s pixels, and each crop starts a few pixels right of its image’s left edge. As Boxes, the rectangles keep their shapes and each crop states where it stands in its image.

DATA_DIR = ensure_data("thoresen")
annotations = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "thoresen_test.tsv", sep="\t")

# Each crop: its image, its left and right x in the image, the image's height
CROPS = [
    ("thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_1.jpeg", 8, 874, 264),
    ("thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_2.jpeg", 7, 874, 270),
    ("thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_3.jpeg", 7, 874, 266),
    ("thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_4.jpeg", 8, 872, 272),
    ("thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page2_1.jpeg", 9, 873, 278),
]

analysis = SegmentLine[DiscreteGraphicalTimeline](
    length=0, unit="pixels", uid="dgt_2", name="Thoresen 2010"
)
for number, (image, x0, x1, height) in enumerate(CROPS, start=1):
    area = BoundingBox.from_xywh(x0, 0, x1 - x0, height, unit="pixels")
    crop = DiscreteGraphicalTimeline(
        length=x1 - x0,
        unit="pixels",
        uid=f"crop_{number}",
        meta={"box": area.to_dict(), "image": image},
    )
    on_crop = annotations[annotations["image_filename"] == image]
    crop.add_events(
        [
            Box.from_shape(
                BoundingBox.from_xywh(**json.loads(rectangle), unit="pixels"),
                origin=x0,
                id=rectangle_id,
            )
            for rectangle_id, rectangle in zip(
                on_crop["graphical_element_id"], on_crop["rect_coords_json"]
            )
        ]
    )
    analysis.append_segment(crop, name=f"seg_{number}")

DMOS writes the layout it recognises on each page as JSON: per page its image (page_url) and its systems, per system its region and its measures, each with its region. Region corners are in the orders seen above. DMOS gives each page its time path: the systems, read one after the other. create_paths() returns it per page number (no_page), every stated system one piece over the x extent of its region. Page 1 has the path made by hand above.

dmos = DmosLoader.from_file(FILES / "dmos_pages.json")

create_timeline() reads the whole file as one volume: a segment line of its pages, each page a segment line of its systems’ accolades, each measure a Box of its system’s accolade with its quadrilateral. The identifiers are given in the same call. uid names the volume; page_ids, accolade_ids and box_ids each name every element of their kind, as a sequence of IDs in document order or as a template filled from page (the page’s position, from 1), accolade (its position on its page), box (its position in its accolade) and n (the running count). DMOS states no measure numbers, so box_ids="m{n}" numbers the measures through the score.

scan = dmos.create_timeline(
    uid="scan",
    name="Gallica bpt6k11620688",
    page_ids="page_{page}",
    accolade_ids="p{page}_s{accolade}",
    box_ids="m{n}",
)

create_timelines() reads one root timeline per surface, a page built of the accolades of that path: its ID is the surface’s xml:id, its name the surface’s @n, its meta["image"] the graphic’s target. The graphic’s size is on no timeline. Each accolade is named accolade_K and states the strip of its piece as meta["box"]. Each zone becomes a Box of the accolade it lies on, with the zone’s xml:id as its ID: a BoundingBox from ulx … lry, or a Quadrilateral where the zone has points. Here the accolades are named in the call, with accolade_ids.

Where the rule of the left edges does not find a page’s accolades (zones not listed accolade by accolade, say), the path returned by create_paths() is corrected or written anew and given back as paths=, keyed by the surface’s xml:id. zone_types= selects the zones taking part by their @type, and box_ids= replaces the zones’ xml:ids, as in the DMOS section; create_timeline() gives the whole facsimile as one volume.



An IIIF Presentation manifest lists the page images of a volume as canvases, each with its width and height. It states no areas, so nothing in it says where the page is read: IIIFManifestLoader builds a timeline only along the time path it is given for a canvas. The excerpt below is the Gallica manifest of the score above (Presentation 2), trimmed to its first three canvases.

CANVAS = SCORE_URL + "/canvas/f{}"

                        {

                            "@type": "sc:Canvas",
                            "label": label,
                            "width": width,
                            "height": height,
                        }
                        for number, label, width, height in [
                            (1, "NP", 4564, 6174),
                            (2, "2", 4512, 6174),
                            (3, "3", 4564, 6174),
                        ]
                    ],
                }
            ],
        },
        indent=1,
    ),
)

The first canvas is an unnumbered page without music; the second and third are the pages DMOS read, and DMOS’s no_page is the canvas’s position, so the paths of create_paths() fit as they are. The volume is the segment line of the selected pages, each page the segment line of its accolades. IDs are given in the call, as above.

A bundle keeps its timelines in a TimeToShare manifest; the Boxes are events and live beside it. The registry (registry.parquet) holds one row per Box with its timeline’s ID and its position on the axis of the timeline’s root (a measure of an accolade at its place on the page), and the Box table (boxes.parquet) its shape, keyed by its ID; the manifest names the registry among its resources with the type Registry. The bundle below holds the page built by hand, with its two accolades and their three measures, and a logical timeline beside it.

score = ContinuousLogicalTimeline(length=Fraction(8), uid="score", name="Score")
bundle = AlignmentBundle(name="Page and score")
bundle.add_timeline(page)
bundle.add_timeline(score)

title: How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes
text:
A shape is an area of an image in image space: the origin is the image’s top-left corner, x runs right and y down, and every number is in one unit and one number type. On pixels the numbers are integers.
A BoundingBox is built from its top-left corner and its extent with from_xywh(). This one is a rectangle of the graphical analysis used below: x 385, y 46, 139 pixels wide, 20 high.

rect = BoundingBox.from_xywh(385, 46, 139, 20, unit="pixels")
rect

BoundingBox(x=Coordinate(385, pixels), y=Coordinate(46, pixels), width=Duration(139, pixels), height=Duration(20, pixels))


A shape writes itself in the forms other formats use: its dict form (as a manifest holds it), a Media Fragments and IIIF selector, the points of an SVG polygon (corners in the order top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left), and the attributes of an MEI zone, whose lrx and lry are the lower-right corner (x + width, y + height).

{
    "dict form": rect.to_dict(),
    "media fragment": rect.as_media_fragment(),
    "SVG points": rect.as_svg_points(),
    "MEI zone": rect.as_mei_zone(),
}

{'dict form': {'x': 385, 'y': 46, 'width': 139, 'height': 20},
 'media fragment': 'xywh=385,46,139,20',
 'SVG points': '385,46 524,46 524,66 385,66',
 'MEI zone': {'ulx': '385', 'uly': '46', 'lrx': '524', 'lry': '66'}}


Each form reads back into the same box: from_media_fragment() reads the selector, from_corners() the corners an MEI zone states.

(
    BoundingBox.from_media_fragment("xywh=385,46,139,20", unit="pixels") == rect,
    BoundingBox.from_corners(385, 46, 524, 66, unit="pixels") == rect,
)

(True, True)


A Quadrilateral holds four corners, so it can follow a measure whose sides are not upright. from_points() takes the points in any order the source writes them, with order= naming the corner each one is; the optical music recognition tool DMOS writes a measure top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right. These are the corners of the first measure of the first system on page 2 of a printed score in Gallica (ark:/12148/bpt6k11620688), as DMOS states them; measure 2 follows it on that system, and measure 3 is the first of the second system. The quadrilateral keeps the corners in the canonical order.

DMOS_MEASURE_ORDER = ("top_left", "top_right", "bottom_left", "bottom_right")
MEASURE_1 = [[1221, 1589], [2151, 1589], [1221, 2266], [2161, 2266]]
MEASURE_2 = [[2151, 1589], [2766, 1589], [2161, 2266], [2775, 2266]]
MEASURE_3 = [[971, 2493], [1935, 2493], [971, 3192], [1945, 3192]]

measure_1, measure_2, measure_3 = (
    Quadrilateral.from_points(corners, order=DMOS_MEASURE_ORDER, unit="pixels")
    for corners in (MEASURE_1, MEASURE_2, MEASURE_3)
)
measure_1

Quadrilateral(top_left=(1221, 1589), top_right=(2151, 1589), bottom_right=(2161, 2266), bottom_left=(1221, 2266), unit=pixels)


Its top edge is 930 pixels long and its bottom edge 940: the scan is slightly skewed. The quadrilateral’s bounding box is the smallest upright box holding it, and its MEI zone carries both, the box as ulx to lry and the corners as points.

measure_1.bounding_box

BoundingBox(x=Coordinate(1221, pixels), y=Coordinate(1589, pixels), width=Duration(940, pixels), height=Duration(677, pixels))



{"SVG points": measure_1.as_svg_points(), "MEI zone": measure_1.as_mei_zone()}

{'SVG points': '1221,1589 2151,1589 2161,2266 1221,2266',
 'MEI zone': {'ulx': '1221',
  'uly': '1589',
  'lrx': '2161',
  'lry': '2266',
  'points': '1221,1589 2151,1589 2161,2266 1221,2266'}}


SVG and MEI points may start at any corner and run in either direction. from_svg_points() reads such a list and brings it into the canonical order; here the list starts at the bottom-right corner and runs anticlockwise.

Quadrilateral.from_svg_points(
    "2161,2266 2151,1589 1221,1589 1221,2266", unit="pixels"
) == (measure_1)

True


A shape’s numbers are never rounded. A whole number given as a float is taken (385.0 is 385); a pixel position of 385.5 cannot be held on an integer axis and is refused.

BoundingBox.from_xywh(385.0, 46, 139, 20, unit="pixels") == rect

True



refusal(lambda: BoundingBox.from_xywh(385.5, 46, 139, 20, unit="pixels"))

A shape's x is 385.5, which pixels as int cannot hold exactly: geometry is never rounded.

title: How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes
text:
No image has a time axis until its path through the image is defined. A set of boxes makes one: TimeAxisPath.from_boxes() takes the areas of one page in reading order and returns a PiecewisePath, one horizontal piece per accolade.
DMOS states the systems of the page as areas too (corners top-left, bottom-left, top-right, bottom-right). Each system is one accolade, so accolades= gives every box its own label.

PAGE_URL = "https://gallica.bnf.fr/iiif/ark:/12148/bpt6k11620688/f2"
DMOS_SYSTEM_ORDER = ("top_left", "bottom_left", "top_right", "bottom_right")
SYSTEM_1 = [[1221, 1589], [1221, 2266], [4097, 1589], [4101, 2266]]
SYSTEM_2 = [[971, 2493], [971, 3192], [4104, 2493], [4112, 3192]]
system_areas = [
    Quadrilateral.from_points(corners, order=DMOS_SYSTEM_ORDER, unit="pixels")
    for corners in (SYSTEM_1, SYSTEM_2)
]

path = TimeAxisPath.from_boxes(system_areas, accolades=[1, 2])
path.pieces

(HorizontalLinePath(x0=1221, x1=4101, y=Fraction(3855, 2), tolerance=Fraction(677, 2)),
 HorizontalLinePath(x0=971, x1=4112, y=Fraction(5685, 2), tolerance=Fraction(699, 2)))


A piece spans its boxes exactly: x0 is their least x and x1 their greatest, y is the middle of their y extent and tolerance half of it, so the strip y ± tolerance is the accolade’s height. Nothing is rounded: the first system spans y 1589 to 2266, whose middle is 3855/2.
The path’s length is the sum of its pieces, 2880 + 3141 pixels, and each piece starts on the path where the ones before it end.

(path.offsets, path.length)

((0, 2880), 6021)


The path converts between its own coordinate and the image’s (x, y). Coordinate 2880 is the left end of the second accolade, x 971; the point (2151, 1900) lies in the first accolade’s strip, 930 pixels from its left end; a point between the two strips is on no piece.

(path.to_2d(2880), path.from_2d(2151, 1900), path.from_2d(2151, 2400))

((971, Fraction(5685, 2)), 930, None)


Where a source states no accolades, accolades= is left out and from_boxes() finds them: reading on, the left edges of the boxes grow within an accolade and fall back at the start of the next, so a box begins a new accolade when its left edge lies left of the previous box’s by more than half the span of all left edges. Of the three measures, the third falls back from x 2151 to 971 and begins the second piece; each piece spans the measures given, not the whole system.

TimeAxisPath.from_boxes([measure_1, measure_2, measure_3]).pieces

(HorizontalLinePath(x0=1221, x1=2775, y=Fraction(3855, 2), tolerance=Fraction(677, 2)),
 HorizontalLinePath(x0=971, x1=1945, y=Fraction(5685, 2), tolerance=Fraction(699, 2)))

title: How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes
text:
The timelines mirror the path. An accolade is a timeline as long as its piece, and it says which area of which image it stands for in its meta: meta["box"] is that area as a shape’s dict form, in the image’s space, and meta["image"] names the image. Identifiers are given at creation: uid= for a timeline, id= for a Box.
Box.from_shape() makes the Box of a shape on a timeline. Its origin is the x at which the timeline stands in the image, here the accolade’s x_min. The Box’s interval follows from the shape:

start = the shape’s x_min − the timeline’s origin,
duration = the shape’s x_max − x_min.


system_1, system_2 = (
    DiscreteGraphicalTimeline(
        length=(area.x_max - area.x_min).value,
        unit="pixels",
        uid=f"system_{number}",
        name=f"System {number}",
        meta={"box": area.to_dict(), "image": PAGE_URL},
    )
    for number, area in enumerate(system_areas, start=1)
)
system_1.add_events(
    [
        Box.from_shape(measure_1, origin=system_areas[0].x_min, id="m1"),
        Box.from_shape(measure_2, origin=system_areas[0].x_min, id="m2"),
    ]
)
system_2.add_events([Box.from_shape(measure_3, origin=system_areas[1].x_min, id="m3")])
box_table(system_1)

The page is the segment line of its accolades, in reading order. It names its image and states no meta["box"]: its axis is the accolades laid end to end, which is no area of the image.

The page is as long as the path, 6021 pixels, and its accolades start at the path’s offsets. A coordinate on the page is therefore a position along the path, not an x of the image: measure 3 starts at x 971 of the image, at 0 on its accolade, and at 2880 on the page.

A Box whose interval contradicts its shape is refused, on every path that adds events. Forgetting the origin is the common case: the Box below starts at 1221, the shape’s x in the image, but on an accolade standing at x 1221 of its image the shape starts at 0.

refusal(lambda: system_1.add_events([Box.from_shape(measure_1, id="m1_again")]))

Box 'm1_again' starts at 1221 on timeline 'system_1', but its shape starts at x 1221 and the timeline stands at x 1221 of its image (meta["box"]): its start is 0.

title: How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes
text:
How to Transfer Annotations Between Graphical Analyses places eleven rectangles, drawn on five image crops of an analytical diagram, on a segment line of those crops. The diagram is read along one horizontal line per crop, one crop after the other, so the crops are to the analysis what accolades are to a page. Each rectangle is stated in its image’s pixels, and each crop starts a few pixels right of its image’s left edge. As Boxes, the rectangles keep their shapes and each crop states where it stands in its image.

DATA_DIR = ensure_data("thoresen")
annotations = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "thoresen_test.tsv", sep="\t")

# Each crop: its image, its left and right x in the image, the image's height
CROPS = [
    ("thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_1.jpeg", 8, 874, 264),
    ("thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_2.jpeg", 7, 874, 270),
    ("thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_3.jpeg", 7, 874, 266),
    ("thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_4.jpeg", 8, 872, 272),
    ("thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page2_1.jpeg", 9, 873, 278),
]

analysis = SegmentLine[DiscreteGraphicalTimeline](
    length=0, unit="pixels", uid="dgt_2", name="Thoresen 2010"
)
for number, (image, x0, x1, height) in enumerate(CROPS, start=1):
    area = BoundingBox.from_xywh(x0, 0, x1 - x0, height, unit="pixels")
    crop = DiscreteGraphicalTimeline(
        length=x1 - x0,
        unit="pixels",
        uid=f"crop_{number}",
        meta={"box": area.to_dict(), "image": image},
    )
    on_crop = annotations[annotations["image_filename"] == image]
    crop.add_events(
        [
            Box.from_shape(
                BoundingBox.from_xywh(**json.loads(rectangle), unit="pixels"),
                origin=x0,
                id=rectangle_id,
            )
            for rectangle_id, rectangle in zip(
                on_crop["graphical_element_id"], on_crop["rect_coords_json"]
            )
        ]
    )
    analysis.append_segment(crop, name=f"seg_{number}")

crop_2 = analysis.get_child("crop_2")
crop_2.meta

title: How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes
text:
DMOS writes the layout it recognises on each page as JSON: per page its image (page_url) and its systems, per system its region and its measures, each with its region. Region corners are in the orders seen above. The excerpt below is pages 2 and 3 of the Gallica score, trimmed to the first two systems of page 2 and the first of page 3, to the measures used above and the first measure of page 3, and to the keys the loader reads.

SCORE_URL = "https://gallica.bnf.fr/iiif/ark:/12148/bpt6k11620688"
SYSTEM_3 = [[519, 896], [519, 1647], [3661, 896], [3655, 1647]]
MEASURE_4 = [[519, 896], [1520, 896], [519, 1647], [1522, 1647]]

write(
    "dmos_pages.json",
    json.dumps(
        {
            "score_image_url": SCORE_URL,
            "pages": [
                {
                    "page_url": PAGE_URL,
                    "no_page": 1,
                    "systems": [
                        {
                            "id": 1,
                            "region": SYSTEM_1,
                            "measures": [{"region": MEASURE_1}, {"region": MEASURE_2}],
                        },
                        {
                            "id": 2,
                            "region": SYSTEM_2,
                            "measures": [{"region": MEASURE_3}],
                        },
                    ],
                },
                {
                    "page_url": f"{SCORE_URL}/f3",
                    "no_page": 2,
                    "systems": [
                        {
                            "id": 1,
                            "region": SYSTEM_3,
                            "measures": [{"region": MEASURE_4}],
                        }
                    ],
                },
            ],
        },
        indent=1,
    ),
)

DMOS gives each page its time path: the systems, read one after the other. create_paths() returns it per page number (no_page), every stated system one piece over the x extent of its region. Page 1 has the path made by hand above.

dmos = DmosLoader.from_file(FILES / "dmos_pages.json")
dmos_paths = dmos.create_paths()
(dmos_paths[1] == path, dmos_paths[2].pieces)

(True,
 (HorizontalLinePath(x0=519, x1=3661, y=Fraction(2543, 2), tolerance=Fraction(751, 2)),))


create_timeline() reads the whole file as one volume: a segment line of its pages, each page a segment line of its systems’ accolades, each measure a Box of its system’s accolade with its quadrilateral. The identifiers are given in the same call. uid names the volume; page_ids, accolade_ids and box_ids each name every element of their kind, as a sequence of IDs in document order or as a template filled from page (the page’s position, from 1), accolade (its position on its page), box (its position in its accolade) and n (the running count). DMOS states no measure numbers, so box_ids="m{n}" numbers the measures through the score.

scan = dmos.create_timeline(
    uid="scan",
    name="Gallica bpt6k11620688",
    page_ids="page_{page}",
    accolade_ids="p{page}_s{accolade}",
    box_ids="m{n}",
)
scan

SegmentLine[SegmentLine[DiscreteGraphicalTimeline]][scan] (2 children)

title: How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes
text:
An MEI facsimile holds one surface per page image, with a graphic naming the image and one zone per area; elements of the encoding point to their zones with @facs. The first surface below is a page of a chorale of the Anhaltisches Choralbuch digital edition (CC BY 4.0) with its nine measure zones, and two measures pointing to the first two. The second surface is page 2 of the Gallica score, holding measure 1 as the zone as_mei_zone() wrote above, its corners as points.

SURFACE = "surface_01M7DF2D8Q8FYGETPJXXMG03QP"
ZONES = [
    ("zone_01M7DF2D8RNCKHKF6SMCWB94Z5", 490, 344, 973, 877),
    ("zone_01M7DF2D8R00HP8JYGXRTE13G3", 944, 368, 1523, 864),
    ("zone_01M7DF2D8R4E9KQCXCPC9RV59F", 1481, 388, 2082, 912),
    ("zone_01M7DF2D8S9S18YJ6CYJVF4QCJ", 2034, 402, 2694, 884),
    ("zone_01M7DF2D8SY6CN7SFAZFPE58FT", 2669, 389, 3296, 916),
    ("zone_01M7DF2D8SF9X38YEGDA0JCD04", 498, 858, 1496, 1337),
    ("zone_01M7DF2D8S1F9S83VHS68E6N7W", 1465, 885, 2146, 1353),
    ("zone_01M7DF2D8TV0F9DCHY6QNWYTDX", 2110, 886, 2748, 1357),
    ("zone_01M7DF2D8TSXCHCSA07C235VTV", 2704, 886, 3302, 1387),
]
chorale_zones = "\n        ".join(
    f'<zone xml:id="{zone_id}" type="measure" ulx="{ulx}" uly="{uly}" '
    f'lrx="{lrx}" lry="{lry}"/>'
    for zone_id, ulx, uly, lrx, lry in ZONES
)
zone_attributes = " ".join(
    f'{name}="{value}"' for name, value in measure_1.as_mei_zone().items()
)

write(
    "facsimile.mei",
    f"""<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<mei xmlns="http://www.music-encoding.org/ns/mei" meiversion="5.1">
  <meiHead><fileDesc><titleStmt><title>Ach bleib bei uns, Herr Jesu Christ</title></titleStmt>
  <pubStmt/></fileDesc></meiHead>
  <music>
    <facsimile>
      <surface xml:id="{SURFACE}" n="15" ulx="0" uly="0" lrx="3999" lry="2999">
        <graphic xml:id="graphic_01M7DF2D8RMG9SGXTZRR3S1BA3"
                 target="facsimile/20251230_180023.jpg" width="4000" height="3000"/>
        {chorale_zones}
      </surface>
      <surface xml:id="gallica_f2" n="2">
        <graphic target="{PAGE_URL}" width="4512" height="6174"/>
        <zone xml:id="m1" type="measure" {zone_attributes}/>
      </surface>
    </facsimile>
    <body>
      <mdiv>
        <score>
          <section>
            <measure xml:id="m-43" metcon="false" n="0" facs="#{ZONES[0][0]}"/>
            <measure xml:id="m-57" n="1" facs="#{ZONES[1][0]}"/>
          </section>
        </score>
      </mdiv>
    </body>
  </music>
</mei>
""",
)

MEI zones name no accolade, so MeiFacsimileLoader makes each surface’s time path from its zones, with TimeAxisPath.from_boxes() and the rule of the left edges. On the chorale page the sixth zone falls back from x 2669 to 498: the page has two accolades, of five and four measures.

mei = MeiFacsimileLoader.from_file(FILES / "facsimile.mei")
mei.create_paths()[SURFACE].pieces

(HorizontalLinePath(x0=490, x1=3296, y=630, tolerance=286),
 HorizontalLinePath(x0=498, x1=3302, y=Fraction(2245, 2), tolerance=Fraction(529, 2)))


create_timelines() reads one root timeline per surface, a page built of the accolades of that path: its ID is the surface’s xml:id, its name the surface’s @n, its meta["image"] the graphic’s target. The graphic’s size is on no timeline. Each accolade is named accolade_K and states the strip of its piece as meta["box"]. Each zone becomes a Box of the accolade it lies on, with the zone’s xml:id as its ID: a BoundingBox from ulx … lry, or a Quadrilateral where the zone has points. Here the accolades are named in the call, with accolade_ids.

chorale, gallica_page = mei.create_timelines(accolade_ids="p{page}_a{accolade}")
{
    surface.id: (surface.name, surface.length, surface.meta)
    for surface in (chorale, gallica_page)
}

title: How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes
text:
An IIIF Presentation manifest lists the page images of a volume as canvases, each with its width and height. It states no areas, so nothing in it says where the page is read: IIIFManifestLoader builds a timeline only along the time path it is given for a canvas. The excerpt below is the Gallica manifest of the score above (Presentation 2), trimmed to its first three canvases.

MANIFEST_ID = f"{SCORE_URL}/manifest.json"
CANVAS = SCORE_URL + "/canvas/f{}"
write(
    "manifest.json",
    json.dumps(
        {
            "@context": "http://iiif.io/api/presentation/2/context.json",
            "@id": MANIFEST_ID,
            "@type": "sc:Manifest",
            "label": "Exemplaire localisé à la Médiathèque Hector Berlioz (CNSMDP), D-9658 (1)",
            "sequences": [
                {
                    "@type": "sc:Sequence",
                    "canvases": [
                        {
                            "@id": CANVAS.format(number),
                            "@type": "sc:Canvas",
                            "label": label,
                            "width": width,
                            "height": height,
                        }
                        for number, label, width, height in [
                            (1, "NP", 4564, 6174),
                            (2, "2", 4512, 6174),
                            (3, "3", 4564, 6174),
                        ]
                    ],
                }
            ],
        },
        indent=1,
    ),
)

create_timeline() takes the paths as a mapping from a canvas, named by its position from 0 or by its ID, to its path, and canvases= selects the canvases to read. The first canvas is an unnumbered page without music; the second and third are the pages DMOS read, and DMOS’s no_page is the canvas’s position, so the paths of create_paths() fit as they are. The volume is the segment line of the selected pages, each page the segment line of its accolades. IDs are given in the call, as above.

volume = IIIFManifestLoader.from_file(FILES / "manifest.json").create_timeline(
    dmos_paths,
    canvases=[1, 2],
    uid="volume",
    page_ids=["f2", "f3"],
    accolade_ids="p{page}_s{accolade}",
)
volume

  │  ├─ accolade_1     0 ∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶                        2880
  │  └─ accolade_2  2880           ∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶             6021
  └─ 3              6021                      ∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶ 9163
     └─ accolade_1  6021                      ∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶ 9163

pages["dcterms:source"] = [

title: How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes
text:
A bundle keeps its timelines in a TimeToShare manifest; the Boxes are events and live beside it. The registry (registry.parquet) holds one row per Box with its timeline’s ID and its position on the axis of the timeline’s root (a measure of an accolade at its place on the page), and the Box table (boxes.parquet) its shape, keyed by its ID; the manifest names the registry among its resources with the type Registry. The bundle below holds the page built by hand, with its two accolades and their three measures, and a logical timeline beside it.

score = ContinuousLogicalTimeline(length=Fraction(8), uid="score", name="Score")
bundle = AlignmentBundle(name="Page and score")
bundle.add_timeline(page)
bundle.add_timeline(score)

manifest_path = bundle.to_file(FILES / "package" / "page.yaml")
sorted(path.name for path in manifest_path.parent.iterdir())

['boxes.parquet', 'extractions.parquet', 'page.yaml', 'registry.parquet']


The manifest holds the timelines and their meta, and names the registry:

show(manifest_path, "resources")

resources:
  -
    id: "#resource_0e99m58psb85r"
    integrity:
      algorithm: SHA-256
      digest: ca4c64e738f12c306eb5578289dea187d7e3be542765416fcb913498801e7dfc
    media_type: application/vnd.apache.parquet
    size: 5267
    timelines: ["#system_1", "#system_2"]
    type: Registry
    url: registry.parquet


from_file() reads the manifest and the tables. Every Box comes back on its timeline with the same ID, interval (on the timeline’s own axis) and shape, and is checked against its shape on the way in.

read = AlignmentBundle.from_file(manifest_path)
read_page = read.timelines["page"]
[
    (
        accolade.id,
        list(
            read_page.get_child(accolade.id).get_events(event_type="Box").get_field(Box)
        )
        == list(accolade.get_events(event_type="Box").get_field(Box)),
        read_page.get_child(accolade.id).meta == accolade.meta,
    )
    for accolade in (system_1, system_2)
]

[('system_1', True, True), ('system_2', True, True)]

title: How to Load a parangonada Note Alignment Across Several Performances
text:
parangonar aligns a symbolic score to a performance and exports the result as a parangonada triple of CSV files — the score notes, the performed notes, and the note-level correspondences between them. This guide loads such an export for one work performed five different times into a single multimodal AlignmentBundle.
We load an existing alignment; nothing here runs an aligner. The correspondences were computed once, offline, and written to disk; the loader’s job is to read them faithfully and arrange them as timelines and MatchClaims.
The work is Beethoven’s Eroica Variations, Op. 35 — Var. XIV — in five recordings spanning six decades: Szegedi (1966), Gould (1970), Curzon (1971), Brendel (1985), and Hewitt (2023). One score, five performances, and the note-by-note alignment that ties each performance back to the score.
The arc:

Load the whole export in one call.
Read the shared logical score, in two units, linked by a ConversionMap.
Read one performer’s physical timelines, in two units, linked by a ConversionMap.
Inspect the cross-group MatchClaims — both the synchronous matches and the NOMATCH sentinels — and read one shared score position across all five performances.
Read each performance’s measured per-beat tempo and dynamics, carried as events on its own timeline.




from __future__ import annotations

import pandas as pd

from timetoalign.core import TimeUnit
from timetoalign.loader.alignment import ParangonadaLoader
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

root = ensure_data("parangonar")
dataset_dir = root / "Beethoven_Eroica_op35-cpjku"




ParangonadaLoader discovers every performance under the export’s directory, parses the shared score once and each performance’s notes and alignment, and binds each recording’s audio for its sample rate. from_file() is the one-line form of the standard two-phase loader pattern.

bundle = ParangonadaLoader.from_file(dataset_dir).create_bundle()
bundle

Twelve timelines arranged in six groups: one shared "score" group, and one "perf:<key>" group per recording. Everything below reads from this single bundle.

{
    "timelines": bundle.n_timelines,
    "groups": bundle.n_groups,

The score is identical across all five performances, so it is parsed once and placed in its own group. It appears in two logical units — the same notes, measured two ways:

score:clt_… carries quarter-note onsets (an exact rational).
score:dlt_… carries division-grid onsets (the integer tick grid the score was notated on).

The loader leads every timeline ID with its role, score: or perf:, before an ID minted from the export’s files, so the same export gives the same IDs on every run. A regular expression matching whole IDs finds a timeline by its role and kind:

score_clt = bundle.get_timeline("score:clt_.*")
score_clt

The two logical timelines are not independent: a single ConversionMap on score:dlt_… carries the division grid to quarters. It is a LinearMap — 32 divisions to the quarter, shifted by the half-quarter anacrusis — and it reproduces the quarter onsets exactly, because divisions are the discrete grid the quarters were notated on:

divs_to_quarters = score_dlt.get_conversion_map(TimeUnit.quarters)

{
    "div 16 -> quarters": divs_to_quarters(16),
    "div 48 -> quarters": divs_to_quarters(48),
    "div 1296 -> quarters": divs_to_quarters(1296),
}

{'div 16 -> quarters': Fraction(0, 1),
 'div 48 -> quarters': Fraction(1, 1),
 'div 1296 -> quarters': Fraction(40, 1)}


The same conversion is what a TimeStamp exposes. Querying score:dlt_… at division 48 and asking for the quarter reading reports 1.0, the continuous↔︎discrete link of the logical domain made visible at a single coordinate:

score_dlt.get_timestamp(48).get_unit(TimeUnit.quarters)

IdCoordinate(Fraction(1, 1), quarters, 'score:dlt_2aq31ztdm4t6x')







Each performance lives in its own group, named perf:<key>, again in two units — the same performed notes, measured two ways:

perf:cpt_… carries onsets in seconds.
perf:dpt_… carries the same onsets as sample indices into the recording’s audio.

A performer’s group is found by its name, and each of its two timelines by a regular expression within the group. Take Szegedi’s 1966 recording:

def performance(key):
    """The group holding one recording's timelines, named ``perf:<key>``."""
    return next(
        group for group in bundle.groups.values() if group.name == f"perf:{key}"
    )


szegedi = performance("1966_Szegedi")
szegedi_cpt = szegedi.get_timeline("perf:cpt_.*")
szegedi_cpt

The seconds grid and the samples grid are, again, one ConversionMap apart — here a SamplesToSeconds map carrying the recording’s 44.1 kHz sample rate. It is the physical-domain counterpart of the logical divs→quarters map: 44 100 samples is one second.

samples_to_seconds = szegedi_dpt.get_conversion_map(TimeUnit.seconds)

{

The score group and the five performance groups are tied together by cross-group MatchClaims — one per row of each performance’s alignment file. A matched note becomes a synchronous claim relating a score quarter to a performed second; an unmatched note becomes a NOMATCH claim, which records the dangling note rather than discarding it.

claims = bundle.get_match_claims()

{
    "total claims": len(claims),
    "synchronous (matched)": sum(1 for c in claims if c.is_synchronous),
    "NOMATCH (score-only or performance-only)": sum(
        1 for c in claims if not c.is_synchronous
    ),
}

{'total claims': 1275,
 'synchronous (matched)': 1208,
 'NOMATCH (score-only or performance-only)': 67}


A synchronous claim carries an anchor: a score quarter on one side, the performed second on the other. This is Szegedi’s note at score quarter 40, played 38.18 seconds into the recording:

szegedi_synchronous = [
    c
    for c in claims
    if c.is_synchronous
    and c.connects(szegedi_cpt.id)
    and c.start_anchor is not None
    and float(c.start_anchor.coordinate_a) == 40.0
]
