The stamp names each timeline by its ID; each performer’s group names the recording, so the seconds read per performer are:

{
    group.name: stamp.get_coordinate_for(
        group.get_timeline("perf:cpt_.*").id, format="coordinate"
    )
    for group in bundle.groups.values()
    if group.name.startswith("perf:")
}

{'perf:1966_Szegedi': Coordinate(38.183334, seconds),
 'perf:1970_Gould': Coordinate(63.103645, seconds),
 'perf:1971_Curzon': Coordinate(41.247395, seconds),
 'perf:1985_Brendel': Coordinate(37.84375, seconds),
 'perf:2023_Hewitt': Coordinate(47.46875, seconds)}


Read across that MatchStamp: the same notated moment falls at 37.8 s for Brendel and 38.2 s for Szegedi, but at 63.1 s for Gould — the raw material of a tempo comparison, drawn straight from the loaded alignment with no aligner ever run.





The alignment ties each performance to the score note by note, but parangonar also measured, for every recording, a per-beat tempo and dynamics profile. These are not a model or a synthesised constant-tempo grid: they are the variable tempo and loudness actually measured beat by beat in each recording. The loader places them on the performance’s own seconds timeline — perf:cpt_… of the group perf:<key> — as Beat and Dynamics Events, sitting alongside the Note events at their measured onsets. A performance timeline therefore carries three kinds of event: the notes that were played, and the measured tempo and dynamics that describe how.
We read them with the same event query used everywhere else — filter by event_type. The coordinate (start) comes back as a number; the remaining measured columns currently round-trip as strings, so we cast them as we read.


Each Beat event carries the measured beat-per-minute reading at its onset, together with the measure_number and beat it falls on. There are 63 of them — one per measured beat of the variation. Take Szegedi’s:

szegedi_beats = szegedi_cpt.get_events().filter(event_type="Beat").to_dataframe()

szegedi_tempo = szegedi_beats[["start", "measure_number", "beat", "bpm"]].copy()
szegedi_tempo["onset_sec"] = szegedi_tempo.pop("start").astype(float)
szegedi_tempo["measure_number"] = szegedi_tempo["measure_number"].astype(int)
szegedi_tempo["beat"] = szegedi_tempo["beat"].astype(int)
szegedi_tempo["bpm"] = szegedi_tempo["bpm"].astype(float)

{
    "beat events": len(szegedi_tempo),
    "first onset (s)": szegedi_tempo["onset_sec"].iloc[0],
    "measured BPM: min / median / max": (
        round(szegedi_tempo["bpm"].min(), 1),
        round(szegedi_tempo["bpm"].median(), 1),
        round(szegedi_tempo["bpm"].max(), 1),
    ),
}

{'beat events': 63,

 'measured BPM: min / median / max': (np.float64(20.7),

At the same measured onsets sit 63 Dynamics events, each carrying the mean and peak MIDI velocity measured over its beat. The .dyn source rows have no onset of their own; the loader joined each to the Beat row sharing its (measure_number, beat) key, so the dynamics land at exactly the same seconds as the tempo readings:

szegedi_dyn = szegedi_cpt.get_events().filter(event_type="Dynamics").to_dataframe()

szegedi_dynamics = szegedi_dyn[
    ["start", "measure_number", "beat", "velocity_mean", "velocity_max"]
].copy()
szegedi_dynamics["onset_sec"] = szegedi_dynamics.pop("start").astype(float)

Because every performance carries its own measured Beat events, the “five interpretations of one work” claim becomes concrete: the same 63 beats of the variation, measured in each recording. Summarising each performer’s measured tempo shows how differently they take it — Gould stretches the variation across nearly twice the span of Brendel, at roughly half the median tempo:

tempo_by_performer = {}
for group in bundle.groups.values():
    key = group.name
    if not key.startswith("perf:"):
        continue
    cpt = group.get_timeline("perf:cpt_.*")
    beats = cpt.get_events().filter(event_type="Beat").to_dataframe()
    bpm = beats["bpm"].astype(float)
    onset = beats["start"].astype(float)
    tempo_by_performer[key.removeprefix("perf:")] = {
        "beats": len(beats),
        "median BPM": round(bpm.median(), 1),
        "span (s)": round(onset.max() - onset.min(), 1),
    }

These profiles are measured features carried on the performance timelines, not anything TimeToAlign! inferred. Loaded next to the notes and the cross-group MatchClaims, they let one bundle hold both what was played (the aligned notes) and how it was played (the measured tempo and dynamics), for every one of the five recordings.











What the bundle expresses
How




Score, two logical units
score:clt_… (quarters) + score:dlt_… (divs), one divs→quarters LinearMap


Performance, two physical units
perf:cpt_… (s) + perf:dpt_… (samples), one SamplesToSeconds


Score ↔︎ performance
a synchronous MatchClaim per match; a NOMATCH per gap


A shared position read everywhere
bundle.get_matchstamp_at(coord, score_clt.id)


Measured tempo and dynamics
Beat / Dynamics events on perf:cpt_…, read via filter(event_type=...)



Two logical units for the score, two physical units per performance, each pair linked by a ConversionMap, the whole tied together by cross-group MatchClaims, and each performance additionally carrying its measured per-beat tempo and dynamics as events — one AlignmentBundle carrying an existing note alignment of one work across five performances, and a faithful record of how each was played.

title: How to Load a parangonada Note Alignment Across Several Performances
text:
The score is identical across all five performances, so it is parsed once and placed in its own group. It appears in two logical units — the same notes, measured two ways:

score:clt_… carries quarter-note onsets (an exact rational).
score:dlt_… carries division-grid onsets (the integer tick grid the score was notated on).

The loader leads every timeline ID with its role, score: or perf:, before an ID minted from the export’s files, so the same export gives the same IDs on every run. A regular expression matching whole IDs finds a timeline by its role and kind:

score_clt = bundle.get_timeline("score:clt_.*")
score_clt

score_dlt = bundle.get_timeline("score:dlt_.*")
score_dlt

                      0 ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, 2064 ticks

The two logical timelines are not independent: a single ConversionMap on score:dlt_… carries the division grid to quarters. It is a LinearMap — 32 divisions to the quarter, shifted by the half-quarter anacrusis — and it reproduces the quarter onsets exactly, because divisions are the discrete grid the quarters were notated on:

divs_to_quarters = score_dlt.get_conversion_map(TimeUnit.quarters)

{
    "div 16 -> quarters": divs_to_quarters(16),
    "div 48 -> quarters": divs_to_quarters(48),
    "div 1296 -> quarters": divs_to_quarters(1296),
}

The same conversion is what a TimeStamp exposes. Querying score:dlt_… at division 48 and asking for the quarter reading reports 1.0, the continuous↔︎discrete link of the logical domain made visible at a single coordinate:

title: How to Load a parangonada Note Alignment Across Several Performances
text:
Each performance lives in its own group, named perf:<key>, again in two units — the same performed notes, measured two ways:

perf:cpt_… carries onsets in seconds.
perf:dpt_… carries the same onsets as sample indices into the recording’s audio.

A performer’s group is found by its name, and each of its two timelines by a regular expression within the group. Take Szegedi’s 1966 recording:

def performance(key):
    """The group holding one recording's timelines, named ``perf:<key>``."""
    return next(
        group for group in bundle.groups.values() if group.name == f"perf:{key}"
    )


szegedi = performance("1966_Szegedi")
szegedi_cpt = szegedi.get_timeline("perf:cpt_.*")
szegedi_cpt

title: How to Load a parangonada Note Alignment Across Several Performances
text:
The score group and the five performance groups are tied together by cross-group MatchClaims — one per row of each performance’s alignment file. A matched note becomes a synchronous claim relating a score quarter to a performed second; an unmatched note becomes a NOMATCH claim, which records the dangling note rather than discarding it.

claims = bundle.get_match_claims()

{
    "total claims": len(claims),
    "synchronous (matched)": sum(1 for c in claims if c.is_synchronous),
    "NOMATCH (score-only or performance-only)": sum(
        1 for c in claims if not c.is_synchronous
    ),
}

A synchronous claim carries an anchor: a score quarter on one side, the performed second on the other. This is Szegedi’s note at score quarter 40, played 38.18 seconds into the recording:

szegedi_synchronous = [

    if c.is_synchronous
    and c.connects(szegedi_cpt.id)
    and c.start_anchor is not None
    and float(c.start_anchor.coordinate_a) == 40.0
]

title: How to Load a parangonada Note Alignment Across Several Performances
text:
The alignment ties each performance to the score note by note, but parangonar also measured, for every recording, a per-beat tempo and dynamics profile. These are not a model or a synthesised constant-tempo grid: they are the variable tempo and loudness actually measured beat by beat in each recording. The loader places them on the performance’s own seconds timeline — perf:cpt_… of the group perf:<key> — as Beat and Dynamics Events, sitting alongside the Note events at their measured onsets. A performance timeline therefore carries three kinds of event: the notes that were played, and the measured tempo and dynamics that describe how.
We read them with the same event query used everywhere else — filter by event_type. The coordinate (start) comes back as a number; the remaining measured columns currently round-trip as strings, so we cast them as we read.


Each Beat event carries the measured beat-per-minute reading at its onset, together with the measure_number and beat it falls on. There are 63 of them — one per measured beat of the variation. Take Szegedi’s:

szegedi_beats = szegedi_cpt.get_events().filter(event_type="Beat").to_dataframe()

szegedi_tempo = szegedi_beats[["start", "measure_number", "beat", "bpm"]].copy()
szegedi_tempo["onset_sec"] = szegedi_tempo.pop("start").astype(float)
szegedi_tempo["measure_number"] = szegedi_tempo["measure_number"].astype(int)
szegedi_tempo["beat"] = szegedi_tempo["beat"].astype(int)
szegedi_tempo["bpm"] = szegedi_tempo["bpm"].astype(float)

{
    "beat events": len(szegedi_tempo),
    "first onset (s)": szegedi_tempo["onset_sec"].iloc[0],
    "measured BPM: min / median / max": (
        round(szegedi_tempo["bpm"].min(), 1),
        round(szegedi_tempo["bpm"].median(), 1),
        round(szegedi_tempo["bpm"].max(), 1),
    ),
}

tempo_by_performer = {}

Two logical units for the score, two physical units per performance, each pair linked by a ConversionMap, the whole tied together by cross-group MatchClaims, and each performance additionally carrying its measured per-beat tempo and dynamics as events — one AlignmentBundle carrying an existing note alignment of one work across five performances, and a faithful record of how each was played.

title: How to Keep MatchClaims, Projections and Beliefs in a Package
text:
A TimeToShare manifest holds the structure of its timelines. The MatchClaims that relate them are data and live beside it, in the MatchClaim table (match_claims.parquet). The events that stand in for an event a timeline does not hold, Projections, are events like any other: each has a row in the registry (registry.parquet), which holds every event’s ID, timeline and position, and its content, the event it stands for, in the pre-parsed Projection table (projections.parquet); the Extraction table (extractions.parquet) records what made them. The manifest names the registry and the MatchClaim table in its resources; the manifest and the files beside it make a package.
This guide states MatchClaims between the events of a score and a recording, gives a side without an event a Projection, records who believes which claim and filters by those beliefs, writes the bundle as a package with to_file() and reads it back with from_file(), and shows why a package’s claims can be added to but never removed.


Install the library with pip install timetoalign. Two people take part: an editor, who states claims and believes what they state, and an automatic aligner, which states how it made its claims and believes nothing. Every date is a fixed string. The helper claim_rows shows claims one per row with the editor’s belief, files lists a directory, and show prints part of a manifest as the file holds it.

import tempfile
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from timetoshare import dumps, loads

from timetoalign import (
    AlignmentBundle,
    ContinuousLogicalTimeline,
    ContinuousPhysicalTimeline,
    Coordinate,
    EventReference,
    Projection,
    Provenance,
)

FILES = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
EDITOR = "https://example.org/people/editor"
ALIGNER = "https://example.org/tools/onset-aligner"
DAY = "2026-11-21"


def claim_rows(claims):
    """One row per claim: its id, its two events, its kind, the editor's belief."""

    def editor_belief(claim):
        beliefs = claim.provenance.beliefs if claim.provenance else ()
        return next((b.belief for b in beliefs if b.actor == EDITOR), None)

    return pd.DataFrame(
        [
            {
                "id": claim.id,
                "event_a_id": claim.event_a_id,
                "event_b_id": claim.event_b_id,
                "claim_type": claim.claim_type.value,
                "editor believes": editor_belief(claim),
            }
            for claim in claims
        ]
    )


def files(directory):
    """The names of the files in a directory, sorted."""
    return sorted(path.name for path in directory.iterdir())


def show(manifest_path, key):
    """Print one key of a manifest file as canonical YAML."""
    print(dumps({key: loads(manifest_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))[key]}), end="")




A score of eight quarters with four notes, and a recording of six seconds in which an onset detector found three onsets. The fourth note, held at the end, was played too softly for the detector.

score = ContinuousLogicalTimeline(length=Fraction(8), uid="score", name="Score")
notes = {"n1": (0, 1), "n2": (1, 1), "n3": (2, 2), "n4": (4, 4)}
score.add_events(
    [
        {
            "id": note,
            "event_type": "Note",
            "start": Fraction(start),
            "duration": Fraction(length),
        }
        for note, (start, length) in notes.items()
    ]
)
recording = ContinuousPhysicalTimeline(length=6.0, uid="recording", name="Recording")
recording.add_events(
    [
        {"id": "o1", "event_type": "Onset", "instant": 0.25},
        {"id": "o2", "event_type": "Onset", "instant": 1.0},
        {"id": "o3", "event_type": "Onset", "instant": 1.75},
    ]
)

bundle = AlignmentBundle(name="Song")
bundle.add_timeline(score, as_group="score")
bundle.add_timeline(recording, as_group="recording")

to_file() writes the MatchClaim table, the registry, the Extraction table and the Projection table beside the manifest, then the manifest naming the registry and the MatchClaim table. A manifest names no event: the claims name the score’s notes and the recording’s onsets by their ids, and by default those events stay with the sources they came from, here the score and the onset list. The package holds the events it made itself, the Projections. To keep the notes and onsets in the package as well, to_file(events=True) writes them into the registry and a pre-parsed table per event type, never into the manifest itself: see How to Write the Registry and Share Tables in a Package.

An event’s id is unique among all the events of the package, whichever timeline holds it, so the registry and the table name each id once. Here they hold one Projection, the recording’s for the fourth note (its projection_of names the note); the claim between two positions added none. Each id is minted (projection_…) and never re-minted, and a Projection given an id another timeline’s Projection holds is refused.



from_file() reads the manifest, then the tables it names: each Projection’s registry row onto its timeline (its content read from the Projection table when the timeline’s events are read), then the MatchClaim table. Its timelines hold their Projections but not the notes and onsets, which the manifest does not carry (the score read holds no event at all). A bundle that lacks claims the table holds cannot be written over it.     print(refusal)

A score of eight quarters with four notes, and a recording of six seconds in which an onset detector found three onsets. The fourth note, held at the end, was played too softly for the detector.

    [
        {
            "id": note,
            "event_type": "Note",
            "start": Fraction(start),
            "duration": Fraction(length),
        }
        for note, (start, length) in notes.items()
    ]
)
recording = ContinuousPhysicalTimeline(length=6.0, uid="recording", name="Recording")
recording.add_events(
    [
        {"id": "o1", "event_type": "Onset", "instant": 0.25},
        {"id": "o2", "event_type": "Onset", "instant": 1.0},
        {"id": "o3", "event_type": "Onset", "instant": 1.75},
    ]
)

bundle = AlignmentBundle(name="Song")
bundle.add_timeline(score, as_group="score")
bundle.add_timeline(recording, as_group="recording")

title: How to Keep MatchClaims, Projections and Beliefs in a Package
text:
to_file() writes the MatchClaim table, the registry, the Extraction table and the Projection table beside the manifest, then the manifest naming the registry and the MatchClaim table. A manifest names no event: the claims name the score’s notes and the recording’s onsets by their ids, and by default those events stay with the sources they came from, here the score and the onset list. The package holds the events it made itself, the Projections. To keep the notes and onsets in the package as well, to_file(events=True) writes them into the registry and a pre-parsed table per event type, never into the manifest itself: see How to Write the Registry and Share Tables in a Package.

package = FILES / "song"
package.mkdir()
manifest_path = bundle.to_file(package / "song.yaml")
files(package)

The MatchClaim table has one row per claim and one column per property of a MatchClaim: its two timelines and two events, the anchors’ coordinates, its provenance with the beliefs, and more. An event ID cell is never empty: a side without an event holds a sentinel, NOMATCH_SENTINEL for the absent side of a NOMATCH and CHUNK_SENTINEL for a side whose coordinate the anchor states, as on both sides of the doubted claim. A Projection’s registry row holds its id, its timeline and its position on the axis of the timeline’s root (start, and duration for a span), with that axis’s unit and number type once, each number written once, as that number type says: an int as its numerator alone, a fraction as numerator and denominator, a float as its value alone. The registry’s other rows, its non-event rows, name the manifest’s elements, the MatchClaims and the extraction.

        name: row[name]
        for name in ("id", "kind", "timeline_id", "unit", "number_type", "start")
    }

The Projection table holds the content of each Projection, keyed by its id: the event it stands for, if any.

pq.read_table(package / "projections.parquet").to_pylist()

[{'id': 'projection_1drob75w08pcl',
  'projection_of': {'timeline_id': 'score', 'event_id': 'n4'}}]


An event’s id is unique among all the events of the package, whichever timeline holds it, so the registry and the table name each id once. Here they hold one Projection, the recording’s for the fourth note (its projection_of names the note); the claim between two positions added none. Each id is minted (projection_…) and never re-minted, and a Projection given an id another timeline’s Projection holds is refused.

title: How to Keep MatchClaims, Projections and Beliefs in a Package
text:
from_file() reads the manifest, then the tables it names: each Projection’s registry row onto its timeline (its content read from the Projection table when the timeline’s events are read), then the MatchClaim table. The bundle read holds the same claims and the same manifest, and its belief filter gives the same answers. Its timelines hold their Projections but not the notes and onsets, which the manifest does not carry (the score read holds no event at all). Each claim keeps the coordinates of its two sides, so MatchStamps need no event: under the editor’s beliefs the third note, at quarter 2, still lies at 1.75 seconds.

        claim.id for claim in read.get_match_claims(believer=EDITOR, beliefs=["true"])
    ],
    "events of the score read": len(read.get_timeline(score.id).get_events()),
}

title: How to Keep MatchClaims, Projections and Beliefs in a Package
text:
A MatchClaim is never deleted and its id never changes; whoever disagrees states a belief instead. So writing over a package’s MatchClaim table obeys the succession rule: every claim of the old table is in the new one, with the same timelines, events and anchors; only its provenance may differ. Adding a claim, stating a belief and writing the bundle back is fine. The editor goes on in the bundle that holds the events: a conceptual claim between the second note and the second onset, and a change of mind about the doubted claim.

bundle.create_match_claims(
    [("n2", score.id, "o2", recording.id)], synchronous=False, actor=EDITOR, date=DAY
)
bundle.add_match_claim_belief(doubted.id, actor=EDITOR, belief="false", date=DAY)
bundle.to_file(manifest_path)

title: How to Load Data
text:
This tutorial introduces the Loader pattern and EventStores - the foundation for bringing music data into TimeToAlign!
Learning Objectives: - Use Loaders to ingest music data from various formats - Navigate EventStores and access event data - Understand the harmonized schema that unifies different data sources
Prerequisites: - Basic Python and pandas knowledge - TimeToAlign! installed (pip install timetoalign)


Music data comes in many formats: MusicXML, MIDI, MEI, Humdrum, proprietary TSV exports, and more. Each format has its own structure, terminology, and quirks.
The problem: Without a unified approach, you’d need format-specific code for every data source, making cross-format analysis difficult and error-prone.
The TimeToAlign! solution: Loaders normalize heterogeneous formats into a consistent EventStore, enabling downstream processing without format-specific code.
MusicXML ─┐
MIDI ─────┼──> Loader ──> EventStore ──> DataFrame
TSV ──────┘




import json
import os
import tempfile
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

from timetoalign import Ms3Loader
from timetoalign.core.events import EnharmonicPitch
from timetoalign.loader import materialize
from timetoalign.loader.score.music21 import Music21Loader
from timetoalign.loader.score.partitura import PartituraLoader
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

DATA_DIR = ensure_data("vienna_1x22")

# Our test piece: Chopin Etude Op.10 No.3
CHOPIN_XML = DATA_DIR / "Chopin_op10_no3.musicxml"
CHOPIN_TSV = DATA_DIR / "ms3" / "chopin_op10_no3.notes.tsv"


def source_entry(loader):
    """The `path` and `member` a loader records for its one source, the path by name."""
    entry = loader.metadata["sources"][0]
    return {"path": Path(entry["path"]).name, "member": entry.get("member", "—")}


CHOPIN_XML.name, CHOPIN_TSV.name

('Chopin_op10_no3.musicxml', 'chopin_op10_no3.notes.tsv')





All TimeToAlign! loaders follow the same three-step pattern:

Create a loader instance
Load a file using .load(path)
Access the store containing EventStores

Let’s see this in action with three different loaders, all loading the same Chopin piece:

# Load from three different sources
tsv_loader = Ms3Loader()
tsv_loader.load(CHOPIN_TSV)

partitura_loader = PartituraLoader()
partitura_loader.load(CHOPIN_XML)

music21_loader = Music21Loader()
music21_loader.load(CHOPIN_XML)

# All produce ScoreStores
{
    "TSV": type(tsv_loader.store).__name__,
    "Partitura": type(partitura_loader.store).__name__,
    "Music21": type(music21_loader.store).__name__,
}

{'TSV': 'ScoreStore', 'Partitura': 'ScoreStore', 'Music21': 'ScoreStore'}





One of the key benefits of TimeToAlign! is that different loaders produce comparable output. Let’s verify that all three loaders found the same number of notes:

# Convert to DataFrames
tsv_df = tsv_loader.store.notes.to_dataframe()
partitura_df = partitura_loader.store.notes.to_dataframe()
music21_df = music21_loader.store.notes.to_dataframe()

# Count only Note events (not rests or other event types)
counts = {
    "TSV": len(tsv_df[tsv_df["event_type"] == "Note"]),
    "Partitura": len(partitura_df[partitura_df["event_type"] == "Note"]),
    "Music21": len(music21_df[music21_df["event_type"] == "Note"]),
}

# Validate against gold standard
assert all(c == 498 for c in counts.values()), f"Note count mismatch: {counts}"

pd.Series(counts, name="note_count")

TSV          498
Partitura    498

Name: note_count, dtype: int64





Each ScoreStore contains EventStores - efficient, PyArrow-backed tables that hold musical events.
Key characteristics: - High Performance: Built on Apache Arrow for fast columnar operations - Type Safety: Schema metadata preserves units and types - Pandas Interop: Easy conversion with .to_dataframe()

notes_store = tsv_loader.store.notes

{
    "type": type(notes_store).__name__,
    "n_events": len(notes_store),
    "storage": type(notes_store.table).__name__,
}

{'type': 'NoteEventData', 'n_events': 498, 'storage': 'Table'}



# Examine the schema with metadata
schema_info = []
for field in notes_store.table.schema:
    meta = field.metadata or {}
    # Column metadata is one `timetoalign` JSON blob; unpack it so the table
    # shows the declared unit and number type rather than a serialized string.
    blob = json.loads(meta[b"timetoalign"]) if b"timetoalign" in meta else {}
    extra = {k.decode(): v.decode() for k, v in meta.items() if k != b"timetoalign"}
    meta_str = ", ".join(
        f"{k}={v}" for k, v in {**blob, **extra}.items() if k != "version"
    )
    schema_info.append(
        {"name": field.name, "type": str(field.type)[:30], "metadata": meta_str}
    )

A spelled score faithfully supports a fully specific pitch, so pitch is represented exactly once: specific_pitch (step + alter + octave) is the single default pitch field, and it preserves the enharmonic spelling (e.g. G♯ vs A♭) that a bare MIDI pitch cannot.
The source MIDI pitch survives as a plain midi integer column. It is redundant with the spelling, so it is not stored as a second pitch field; instead the EventStore affords an EnharmonicPitch view over it on request via get_field(EnharmonicPitch) (or the enharmonic_pitch_field accessor). The spelled and enharmonic views diverge exactly where it matters — an accidental-bearing note.

# The default pitch field: fully spelled SpecificPitch scalars.
specific_pitch = notes_store.specific_pitch_field

# The afforded EnharmonicPitch view over the raw `midi` integer column.
enharmonic_pitch = notes_store.get_field(EnharmonicPitch)

# Index 3 is an accidental-bearing note, where spelling (SP) and the
# MIDI pitch (EP) part ways.
{

A few things to keep in mind:

Only a zipfile.Path names a member. A string such as "chopin.zip/ms3/chopin_op10_no3.notes.tsv" is a filesystem path, and loading it raises FileNotFoundError because no such file exists.
A member the archive does not hold raises FileNotFoundError naming both the archive and the member.
RDF read from a member (MelodyLoader) resolves relative IRIs against the member’s URI, jar:<archive file URI>!/<member>.

To hand a member to your own code that needs a file on disk, call materialize. It copies a member once into the cache, in the folder the environment variable TTA_CACHE_DIR names (by default ~/.cache/timetoalign), and returns the copy’s path; a later call returns the same copy, and a filesystem path comes back unchanged. The cache is never pruned: delete the folder by hand to reclaim the space.

copy = materialize(XML_MEMBER)
{
    "copy in the cache": copy.is_relative_to(ARCHIVE_DIR / "cache"),
    "same bytes as the member": copy.read_bytes() == XML_MEMBER.read_bytes(),
    "second call, same copy": materialize(XML_MEMBER) == copy,
    "a path comes back unchanged": materialize(CHOPIN_XML) == CHOPIN_XML,
}

title: How to Load Data
text:
Music data comes in many formats: MusicXML, MIDI, MEI, Humdrum, proprietary TSV exports, and more. Each format has its own structure, terminology, and quirks.
The problem: Without a unified approach, you’d need format-specific code for every data source, making cross-format analysis difficult and error-prone.
The TimeToAlign! solution: Loaders normalize heterogeneous formats into a consistent EventStore, enabling downstream processing without format-specific code.
MusicXML ─┐
MIDI ─────┼──> Loader ──> EventStore ──> DataFrame
TSV ──────┘

import json

from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

from timetoalign import Ms3Loader
from timetoalign.core.events import EnharmonicPitch

from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

DATA_DIR = ensure_data("vienna_1x22")

# Our test piece: Chopin Etude Op.10 No.3
CHOPIN_XML = DATA_DIR / "Chopin_op10_no3.musicxml"
CHOPIN_TSV = DATA_DIR / "ms3" / "chopin_op10_no3.notes.tsv"


def source_entry(loader):
    """The `path` and `member` a loader records for its one source, the path by name."""
    entry = loader.metadata["sources"][0]
    return {"path": Path(entry["path"]).name, "member": entry.get("member", "—")}

Each ScoreStore contains EventStores - efficient, PyArrow-backed tables that hold musical events.
Key characteristics: - High Performance: Built on Apache Arrow for fast columnar operations - Type Safety: Schema metadata preserves units and types - Pandas Interop: Easy conversion with .to_dataframe()

notes_store = tsv_loader.store.notes

{

# Examine the schema with metadata
schema_info = []
for field in notes_store.table.schema:
    meta = field.metadata or {}
    # Column metadata is one `timetoalign` JSON blob; unpack it so the table
    # shows the declared unit and number type rather than a serialized string.
    blob = json.loads(meta[b"timetoalign"]) if b"timetoalign" in meta else {}
    extra = {k.decode(): v.decode() for k, v in meta.items() if k != b"timetoalign"}
    meta_str = ", ".join(
        f"{k}={v}" for k, v in {**blob, **extra}.items() if k != "version"
    )
    schema_info.append(
        {"name": field.name, "type": str(field.type)[:30], "metadata": meta_str}
    )

title: How to Load Data
text:
A spelled score faithfully supports a fully specific pitch, so pitch is represented exactly once: specific_pitch (step + alter + octave) is the single default pitch field, and it preserves the enharmonic spelling (e.g. G♯ vs A♭) that a bare MIDI pitch cannot.
The source MIDI pitch survives as a plain midi integer column. It is redundant with the spelling, so it is not stored as a second pitch field; instead the EventStore affords an EnharmonicPitch view over it on request via get_field(EnharmonicPitch) (or the enharmonic_pitch_field accessor). The spelled and enharmonic views diverge exactly where it matters — an accidental-bearing note.

# The default pitch field: fully spelled SpecificPitch scalars.
specific_pitch = notes_store.specific_pitch_field

# The afforded EnharmonicPitch view over the raw `midi` integer column.
enharmonic_pitch = notes_store.get_field(EnharmonicPitch)

# Index 3 is an accidental-bearing note, where spelling (SP) and the
# MIDI pitch (EP) part ways.
{
    "specific_pitch[3] (default)": repr(specific_pitch[3]),
    "enharmonic_pitch[3] (afforded view)": repr(enharmonic_pitch[3]),
    "raw midi int[3]": tsv_df.iloc[3]["midi"],
}

title: How to Load CSV/TSV with column_specs and field_specs
text:
Tabular loaders in TimeToAlign! turn columns into fields in two explicit steps:







Term
Meaning




column
A column in the original source (CSV / TSV / DataFrame / pa.Table).


field
A raw or semantic DataField (TTA-internal). May be nested.



The loader’s job is the column to field mapping:

Step 1 — column_specs processes columns one-by-one. Mandatory for header-based sources; trivial for sources that already carry types.
Step 2 — field_specs combines or promotes the resulting fields. Fully optional — many loaders are complete with Step 1 alone.

This guide walks through the Step-1 resolution chain (every entry ends at a DataField), the CompositeFieldParser mechanism for one-column-to-many-fields, and a worked example in which we build a loader from scratch for the header-less .solo performance-analysis format.



from __future__ import annotations

import tempfile
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any, ClassVar

import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

from timetoalign.core import (
    DenominateNumberField,
    EnharmonicPitch,
    EnharmonicPitchField,
    Id,
    IdField,
    IntField,
    MeasureNumberField,
    NumberType,
    RedundantNumberField,
    StringField,
    TimeUnit,
)
from timetoalign.loader.tabular import (
    CompositeFieldParser,
    CsvLoader,
    resolve_field_parser,
)
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

PERF_PRECISION = ensure_data("performance_precision")
CHOPIN_SOLO = PERF_PRECISION / "Chopin Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2.solo"

# A small temp directory whose lifetime spans the whole notebook.  Synthetic
# CSV / TSV examples in subsequent cells write through here so the standard
# ``Loader.load(path)`` API can pick them up.
TMP = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="how04_"))


def write_csv(name: str, body: bytes) -> Path:
    """Write a synthetic CSV body to ``TMP / name`` and return its path."""
    p = TMP / name
    p.write_bytes(body)
    return p


def head_table(table: pa.Table, n: int = 5) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Return the first ``n`` rows of ``table`` as a DataFrame.

    DataFrames render as proper HTML tables in Jupyter, which is far more
    legible than dumping a column-keyed dict.  The helper sits at the top
    of the notebook so every preview cell uses the same display path.
    """
    return table.slice(0, n).to_pandas()




We start with the simplest case — a CSV with a header line and one Python type per column. The keys of column_specs are source-column names; the values are anything that resolves through the Step-1 resolution chain (Section 2). Here, a bare int / str is enough for the columns that aren’t already canonical (the loader still resolves start / end from the underlying source on its own):

mini_csv = (
    b"id,start,end,pitch,label\n"
    b"e0,0.0,0.5,60,intro\n"
    b"e1,0.5,1.0,64,intro\n"
    b"e2,1.0,1.5,67,verse\n"
    b"e3,1.5,2.0,72,verse\n"
)
mini_path = write_csv("mini.csv", mini_csv)


class MiniLoader(CsvLoader):
    column_specs = {"pitch": int, "label": str}


mini = MiniLoader()
mini.load(mini_path)
events = mini.get_events()
head_table(events.table)

Step 1 has produced one raw field per declared source column. The raw fields are reachable through get_raw(); get_field() is reserved for semantic fields with paired-class metadata (we meet that path in Section 4):

{
    "pitch": events.get_raw("pitch"),
    "label": events.get_raw("label"),
}

{'pitch': NumericField(name='pitch', type=int64, len=4),
 'label': StringField(name='label', type=string, len=4)}


Note the asymmetry: columns are a source artefact, fields are a TTA artefact. A loader without column_specs leaves the non-canonical source columns alone as opaque property columns; with column_specs, each named column is processed into a typed field whose semantics travel with it.



Every entry in column_specs (and every entry in a CompositeFieldParser’s parts) goes through a single resolver, resolve_field_parser. The resolver is best read as a chain, not a lookup table: whatever the user passes, the chain ends at one of two producers:

a DataField blueprint — an empty instance carrying just a name and (for semantic fields) the paired scalar class. The blueprint’s emit(source, name=...) consumes the raw pa.Array from the source table and returns a fully materialised field.
a FieldParser instance — a genuine processor with its own emit(source, name=...). Parsers are reserved for the cases that don’t reduce to a typed cast: CompositeFieldParser for one column to many fields, CallableFieldParser for arbitrary user callables.

Both terminals expose the same emit() signature, so the loader does not care which one came out of the chain.
The chain, top-to-bottom:







User passes
Resolves to




a FieldParser instance
itself (genuine processor)


a DataField blueprint instance (e.g. IntField(name="x"))
itself


a DataField subclass (raw or paired SemanticField)
a blueprint with name=<dict key>


a Python type (int / float / str / Fraction)
the matching raw DataField blueprint


a pa.DataType (pa.int64(), pa.float64(), pa.string())
the matching raw DataField blueprint


any callable (pa.Array) -> DataField
wrapped in a CallableFieldParser



The next cells run resolve_field_parser directly so the chain stops being abstract — every input ends at a concrete DataField blueprint or a FieldParser:

# Python-type input -> matching raw DataField blueprint.  ``default_name``
# stands in for the dict key that a real ``column_specs`` entry would
# carry; here we just supply a placeholder to satisfy the blueprint's
# name requirement.
{
    "int": type(resolve_field_parser(int, default_name="x")).__name__,
    "float": type(resolve_field_parser(float, default_name="x")).__name__,
    "str": type(resolve_field_parser(str, default_name="x")).__name__,
    "Fraction": type(resolve_field_parser(Fraction, default_name="x")).__name__,
}

{'int': 'IntField',
 'float': 'FloatField',
 'str': 'StringField',
 'Fraction': 'RedundantNumberField'}



# pa.DataType input -> matched by-type to the equivalent raw blueprint.
{
    "pa.int64()": type(resolve_field_parser(pa.int64(), default_name="x")).__name__,
    "pa.float64()": type(resolve_field_parser(pa.float64(), default_name="x")).__name__,
    "pa.string()": type(resolve_field_parser(pa.string(), default_name="x")).__name__,
}

{'pa.int64()': 'IntField',
 'pa.float64()': 'FloatField',
 'pa.string()': 'StringField'}



# A pre-built blueprint passes through unchanged (identity check).
bp = IntField(name="channel")
resolve_field_parser(bp) is bp

typed_path = write_csv("typed.csv", typed_csv)

    column_specs = {"x": IntField(name="x_renamed")}


typed = TypedLoader()

Two terminal categories are worth restating, because they cover the overwhelming majority of real loaders:

DataField blueprints are what you reach for whenever the source column maps to a single typed value — possibly with semantic metadata. IntField, FloatField, StringField, RedundantNumberField cover the raw side; every paired SemanticField subclass (DenominateNumberField, EnharmonicPitchField, IdField, …) is blueprint-constructible in exactly the same way: name= plus whatever extra kwargs the scalar requires.
FieldParsers show up when the column-to-field map is genuinely procedural — when a typed cast is not enough.

The next section meets the only FieldParser you’ll need in practice.



Some source columns pack several values into one string. The classic musicological example is 1+3/8 — a measure number, a literal +, and a fractional offset inside the measure. CompositeFieldParser is the universal splitter: a separator (or regex pattern) plus a parts declaration that follows the same resolution chain as column_specs:

composite_csv = (
    b"id,start,end,position\n"
    b"e0,0.0,0.5,1+0/8\n"
    b"e1,0.5,1.0,1+3/8\n"
    b"e2,1.0,1.5,2+1/4\n"
    b"e3,1.5,2.0,2+5/8\n"
)
composite_path = write_csv("composite.csv", composite_csv)


class CompositeLoader(CsvLoader):
    column_specs = {
        "position": CompositeFieldParser(
            separator="+",
            parts={
                "measure": int,
                "offset": Fraction,
            },
        ),
    }

comp.load(composite_path)

Each entry of parts is resolved through the same chain — so int becomes an IntField blueprint and Fraction becomes a RedundantNumberField blueprint. Composites also nest: a parts entry may itself be a CompositeFieldParser.
RedundantNumberField parses string entries like "3/8" into a Fraction, storing the exact numerator/denominator pair alongside a float mirror; DenominateNumberField does the same and binds the result to a TimeUnit, so the field arrives at the next pipeline stage already carrying time-unit semantics:

denom_csv = b"id,start,end,duration\n" b"e0,0.0,0.5,1/2\n" b"e1,0.5,0.75,1/4\n"

Performance-analysis pipelines emit .solo files: a header-less, tab-separated format in which each row carries six columns:

Measure-plus-offset (1+3/8) — measure number, a literal +, then a fractional onset within the measure (in quarters).
Duration as a fraction of a quarter note (1/4).
Channel (integer).
MIDI pitch (integer, 0–127).
Velocity (integer, 0–127; 0 marks a note-off).
Opaque alphanumeric note identifier ("n1b8xktz").

Here is the head of the Chopin specimen:

{"first lines": CHOPIN_SOLO.read_text().splitlines()[:5]}

{'first lines': ['0+11/8\t0/1\t90\t70\t80\tn1b8xktz',
  '1+0/1\t1/8\t90\t70\t0\tn1b8xktz',
  '1+0/1\t1/8\t90\t39\t80\tnh9xux4',
  '1+0/1\t1/8\t90\t79\t80\tn4g35y0',
  '1+1/8\t1/4\t90\t39\t0\tnh9xux4']}


We’re going to write a CsvLoader subclass for this format from scratch — exercising every mechanism in this guide. Two things make .solo non-trivial:

There is no header line, so the dataframe-reading step needs to be overridden to supply positional column names.
The first column packs measure number + onset together — exactly the case CompositeFieldParser is for.

The pattern for overriding the dataframe read is to set header_row = -1 (the sentinel for “no header”) and override _read_dataframe to call pd.read_csv(..., header=None, names=[...]) with positional names matching the column_specs declaration order. Everything else — Step 1 emissions, Step 2 promotions, property columns — works exactly as in the header-based examples above.

class ChopinSoloLoader(CsvLoader):
    """Loader for the header-less ``.solo`` performance-analysis format."""

    # Header-less, tab-delimited source.
    delimiter: ClassVar[str] = "\t"
    header_row: ClassVar[int] = -1  # sentinel for "no header"

    # Canonical column wiring.  ``mn_onset`` is the fractional onset within
    # the measure, produced by Step 1's composite split; measure-number
    # resolution against a MetricMap is left to downstream consumers.
    id_column: ClassVar[str | None] = None  # auto-generated
    name_column: ClassVar[str | None] = None
    start_column: ClassVar[str] = "mn_onset"
    end_column: ClassVar[str | None] = None
    duration_column: ClassVar[str | None] = "duration"
    event_type_column: ClassVar[str | None] = None
    default_event_type: ClassVar[str] = "Note"

    _default_unit: ClassVar[TimeUnit] = TimeUnit.quarters
    coordinate_type: ClassVar[NumberType] = NumberType.fraction

    # Step 1: one entry per source column, in declaration order.  An
    # iterable form is used because the source has no header to key on.
    column_specs: ClassVar[list[Any]] = [
        # col 0: measure_number + fractional onset within the measure.
        CompositeFieldParser(
            separator="+",
            parts=[
                MeasureNumberField,  # default name 'measure_number'
                RedundantNumberField(name="mn_onset"),
            ],
            name="position",
        ),
        # col 1: duration as a fraction of a quarter note (semantic).
        DenominateNumberField(name="duration", unit=TimeUnit.quarters),
        # cols 2-5: simple typed blueprints.
        IntField(name="channel"),
        IntField(name="pitch"),
        IntField(name="velocity"),
        StringField(name="note_id"),
    ]

    # Step 2: promote two raw Step-1 fields to semantic ones using the
    # ``source_fields=<name>`` blueprint shorthand — "one raw field by
    # this name, fed into the target's canonical 'value'".
    field_specs: ClassVar[list[Any]] = [
        EnharmonicPitchField(source_fields="pitch"),
        IdField(source_fields="note_id"),
    ]

    def _read_dataframe(self, source):  # type: ignore[override]
        """Read a header-less ``.solo`` file with positional column names."""
        names = ["position", "duration", "channel", "pitch", "velocity", "note_id"]
        return pd.read_csv(
            source,
            sep=self.delimiter,
            header=None,
            names=names,
            encoding=self.encoding,
            dtype=str,
        )

After Step 1, the working table holds typed fields — measure number and fractional offset broken out into the position struct, duration bound to quarters, the three integer columns, and the string ID. Step 2 then promotes the raw pitch int into a semantic EnharmonicPitchField and the raw note_id string into a paired IdField:

events.table.column_names

['id',
 'name',
 'temporal_type',
 'event_type',
 'start',
 'end',
 'duration',
 'position',
 'channel',
 'pitch',
 'velocity',
 'note_id',
 'measure_number',
 'mn_onset',
 'locator',
 'extraction_id']


EnharmonicPitchField is now reachable by type, and indexing it returns EnharmonicPitch scalars. The faithfulness rule applies: the field records the MIDI pitch number that the source data carried, not anything inferred about spelling — both G♯3 and A♭3 show as MIDI 56 because .solo does not carry an accidental:

ep_field = events.get_field(EnharmonicPitch)
{"first 5": [ep_field[i] for i in range(5)]}

{'first 5': [EP(A♯/B♭4), EP(A♯/B♭4), EP(D♯/E♭2), EP(G5), EP(D♯/E♭2)]}


IdField holds the original note identifiers. The Chopin specimen re-uses some IDs across event onsets/offsets, which the shallow form preserves verbatim:

id_field = events.get_field(Id)
{"first 5": [id_field[i] for i in range(5)]}

{'first 5': [Id('n1b8xktz'),
  Id('n1b8xktz'),
  Id('nh9xux4'),
  Id('n4g35y0'),
  Id('nh9xux4')]}


That is the entire loader. No subclassing of internal types, no struct dicts, no special-casing — every column flowed through the same Step 1 resolution chain, and two raw fields graduated to semantic via Step 2 blueprints.



By default, source columns that are NOT consumed by any column_specs entry survive in the EventData as property columns — convenient for ad-hoc inspection but excluded from the field machinery. The properties= kwarg on get_events() controls which ones make it through:







Value
Meaning




True (default)
all remaining source columns survive as properties


False
no property columns; the EventData carries only fields


"col"
shorthand for a one-element tuple


(col1,col2, …)
explicit named subset



To exercise this we need a CSV that genuinely carries an unconsumed column. Here page and scribbled_note are present in the source but absent from column_specs, so they default to property columns:

extras_csv = (

    b"e2,1.0,1.5,67,verse,three,2\n"
)
extras_path = write_csv("extras.csv", extras_csv)


class ExtrasLoader(CsvLoader):
    column_specs = {"pitch": int, "label": str}


ex = ExtrasLoader()
ex.load(extras_path)

title: How to Load CSV/TSV with column_specs and field_specs
text:
from __future__ import annotations

import tempfile
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any, ClassVar

import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

from timetoalign.core import (
    DenominateNumberField,
    EnharmonicPitch,
    EnharmonicPitchField,
    Id,
    IdField,
    IntField,
    MeasureNumberField,
    NumberType,
    RedundantNumberField,
    StringField,
    TimeUnit,
)
from timetoalign.loader.tabular import (
    CompositeFieldParser,
    CsvLoader,
    resolve_field_parser,
)
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

PERF_PRECISION = ensure_data("performance_precision")
CHOPIN_SOLO = PERF_PRECISION / "Chopin Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2.solo"

# A small temp directory whose lifetime spans the whole notebook.  Synthetic
# CSV / TSV examples in subsequent cells write through here so the standard
# ``Loader.load(path)`` API can pick them up.
TMP = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="how04_"))


def write_csv(name: str, body: bytes) -> Path:
    """Write a synthetic CSV body to ``TMP / name`` and return its path."""
    p = TMP / name
    p.write_bytes(body)
    return p


def head_table(table: pa.Table, n: int = 5) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Return the first ``n`` rows of ``table`` as a DataFrame.

    DataFrames render as proper HTML tables in Jupyter, which is far more
    legible than dumping a column-keyed dict.  The helper sits at the top
    of the notebook so every preview cell uses the same display path.
    """
    return table.slice(0, n).to_pandas()

title: How to Load CSV/TSV with column_specs and field_specs
text:
Every entry in column_specs (and every entry in a CompositeFieldParser’s parts) goes through a single resolver, resolve_field_parser. The resolver is best read as a chain, not a lookup table: whatever the user passes, the chain ends at one of two producers:

a DataField blueprint — an empty instance carrying just a name and (for semantic fields) the paired scalar class. The blueprint’s emit(source, name=...) consumes the raw pa.Array from the source table and returns a fully materialised field.
a FieldParser instance — a genuine processor with its own emit(source, name=...). Parsers are reserved for the cases that don’t reduce to a typed cast: CompositeFieldParser for one column to many fields, CallableFieldParser for arbitrary user callables.

Both terminals expose the same emit() signature, so the loader does not care which one came out of the chain.
The chain, top-to-bottom:







User passes
Resolves to




a FieldParser instance
itself (genuine processor)


a DataField blueprint instance (e.g. IntField(name="x"))
itself


a DataField subclass (raw or paired SemanticField)
a blueprint with name=<dict key>


a Python type (int / float / str / Fraction)
the matching raw DataField blueprint


a pa.DataType (pa.int64(), pa.float64(), pa.string())
the matching raw DataField blueprint


any callable (pa.Array) -> DataField
wrapped in a CallableFieldParser



The next cells run resolve_field_parser directly so the chain stops being abstract — every input ends at a concrete DataField blueprint or a FieldParser:

# Python-type input -> matching raw DataField blueprint.  ``default_name``
# stands in for the dict key that a real ``column_specs`` entry would
# carry; here we just supply a placeholder to satisfy the blueprint's
# name requirement.
{
    "int": type(resolve_field_parser(int, default_name="x")).__name__,
    "float": type(resolve_field_parser(float, default_name="x")).__name__,
    "str": type(resolve_field_parser(str, default_name="x")).__name__,
    "Fraction": type(resolve_field_parser(Fraction, default_name="x")).__name__,
}

{'int': 'IntField',
 'float': 'FloatField',
 'str': 'StringField',
 'Fraction': 'RedundantNumberField'}



# pa.DataType input -> matched by-type to the equivalent raw blueprint.
{
    "pa.int64()": type(resolve_field_parser(pa.int64(), default_name="x")).__name__,
    "pa.float64()": type(resolve_field_parser(pa.float64(), default_name="x")).__name__,
    "pa.string()": type(resolve_field_parser(pa.string(), default_name="x")).__name__,
}

{'pa.int64()': 'IntField',
 'pa.float64()': 'FloatField',
 'pa.string()': 'StringField'}



# A pre-built blueprint passes through unchanged (identity check).
bp = IntField(name="channel")
resolve_field_parser(bp) is bp

True

Two terminal categories are worth restating, because they cover the overwhelming majority of real loaders:

DataField blueprints are what you reach for whenever the source column maps to a single typed value — possibly with semantic metadata. IntField, FloatField, StringField, RedundantNumberField cover the raw side; every paired SemanticField subclass (DenominateNumberField, EnharmonicPitchField, IdField, …) is blueprint-constructible in exactly the same way: name= plus whatever extra kwargs the scalar requires.
FieldParsers show up when the column-to-field map is genuinely procedural — when a typed cast is not enough.

The next section meets the only FieldParser you’ll need in practice.

Some source columns pack several values into one string. The classic musicological example is 1+3/8 — a measure number, a literal +, and a fractional offset inside the measure. title: How to Load CSV/TSV with column_specs and field_specs
text:
Performance-analysis pipelines emit .solo files: a header-less, tab-separated format in which each row carries six columns:

Measure-plus-offset (1+3/8) — measure number, a literal +, then a fractional onset within the measure (in quarters).
Duration as a fraction of a quarter note (1/4).
Channel (integer).
MIDI pitch (integer, 0–127).
Velocity (integer, 0–127; 0 marks a note-off).
Opaque alphanumeric note identifier ("n1b8xktz").

Here is the head of the Chopin specimen:

{"first lines": CHOPIN_SOLO.read_text().splitlines()[:5]}

{'first lines': ['0+11/8\t0/1\t90\t70\t80\tn1b8xktz',
  '1+0/1\t1/8\t90\t70\t0\tn1b8xktz',
  '1+0/1\t1/8\t90\t39\t80\tnh9xux4',
  '1+0/1\t1/8\t90\t79\t80\tn4g35y0',
  '1+1/8\t1/4\t90\t39\t0\tnh9xux4']}


We’re going to write a CsvLoader subclass for this format from scratch — exercising every mechanism in this guide. Two things make .solo non-trivial:

There is no header line, so the dataframe-reading step needs to be overridden to supply positional column names.
The first column packs measure number + onset together — exactly the case CompositeFieldParser is for.

The pattern for overriding the dataframe read is to set header_row = -1 (the sentinel for “no header”) and override _read_dataframe to call pd.read_csv(..., header=None, names=[...]) with positional names matching the column_specs declaration order. Everything else — Step 1 emissions, Step 2 promotions, property columns — works exactly as in the header-based examples above.

class ChopinSoloLoader(CsvLoader):
    """Loader for the header-less ``.solo`` performance-analysis format."""

    # Header-less, tab-delimited source.
    delimiter: ClassVar[str] = "\t"
    header_row: ClassVar[int] = -1  # sentinel for "no header"

    # Canonical column wiring.  ``mn_onset`` is the fractional onset within
    # the measure, produced by Step 1's composite split; measure-number
    # resolution against a MetricMap is left to downstream consumers.
    id_column: ClassVar[str | None] = None  # auto-generated
    name_column: ClassVar[str | None] = None
    start_column: ClassVar[str] = "mn_onset"
    end_column: ClassVar[str | None] = None
    duration_column: ClassVar[str | None] = "duration"
    event_type_column: ClassVar[str | None] = None
    default_event_type: ClassVar[str] = "Note"

    _default_unit: ClassVar[TimeUnit] = TimeUnit.quarters
    coordinate_type: ClassVar[NumberType] = NumberType.fraction

    # Step 1: one entry per source column, in declaration order.  An
    # iterable form is used because the source has no header to key on.
    column_specs: ClassVar[list[Any]] = [
        # col 0: measure_number + fractional onset within the measure.
        CompositeFieldParser(
            separator="+",
            parts=[
                MeasureNumberField,  # default name 'measure_number'
                RedundantNumberField(name="mn_onset"),
            ],
            name="position",
        ),
        # col 1: duration as a fraction of a quarter note (semantic).
        DenominateNumberField(name="duration", unit=TimeUnit.quarters),
        # cols 2-5: simple typed blueprints.
        IntField(name="channel"),
        IntField(name="pitch"),
        IntField(name="velocity"),
        StringField(name="note_id"),
    ]

    # Step 2: promote two raw Step-1 fields to semantic ones using the
    # ``source_fields=<name>`` blueprint shorthand — "one raw field by
    # this name, fed into the target's canonical 'value'".
    field_specs: ClassVar[list[Any]] = [
        EnharmonicPitchField(source_fields="pitch"),
        IdField(source_fields="note_id"),
    ]

    def _read_dataframe(self, source):  # type: ignore[override]
        """Read a header-less ``.solo`` file with positional column names."""
        names = ["position", "duration", "channel", "pitch", "velocity", "note_id"]
        return pd.read_csv(
            source,
            sep=self.delimiter,
            header=None,
            names=names,
            encoding=self.encoding,
            dtype=str,
        )

After Step 1, the working table holds typed fields — measure number and fractional offset broken out into the position struct, duration bound to quarters, the three integer columns, and the string ID. Step 2 then promotes the raw pitch int into a semantic EnharmonicPitchField and the raw note_id string into a paired IdField:

events.table.column_names

['id',
 'name',
 'temporal_type',
 'event_type',
 'start',
 'end',
 'duration',
 'position',
 'channel',
 'pitch',
 'velocity',
 'note_id',
 'measure_number',
 'mn_onset',
 'locator',
 'extraction_id']


EnharmonicPitchField is now reachable by type, and indexing it returns EnharmonicPitch scalars. The faithfulness rule applies: the field records the MIDI pitch number that the source data carried, not anything inferred about spelling — both G♯3 and A♭3 show as MIDI 56 because .solo does not carry an accidental:

ep_field = events.get_field(EnharmonicPitch)
{"first 5": [ep_field[i] for i in range(5)]}

{'first 5': [EP(A♯/B♭4), EP(A♯/B♭4), EP(D♯/E♭2), EP(G5), EP(D♯/E♭2)]}


IdField holds the original note identifiers. The Chopin specimen re-uses some IDs across event onsets/offsets, which the shallow form preserves verbatim:

id_field = events.get_field(Id)
{"first 5": [id_field[i] for i in range(5)]}

{'first 5': [Id('n1b8xktz'),
  Id('n1b8xktz'),
  Id('nh9xux4'),
  Id('n4g35y0'),
  Id('nh9xux4')]}


That is the entire loader. No subclassing of internal types, no struct dicts, no special-casing — every column flowed through the same Step 1 resolution chain, and two raw fields graduated to semantic via Step 2 blueprints.

title: How to Load CSV/TSV with column_specs and field_specs
text:
By default, source columns that are NOT consumed by any column_specs entry survive in the EventData as property columns — convenient for ad-hoc inspection but excluded from the field machinery. The properties= kwarg on get_events() controls which ones make it through:







Value
Meaning




True (default)
all remaining source columns survive as properties


False
no property columns; the EventData carries only fields


"col"
shorthand for a one-element tuple


(col1,col2, …)
explicit named subset



To exercise this we need a CSV that genuinely carries an unconsumed column. Here page and scribbled_note are present in the source but absent from column_specs, so they default to property columns:

extras_csv = (
    b"id,start,end,pitch,label,scribbled_note,page\n"
    b"e0,0.0,0.5,60,intro,one,1\n"
    b"e1,0.5,1.0,64,intro,two,1\n"
    b"e2,1.0,1.5,67,verse,three,2\n"
)
extras_path = write_csv("extras.csv", extras_csv)


class ExtrasLoader(CsvLoader):
    column_specs = {"pitch": int, "label": str}


ex = ExtrasLoader()
ex.load(extras_path)






Sources
1 file(s): extras.csv


Events
3


Unit
seconds


Try
create_timeline(), get_events(...)





properties=True (the default) keeps every unconsumed column; properties=False drops them all. The string shorthand properties="page" and the tuple form properties=("page",) are equivalent — both keep just page as a property and drop scribbled_note:

{
    "properties=True  (default)": ex.get_events(properties=True).table.column_names,
    "properties=False": ex.get_events(properties=False).table.column_names,
    "properties='page'": ex.get_events(properties="page").table.column_names,
    "properties=('page',)": ex.get_events(properties=("page",)).table.column_names,
}

{'properties=True  (default)': ['id',
  'name',
  'temporal_type',
  'event_type',
  'start',
  'end',
  'duration',
  'pitch',
  'label',
  'scribbled_note',
  'page',
  'locator',
  'extraction_id'],
 'properties=False': ['id',
  'name',
  'temporal_type',
  'event_type',
  'start',
  'end',
  'duration',
  'pitch',
  'label'],
 "properties='page'": ['id',
  'name',
  'temporal_type',
  'event_type',
  'start',
  'end',
  'duration',
  'pitch',
  'label',
  'page'],
 "properties=('page',)": ['id',
  'name',
  'temporal_type',
  'event_type',
  'start',
  'end',
  'duration',
  'pitch',
  'label',
  'page']}


Property columns let users keep source-side metadata alongside the fields without forcing every loose annotation through column_specs. When a property column needs to gain semantic identity — to become a DataField proper — that’s exactly when field_specs enters: name the column in Step 1 with the appropriate spec, and Step 2 promotes it (as it did with pitch and note_id in the .solo loader above).
