TimeStamps


Definition: TimeStamp

A TimeStamp is a set of values reflecting the coordinate of a root timeline, the synchronous coordinates of all Children, and the conversion results of all ConversionMaps associated respectively.

A TimeStamp is a cross-section through a timeline hierarchy at a given coordinate. It answers the question: “At coordinate c of the root timeline, what are the local coordinates in each Child, and what do all C-maps produce?”
Which Children answer follows one containment rule. A Child holds the parent positions from its start up to, but not including, its end, and its end as well where no sibling starts there. A boundary two siblings share therefore belongs to the one starting at it, so one parent position names one segment, while a Child that nothing follows still answers at its own end. The rule applies along the path: a position reaches a nested timeline only if every timeline on the way down holds it, so a grandchild never answers where its own parent leaves the position to a sibling. TimeStamps, timestamp tables, get_children_at() and the MatchStamps of an AlignmentBundle all apply this rule, to every timeline of a tree, nested ones included.
By analogy, a TimeIntervalStamp combines a start TimeStamp and an end TimeStamp, representing the cross-section of an interval through the hierarchy.


Visualisation: TimeStamp

TimeStamps are visualised as a vertical cross-section through a timeline that intersects all Children and ConversionMaps at their synchronous points.







Figure 5: A timeline’s internal data structures. The instants table records all Instants with their coordinates, IDs, and types. The intervals table is derived from the instants table and supports interval queries.

title: Conceptual Model
text:
Regions and Derivative Timelines

Regions
A Region is a named part of a timeline defined by a TimeInterval. Regions are useful for referring to parts of a timeline by name (e.g., “Chorus”, “Verse”, “Development”) or by generic labels (e.g., alphabetical letters for representing traversal paths).
Regions are not timelines: they do not accommodate events or C-maps. They can, however, be used as the basis for partitioning a timeline into Children—creating a Child whose boundaries correspond to the Region’s TimeInterval.


Derivative Timelines
Three kinds of derived timelines play a central role in alignment:

FlowMap and virtual timeline

A FlowMap lists stretches of a root timeline— Regions, child timelines, virtual timelines—in the order they are played, with gaps between them where nothing of the timeline is played. It is computed from the timeline’s flow control (Breaks, Jumps and the other elements), or written by hand for a cut, an order of movements or a set list. Applied, it gives a Virtual timeline: the played order as a timeline with an ID, a unit and a length of its own and nothing else, through which positions convert in both directions. Unfolding a position of the score gives every position where it is played; folding a played position gives the one position of the score.
For example, a score with a repeat and a dal segno al coda has a FlowMap like [A, B, A, B, C, D] where some sections appear more than once: a position in A unfolds to two positions of the virtual timeline.

Converted timeline

A timeline whose coordinates have been transformed to another unit via a ConversionMap or ChainMap, potentially after applying a FlowMap.

WarpMap

A derived timeline where coordinates have been re-adjusted to align with those of another timeline on the basis of AlignmentAnchors. See Alignment for the full definition of WarpMap and the pipeline that produces it.

title: Conceptual Model
text:
Alignment
The alignment layer is where the model’s cross-domain capability comes together.

MatchClaim


Definition: MatchClaim

A MatchClaim is a claim of equivalence between two events on different timelines, each coordinate on its own timeline’s axis, with its Provenance: how it was made and who believes it. A MatchClaim may be synchronous (producing AlignmentAnchors) or conceptual (structural equivalence without temporal commitment). The sentinel NOMATCH on one side explicitly encodes the absence of a corresponding event on the other timeline.

A MatchClaim names its two events by their IDs, each with its timeline. The model matches events, not coordinates: the claim’s coordinates are its events’ coordinates, and the events stay addressable for everything else that is said about them. A side without an event of its own is given a Projection: an event added to that timeline at the stated position, standing for the other side’s event (its projection_of), or for none where no such event is known. A synchronous claim between two bare positions is instead CHUNK on both sides: its anchors state the coordinates and no Projection is added. Each side of a stated MatchClaim therefore names an event or a sentinel. AlignmentBundle.create_match_claims() adds the Projections a list of pairs needs and reuses those a timeline already holds. It checks every pair before it adds anything, so a refused list leaves the bundle and its timelines unchanged: a float position on a timeline counting samples, a span that runs backwards, a position past where its timeline can reach (the end of a locked timeline, or an end its parent cannot contain) and a held event’s ID given with a span other than its own are refused.
MatchClaims grow incrementally: an initial claim between events A and B can be extended by adding B-C, creating a match path A -> B -> C that connects three timelines.
Two levels of matching are distinguished:

Synchronous matching: the matched events occupy corresponding temporal positions (e.g., “this beat in the score corresponds to this moment in the recording”).
Conceptual matching: the matched events are semantically equivalent but may not share a temporal correspondence (e.g., “both versions have a Bridge section, but they differ in length and internal structure”).


Provenance and beliefs
A MatchClaim carries a certainty, in [0, 1], and one Provenance entry, the facility statements use as well. The entry records how the claim was made: who stated it (stated_by), the day, the method (manual, reconciled, imported, inferred or an IRI), the service that made it, the sources it rests on and a note. It also holds the beliefs about the claim: at most one per actor, "true", "false" or "unlikely", each dated. A person stating a claim believes it "true" (create_match_claims(..., actor=) records that belief); a loader or a service records how it made the claim and believes nothing.
A MatchClaim is never deleted and its ID never changes. Whoever disagrees records a belief instead (AlignmentBundle.add_match_claim_belief()), and a correction is a new claim. Nothing derives a truth value from the beliefs; the belief filter reads them for one actor. Every query that reads MatchClaims takes it (get_match_claims(), the MatchStamp getters and the bundle’s coordinate getters): believer= names the actor, and beliefs= the states kept, any of "true", "undecided" (the believer holds no belief on the claim), "unlikely" and "false". The default keeps every state but "false", so a claim without a belief and an "unlikely" one pass. Where one believer is spelled twice in a claim’s beliefs (actors compare as the IRIs they stand for), the claim is read as the most critical of the two. Without believer= nothing is filtered.


The MatchClaim table and the package
An AlignmentBundle holds all its claims in one MatchClaim table, a MatchClaimField (match_claim_table): one row per claim, one column per property of a MatchClaim. A claim given no ID is minted one when it is constructed, and joining a bundle renames none. A MatchClaim is addressed by its ID alone, so AlignmentBundle.from_bundles() refuses two sources holding one ID. On disk the MatchClaim table is match_claims.parquet, and the Projections of every timeline are rows of the Registry, registry.parquet, with their content in the Projection table, projections.parquet. The MatchClaim table and the registry write each number once, in the member its number type names (a fraction as numerator and denominator), where memory keeps the float beside the exact ratio; this package form is what MatchClaimField.package_table gives and from_package_table() reads. Both lie beside the TimeToShare manifest, which names each in its resources (see Resource); a manifest and the files it names make a Package. The manifest names no event: the claims name events by their IDs, and by default the events stay with the sources they come from while the package holds the events it made itself, the Projections (and the Boxes of a page). to_file(events=True) writes every other event type as well, into the registry and a Pre-parsed table per type beside the manifest. to_file() writes the package and from_file() reads it back. Several manifests share their tables in a package whose package.yaml lists them, which the Package class writes and opens. Writing over a MatchClaim table obeys the succession rule: every claim of the old table is in the new one, with the same timelines, events and anchors; only the provenance may differ.



AlignmentAnchors


Definition: AlignmentAnchor

An AlignmentAnchor is a pure coordinate pair associating one coordinate on timeline A with one coordinate on timeline B. It is a neutral record with no claim semantics—provenance and interpretation are carried by the enclosing MatchClaim. Only synchronous MatchClaims produce AlignmentAnchors.

From a MatchClaim that associates TimeIntervalEvents, two anchors are derived: a StartAnchor and an EndAnchor. Based on the units present in the aligned timelines, WarpMaps can be constructed.


Visualisation: AlignmentAnchor

AlignmentAnchors are visualised as connecting lines between TimeStamps, using the same or a similar visual style as the Matches they derive from.


MatchClaim cases
A MatchClaim always knows which pair of timelines it connects. It contains 0–2 AlignmentAnchors (only if synchronous), the synchrony flag, its provenance and its certainty. Its kind, the ClaimType, is derived from that structure and never stored. Three kinds are distinguished:

event_match: synchronous, an event or CHUNK on each side, a Projection included—the core alignment operation, and the kind that yields AlignmentAnchors.
nomatch (NOMATCH): non-synchronous, one event and the sentinel—a positive assertion that the event has no equivalent on the other timeline, oriented from the timeline that has it to the one that lacks it.
conceptual: non-synchronous, an event on each side—a structural correspondence without temporal commitment.

What a MatchGraph infers through a TimelineGroup (a match between two timelines implying coordinates on the sibling members of their groups) is not a MatchClaim and has no kind: it is the graph’s own inferred edge.
A Projection is not a kind of claim: it is an event, and a claim joining a Projection is an event_match like any other. Transferring an annotation to a timeline that has no event for it is such a claim.



MatchGraph and MatchStamp
A MatchGraph is an on-demand analytical structure built from MatchClaims. Nodes are (timeline_id, coordinate) tuples; edges derive from the AlignmentAnchors of synchronous claims. Each connected component yields a MatchStamp—a synchronised instant across multiple timelines. A MatchGraph can be extended through TimelineGroup membership; the edges it infers are its own (inferred_edges), apart from the stated ones. In the Hendrix example, each Match box M1–M15 is a MatchGraph, not a single MatchClaim.


Definition: MatchStamp

A MatchStamp is the union of TimeStamps from groups synchronously connected by a MatchGraph. It contains one coordinate per participating timeline and, with conversion_maps=True, the results of all ConversionMaps associated with those timelines. Unlike a TimeStamp, where C-Map results are visible by default, conversion_maps on every MatchStamp-producing getter (bundle.get_matchstamp_at(), get_matchstamps_at(), get_matchstamp_table(), MatchClaim.get_matchstamp()) is opt-in and defaults to False. This differing default is a per-context parameter setting, not a break in stamp uniformity: a MatchStamp exposes the identical Stamp interface — get_coordinate_for(), get_coordinates_for(), the get_coordinate() dispatcher, get_unit(), get_conversion_for(), present_timelines, is_interpolated, to_dict() — as a TimeStamp, so a stamp from any source keeps the same structure and behaviour regardless of which keyword defaults were used to produce it.

A MatchStamp from a single MatchClaim contains the TimeStamps for the claim’s AlignmentAnchor. A MatchStamp from a MatchGraph contains all TimeStamps that the graph connects through its connected components. Like a TimeStamp, it can be expanded with within-group coordinates (delegating to TimelineGroup) and, once opted in, C-map conversions.
get_matchstamp_table() extends the same opt-in flag to tabular output: with conversion_maps=True, one derived column is added per timeline for each of its enabled numeric unit-conversion maps (a map with a target_unit), placed after the timeline columns. A label- or structure-valued conversion map still surfaces in a MatchStamp’s display but never becomes a table column. A converted-unit column name that collides across timelines is qualified as "<timeline_id>:<unit>".


The MatchLine
The MatchLine is an ordered sequence of AlignmentAnchors derived from MatchClaims, sorted by coordinate on a source timeline. It serves as input for WarpMap generation.


WarpMap


Definition: WarpMap

A WarpMap is an interpolation-based coordinate mapping derived from a MatchLine; it enables non-linear coordinate transfer between TimelineGroups.

A WarpMap is generated from a MatchLine by extracting (source_coord, target_coord) pairs and building an interpolation table. If the source and target timelines have different units, the warped copy is in the target’s unit and of the appropriate timeline type (e.g., a ContinuousLogicalTimeline warped to a ContinuousPhysicalTimeline). A WarpMap requires at least two matching coordinate pairs for interpolation. It is the mechanism by which non-linear temporal correspondences—such as those between a rubato performance and a metronomic score—are captured.


AlignmentBundle


Definition: AlignmentBundle

The AlignmentBundle is a collection of TimelineGroups with inter-group MatchClaim connections; it provides coordinate transfer via offset arithmetic, interpolation, and WarpMaps.

The AlignmentBundle provides coordinate transfer at two levels:

Within a group: delegates to TimelineGroup.get_timestamp_at(), which converts linearly and exactly between members that share one start and one end.
Across groups: constructs a MatchLine from the claims between the groups that the belief filter keeps, generates WarpMaps on demand, and uses those WarpMaps for coordinate transfer.

The canonical user-facing query is bundle.get_matchstamp_at(coord, tl_id), which returns a MatchStamp spanning all groups connected to the queried timeline.
The full alignment object hierarchy, from atomic to composite, is:
AlignmentAnchor      (pure coordinate pair, no semantics)
    ↓
MatchClaim           (semantic claim about two timelines)
    ↓
MatchGraph           (on-demand graph from multiple claims)
    ↓
MatchStamp           (synchronised instant across N timelines)
    ↓
MatchLine            (ordered sequence of MatchStamps)
    ↓
WarpMap              (materialised timeline copy)


Coordinate transfer
The model implements three tiers of coordinate transfer:

Offset arithmetic for parent–child relationships: a child’s coordinate is the parent’s coordinate minus the child’s offset. Exact and lossless.
Interpolation within TimelineGroups: members of potentially different units (e.g., seconds and samples) share one start and one end, so a position converts linearly and exactly, from each member’s 0 and length.
WarpMap for cross-group alignment: derived from a MatchLine, a WarpMap materialises a complete copy of a source timeline warped to a target timeline’s coordinates.

Two timelines are commensurable if connected by a chain of C-maps, membership in the same TimelineGroup, or cross-group MatchClaims. Commensurability is the precondition for coordinate transfer.
This layered architecture is what enables TimeToAlign! to propagate annotations, transfer coordinates, and answer queries across arbitrarily many representations of the same musical content—the central promise of the model.

title: How to Work with Graphical Timelines
text:
This notebook demonstrates how to load and work with graphical timelines using the GraphicalLoader.
Graphical timelines map 2D pixel coordinates in images to 1D timeline coordinates. This is essential for: - Musical score analysis (staff systems as timelines) - Spectrograms (time on x-axis) - Graphical analytical diagrams (like Thoresen’s morphological analyses)



TimeAxisPath: Abstract path defining how 1D timeline coordinates map to 2D pixels. No image has a time axis until its path through the image is defined
ImageSource: Unified interface for images (files, PDFs)
GraphicalSegment: Source + path + timeline offset
GraphicalBundle: Collection of sources and segments
GraphicalLoader: Factory for building bundles


# Install dependencies if needed
# !pip install "timetoalign[graphical]"


import math
from pathlib import Path

from timetoalign.loader.graphical import GraphicalLoader




Load a musical score with multiple staff systems (horizontal lines).

# Create loader
loader = GraphicalLoader(metadata={"source": "Example Score"})

# Add the image
image_path = Path("path/to/score.png")

Load a multi-page analysis where each page is a separate image.

# Create loader for multi-page document
loader2 = GraphicalLoader(metadata={"source": "Multi-page Analysis"})

# Add images and segments

# Create timeline from bundle
# timeline = bundle.create_timeline(uid="score_timeline", name="Example Score")

# print(f"Timeline: {timeline.id}")

Draw paths and events on images.

# Draw all segment paths on the source image

# Save visualization

# Draw an event interval (e.g., a note or phrase)

# print(f"Drew event on {len(event_images)} images")




For non-horizontal timelines, use custom TimeAxisPath classes.

from timetoalign.loader.graphical import (  # noqa: E402
    DiagonalLinePath,
    ParametricPath,
    VerticalLinePath,
)

# Vertical timeline (top to bottom)
vertical_path = VerticalLinePath(x=400, y0=50, y1=600)
print(f"Vertical path length: {vertical_path.length} pixels")

# Diagonal timeline
diagonal_path = DiagonalLinePath(start=(100, 100), end=(700, 500))
print(f"Diagonal path length: {diagonal_path.length:.1f} pixels")

# Spiral timeline (parametric)
# r = a + b*t (Archimedean spiral)
a, b = 50, 10
spiral_path = ParametricPath(
    x_func=lambda t: 400 + (a + b * t) * math.cos(t),
    y_func=lambda t: 400 + (a + b * t) * math.sin(t),
    t_start=0,
    t_end=4 * math.pi,  # 2 full rotations
    samples=1000,
)
print(f"Spiral path length: {spiral_path.length:.1f} pixels")

Vertical path length: 550 pixels
Diagonal path length: 721.1 pixels
Spiral path length: 1424.1 pixels





A page of a score is read along its first accolade (system), then along the second, and so on. A PiecewisePath is such a path: consecutive pieces, each starting on the path where the ones before it end. Its numbers are the pieces’ own, so pieces of integers give exact answers.

from timetoalign.loader.graphical import (  # noqa: E402
    HorizontalLinePath,
    PiecewisePath,
    TimeAxisPath,
)

# Two accolades of a page, 490 and 400 pixels long
page_path = PiecewisePath(
    (
        HorizontalLinePath(x0=10, x1=500, y=100, tolerance=40),
        HorizontalLinePath(x0=20, x1=420, y=300, tolerance=40),
    )
)
print(f"Offsets: {page_path.offsets}, length: {page_path.length} pixels")
print(f"Coordinate 489 is at {page_path.to_2d(489)}, 490 at {page_path.to_2d(490)}")
print(f"Image point (120, 320) is at {page_path.from_2d(120, 320)}")
print(f"Image point (120, 200) is at {page_path.from_2d(120, 200)}")

Offsets: (0, 490), length: 890 pixels
Coordinate 489 is at (499, 100), 490 at (20, 300)
Image point (120, 320) is at 590
Image point (120, 200) is at None


The second piece starts at 490 on the path, so the point (120, 320), 100 pixels along it, is at 590; a point between the two strips is on no piece.
TimeAxisPath.from_boxes() makes the path of a page from the areas drawn on it, given in reading order: one horizontal piece per accolade, from its boxes’ least x to their greatest, at the middle of their y extent, with half that extent as tolerance. A box begins a new accolade when its left edge falls back by more than half the span of all left edges (or accolades= assigns the boxes). Below, three measures, the third on a second line.

from timetoalign import BoundingBox  # noqa: E402

measures = [
    BoundingBox.from_corners(100, 50, 300, 90, unit="pixels"),
    BoundingBox.from_corners(300, 52, 520, 95, unit="pixels"),
    BoundingBox.from_corners(90, 150, 400, 190, unit="pixels"),
]
measures_path = TimeAxisPath.from_boxes(measures)
for piece in measures_path.pieces:
    print(piece)
print(f"Offsets: {measures_path.offsets}, length: {measures_path.length} pixels")
print(f"The third measure lies on piece {measures_path.piece_of(measures[2])}")

HorizontalLinePath(x0=100, x1=520, y=Fraction(145, 2), tolerance=Fraction(45, 2))
HorizontalLinePath(x0=90, x1=400, y=170, tolerance=20)
Offsets: (0, 420), length: 730 pixels
The third measure lies on piece 1


The first piece spans x 100 to 520 (420 pixels) and y 50 to 95, whose middle is 145/2; the second spans x 90 to 400 (310 pixels), so the path is 730 pixels long. Pages built of such paths, with the areas as Box events, are the subject of How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes.



The graphical loader provides:

Flexible path definitions - Horizontal, vertical, diagonal, parametric curves, or several pieces in a row
Multiple image support - Single or multi-page analyses
Bidirectional conversion - Timeline ↔︎ Image coordinates
Visualization - Draw paths and events on images
Timeline integration - Convert bundles to DiscreteGraphicalTimeline

Next: See how01_thoresen_annotation_transfer.ipynb for the Thoresen alignment example using these tools.

title: How to Work with Graphical Timelines
text:
For non-horizontal timelines, use custom TimeAxisPath classes.

from timetoalign.loader.graphical import (  # noqa: E402
    DiagonalLinePath,
    ParametricPath,
    VerticalLinePath,
)

# Vertical timeline (top to bottom)
vertical_path = VerticalLinePath(x=400, y0=50, y1=600)
print(f"Vertical path length: {vertical_path.length} pixels")

# Diagonal timeline
diagonal_path = DiagonalLinePath(start=(100, 100), end=(700, 500))
print(f"Diagonal path length: {diagonal_path.length:.1f} pixels")

# Spiral timeline (parametric)
# r = a + b*t (Archimedean spiral)
a, b = 50, 10
spiral_path = ParametricPath(
    x_func=lambda t: 400 + (a + b * t) * math.cos(t),
    y_func=lambda t: 400 + (a + b * t) * math.sin(t),
    t_start=0,
    t_end=4 * math.pi,  # 2 full rotations
    samples=1000,
)
print(f"Spiral path length: {spiral_path.length:.1f} pixels")

title: How to Work with Graphical Timelines
text:
A page of a score is read along its first accolade (system), then along the second, and so on. A PiecewisePath is such a path: consecutive pieces, each starting on the path where the ones before it end. Its numbers are the pieces’ own, so pieces of integers give exact answers.

from timetoalign.loader.graphical import (  # noqa: E402
    HorizontalLinePath,
    PiecewisePath,
    TimeAxisPath,
)

# Two accolades of a page, 490 and 400 pixels long
page_path = PiecewisePath(
    (
        HorizontalLinePath(x0=10, x1=500, y=100, tolerance=40),
        HorizontalLinePath(x0=20, x1=420, y=300, tolerance=40),
    )
)
print(f"Offsets: {page_path.offsets}, length: {page_path.length} pixels")
print(f"Coordinate 489 is at {page_path.to_2d(489)}, 490 at {page_path.to_2d(490)}")
print(f"Image point (120, 320) is at {page_path.from_2d(120, 320)}")
print(f"Image point (120, 200) is at {page_path.from_2d(120, 200)}")

Offsets: (0, 490), length: 890 pixels
Coordinate 489 is at (499, 100), 490 at (20, 300)
Image point (120, 320) is at 590
Image point (120, 200) is at None


The second piece starts at 490 on the path, so the point (120, 320), 100 pixels along it, is at 590; a point between the two strips is on no piece.
TimeAxisPath.from_boxes() makes the path of a page from the areas drawn on it, given in reading order: one horizontal piece per accolade, from its boxes’ least x to their greatest, at the middle of their y extent, with half that extent as tolerance. A box begins a new accolade when its left edge falls back by more than half the span of all left edges (or accolades= assigns the boxes). Below, three measures, the third on a second line.

from timetoalign import BoundingBox  # noqa: E402

measures = [
    BoundingBox.from_corners(100, 50, 300, 90, unit="pixels"),
    BoundingBox.from_corners(300, 52, 520, 95, unit="pixels"),
    BoundingBox.from_corners(90, 150, 400, 190, unit="pixels"),
]
measures_path = TimeAxisPath.from_boxes(measures)
for piece in measures_path.pieces:
    print(piece)
print(f"Offsets: {measures_path.offsets}, length: {measures_path.length} pixels")
print(f"The third measure lies on piece {measures_path.piece_of(measures[2])}")

HorizontalLinePath(x0=100, x1=520, y=Fraction(145, 2), tolerance=Fraction(45, 2))
HorizontalLinePath(x0=90, x1=400, y=170, tolerance=20)
Offsets: (0, 420), length: 730 pixels
The third measure lies on piece 1


The first piece spans x 100 to 520 (420 pixels) and y 50 to 95, whose middle is 145/2; the second spans x 90 to 400 (310 pixels), so the path is 730 pixels long. Pages built of such paths, with the areas as Box events, are the subject of How to Represent Areas of Page Images as Boxes.

title: How to Load the Vienna 4x22 Corpus
text:
This guide demonstrates how to load score-to-performance alignment data from the Vienna 4x22 Corpus using the MatchfileLoader.


The full 4x22 Vienna Corpus (Grachten & Widmer, 2012) contains four classical piano pieces, each performed by 22 pianists, yielding 88 score-to-performance alignments in the .match file format. Each .match file encodes three things simultaneously:

A score representation (note identities, pitch, metrical position, duration in quarter beats).
A performance representation (MIDI pitch, onset/offset in ticks, velocity).
An alignment linking each score note to its performed counterpart (or marking it as a deletion when the pianist omitted it).

What we demonstrate here is a 1x22 sample — one piece (Chopin Etude Op. 10 No. 3 in E major) performed by all 22 pianists. This is one quarter of the full dataset, and it is the specimen that comes with the TimeToAlign! test suite. The workflow generalises straightforwardly to the remaining three pieces.
What you will learn:

Load all 22 .match files through a single MatchfileLoader
Inspect the resulting timelines and their TimeStamps
Assemble the AlignmentBundle and query its MatchClaims
Obtain MatchStamps — the cross-timeline coordinate cross-section





import warnings

from timetoalign import MatchfileLoader
from timetoalign.alignment import MatchGraph
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

DATA_DIR = ensure_data("vienna_1x22")

match_files = sorted(DATA_DIR.glob("*.match"))
len(match_files)

22


22 .match files — one per pianist — all sharing the same score (Chopin Op. 10 No. 3).




The MatchfileLoader processes all .match files for a given piece through a single instance. It builds a shared score timeline from the first file and verifies each subsequent file against it. Incompatible files are rejected with a warning; compatible files contribute their performance timeline and match claims.

loader = MatchfileLoader()
# partitura warns on the corpus's composite quarter durations, which it cannot
# express symbolically. That is a note from the score parser about its own
# symbolic-duration vocabulary, not a rejected file, so it is silenced here.
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.filterwarnings(
        "ignore",
        message=r"Quarter duration .*",
        category=UserWarning,
        module=r"partitura\.utils\.music",
    )
    loader.load(*match_files)
loader

23 timelines: 1 score + 22 performances. Each performance has a slightly different event count because some pianists omit notes (deletions).
Individual timelines are accessed by role shorthand. The stored IDs lead with the role before an ID the loader mints from the files it read: the score’s is score:clt_…, each performance’s perf:dlt_…. The shorthand (score, or perf: and a performance’s number) remains convenient for lookup:

score = loader.create_timeline(uid="score")

The score is a ContinuousLogicalTimeline in quarter-beat coordinates, carrying two conversion maps: raw_quarters (a ShiftMap for anacrusis offset) and quarters_to_divs (a ScalarMap to MIDI divisions).

A TimeStamp is the primary interface for querying what happens at a given coordinate on a timeline. It returns the coordinate itself plus all conversion map results in a single cross-section.

The bundle keeps its MatchClaims in one MatchClaim table, bundle.match_claim_table; get_match_claims() reads them back as MatchClaim objects. Each claim connects a score event to a performance event (synchronous match) or records a deletion (non-synchronous NOMATCH).

from timetoalign import MatchfileLoader
from timetoalign.alignment import MatchGraph

# Load
loader = MatchfileLoader()
loader.load(*sorted(data_dir.glob("*.match")))

# Inspect timelines and their TimeStamps
score = loader.create_timeline(uid="score")
score.get_timestamp(10.0)  # quarters + raw + divs

# Assemble the bundle
bundle = loader.create_bundle()

# Query claims and build MatchStamps
claims = bundle.get_match_claims()
mg = MatchGraph(claims=[c for c in claims if c.is_synchronous])
stamps = mg.get_stamps()  # full cross-section across all timelines

title: How to Load Musical Themes Aligned to Recordings (MTD)
text:
The Musical Theme Dataset (MTD; Zalkow, Balke, Arifi-Müller and Müller, TISMIR 2020, doi:10.5334/tismir.68) takes 2,067 themes from Barlow and Morgenstern’s A Dictionary of Musical Themes. Each theme is sixteen files: its metadata, an excerpt of a commercial recording of its movement, an alignment of the excerpt with an encoding of the theme, and four encodings of the theme as MIDI files, note lists, PDFs, a Sibelius file and a MusicXML file. This guide reads one movement with MtdLoader:

the CD track, a seconds timeline holding each theme’s excerpt as a child;
per theme, one timeline per file, each naming its file and what it was made from;
per theme, four TimelineGroups, one per encoding;
MTD’s alignment as MatchClaims;

and writes the AlignmentBundle as a TimeToShare manifest.


Install the library with pip install timetoalign. The example data is a sample of four themes in the layout of the MTD archive, MTD_sample.zip, fetched by the test-data helper; the full MTD_1.0.0.zip is read the same way, in place, without extracting it. The files that MTD’s licence does not cover (the excerpts, the EDM encodings, the MusicXML files) are stand-ins shaped like MTD’s own; an excerpt is silence as long as MTD’s.
Three helpers show what the loader made: files one row per timeline of a theme, members one row per member of a theme’s groups, and claims one row per MatchClaim from a timeline.

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from timetoshare import loads, validate

from timetoalign import AlignmentBundle, MatchClaim, MtdLoader
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

ARCHIVE = ensure_data("mtd") / "MTD_sample.zip"


def label(timeline, theme):
    """A timeline's name without its theme: ``SCORE MIDI``, the excerpt ``excerpt``."""
    if timeline.name == f"Theme {theme}":
        return "excerpt"
    return timeline.name.removeprefix(f"{theme}, ")


def theme_timelines(bundle, theme):
    """The excerpt and the file timelines of *theme*, as the bundle holds them."""
    timelines = [bundle.get_timeline(uid) for uid in bundle.timeline_ids]
    children = {uid for timeline in timelines for uid in timeline.list_children()}
    excerpt = next(t for t in timelines if t.name == f"Theme {theme}")
    roots = [
        t for t in timelines if t.id not in children and t.name.startswith(f"{theme}, ")
    ]
    return [excerpt, *roots]


def files(bundle, theme):
    """One row per timeline of *theme*: its axis, length, file and source."""
    timelines = theme_timelines(bundle, theme)
    labels = {f"#{t.id}": label(t, theme) for t in timelines}
    rows = []
    for timeline in timelines:
        statements = timeline.statements
        (item,) = statements["lrmoo:R7i_is_exemplified_by"]
        sources = statements.get("dcterms:source", [])
        rows.append(
            {
                "timeline": label(timeline, theme),
                "unit": timeline.unit.value,
                "length": (
                    "unknown" if timeline.length is None else str(timeline.length)
                ),
                "notes": len(timeline.get_events()),
                "file": item["label"],
                "derived from": ", ".join(labels[s["id"]] for s in sources),
                "children": ", ".join(
                    label(timeline.get_child(uid), theme)
                    for uid in timeline.list_children()
                ),
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def members(bundle, theme):
    """One row per member of *theme*'s groups: the group, the member, its length."""
    rows = []
    for group_id in bundle.group_ids:
        group = bundle.get_group(group_id)
        if not group.name.startswith(f"{theme}, "):
            continue
        for uid in group.timeline_ids:
            member = group.get_timeline(uid)
            rows.append(
                {
                    "group": group.name.removeprefix(f"{theme}, "),
                    "member": label(member, theme),
                    "length": (
                        "unknown" if member.length is None else str(member.length)
                    ),
                }
            )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def claims(field, timeline):
    """One row per MatchClaim from *timeline*: the note, the excerpt's side."""
    events = timeline.get_events().table
    pitches = dict(
        zip(events.column("id").to_pylist(), events.column("pitch").to_pylist())
    )
    return pd.DataFrame(
        [
            {
                "onset (ticks)": claim.start_anchor.coordinate_a.value,
                "MIDI pitch": pitches[claim.event_a_id],
                "excerpt side": claim.event_b_id,
                "excerpt (seconds)": claim.start_anchor.coordinate_b.value,
                "claim type": claim.claim_type.value,
            }
            for claim in field
            if claim.timeline_a_id == timeline.id
        ]
    )




A movement is named as MTD names it, <ComposerID>_<WorkID>; the first movement of Beethoven’s Piano Sonata Op. 2 No. 1 is Beethoven_Op002No1-01. The loader reads every theme’s metadata to find the movement’s themes, then only their files. Themes can also be named by their MTD IDs, themes=["MTD0807"]; without either, every theme is read.

The first theme, B689 in Barlow and Morgenstern, is fourteen timelines: the excerpt and one per file of its four encodings. A MIDI file is the ticks timeline the MIDI loader builds of it, on the file’s own axis, with what the file states of that axis: a C-Map to quarters (480 ticks per quarter here), a C-Map to seconds from its tempo map, and a measure map of its bars; the MusicXML file and the Sibelius file are quarters timelines, a note list (CSV) and the excerpt seconds timelines, a PDF a points timeline. Each names its file in the archive (lrmoo:R7i_is_exemplified_by) and, where MTD’s paper states that the file was made from another, that file’s timeline (dcterms:source): the SCORE exports derive from the Sibelius file, EDM-corr’s MIDI file from EDM-orig’s, each EDM encoding’s note list and PDF from its MIDI file, and EDM-alig’s files from EDM-corr’s MIDI file.
A timeline is as long as its file states: a MIDI file its end of track (its timeline is locked at that length), the MusicXML file the end of its last bar, the excerpt its seconds. A note list, a PDF and the Sibelius file state no end: their length is unknown (length is None). Only the MIDI files’ timelines hold notes.

title: How to Load Tabular Data
text:
The fastest way to get music data into TimeToAlign! is through tabular loaders. If your data is in CSV or TSV format, you’re just 3 lines of code away from analysis.
What you’ll learn: - Load music annotations from TSV/CSV files - Access event counts, coordinate ranges, and metadata - Create timelines from loaded data - Write a custom loader that maps your columns to event fields - Promote selected columns to typed fields with column_specs - Reach nested JSON columns with Field
Time: 15 minutes
This is the gentle introduction. For the full column-to-field mechanism — the Step-1 resolution chain, composite columns, and Step-2 field promotion — see the in-depth CSV/TSV how-to.


from timetoalign.loader.tabular import TsvLoader

loader = TsvLoader()
loader.load("beethoven.notes.tsv")

df = loader.events.to_dataframe()    # Get as DataFrame
timeline = loader.create_timeline()  # Create Timeline




from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

BEETHOVEN = ensure_data("score") / "beethoven_woo71"
THORESEN = ensure_data("thoresen")

# Available files
{
    "Beethoven files": [f.name for f in BEETHOVEN.glob("WoO71.*.tsv")],
    "Thoresen files": [f.name for f in THORESEN.glob("*.tsv")],
}

{'Beethoven files': ['WoO71.chords.tsv',
  'WoO71.measures.tsv',
  'WoO71.notes.tsv'],
 'Thoresen files': ['thoresen_test_h.tsv', 'thoresen_test.tsv']}





TsvLoader is the generic starting point for a TSV whose columns you control. Declare the coordinate columns and promote the values you want as typed fields. For a standard ms3 score export, use the score Ms3Loader instead; it understands its notes, measures, chords, and harmonies facets.
The file gives each note’s length twice: duration_qb in quarters, written as a decimal (a twelfth as 0.08333333333333333), and duration in whole notes, written as an exact ratio (1/48). On an exact (Fraction) axis the loader completes each end as start + duration exactly, and for a note starting at 529/12 the sum with that decimal’s binary value needs a numerator wider than the 64 bits an exact value is stored in, so a duration_column = "duration_qb" is refused rather than guessed back into a ratio. Complete the ends from the exact duration column instead, with a ComputedField as below, or declare coordinate_type = NumberType.float for a file that gives its durations only as decimals.

from fractions import Fraction  # noqa: E402

import pyarrow as pa  # noqa: E402

from timetoalign.core import NumberType, RedundantNumberField, TimeUnit  # noqa: E402
from timetoalign.loader import ComputedField  # noqa: E402
from timetoalign.loader.tabular import TsvLoader  # noqa: E402


def end_in_quarters(table: pa.Table) -> pa.Array:
    """A note's end in quarters: its start plus four times its whole-note duration."""
    starts = table["quarterbeats"].to_pylist()
    wholes = table["duration"].to_pylist()
    # Written as "n/d" text, which the loader reads exactly.
    return pa.array(
        [
            None if s is None else str(Fraction(s) + 4 * Fraction(w))
            for s, w in zip(starts, wholes)
        ]
    )


class BeethovenNotesLoader(TsvLoader):
    """Generic TSV configuration for the coordinate and pitch columns used here."""

    start_column = "quarterbeats"
    end_column = ComputedField("end", expr=end_in_quarters)
    _default_unit = TimeUnit.quarters
    coordinate_type = NumberType.fraction
    # The whole-note column keeps its exact values under its own name, so it
    # is not read as the events' duration, which is in quarters.
    column_specs = {
        "duration": RedundantNumberField(name="duration_whole"),
        "midi": int,
        "staff": int,
        "voice": int,
    }


loader = BeethovenNotesLoader()
loader.load(BEETHOVEN / "WoO71.notes.tsv")

f"{len(loader.events):,} notes loaded"

'4,753 notes loaded'

from timetoalign.loader.tabular import TsvLoader  # noqa: E402


class ThoresenLoader(TsvLoader):
    """Minimal loader — maps the core event fields."""

    id_column = "event_id"
    start_column = "start_time_sec"
    duration_column = "duration_sec"
    event_type_column = "event_type"
    name_column = "description"

    _default_unit = TimeUnit.seconds
    coordinate_type = NumberType.float


thoresen = ThoresenLoader()
thoresen.load(THORESEN / "thoresen_test.tsv")
thoresen.events.to_dataframe()

When a property column should become a typed field, name it in column_specs. The keys are source-column names; the values are anything the loader can resolve to a field — a bare Python type (int / float / str) is the simplest form. Here we give two extra columns explicit types:

class ThoresenTypedLoader(TsvLoader):
    """Selected columns promoted to typed fields."""

    id_column = "event_id"
    start_column = "start_time_sec"
    duration_column = "duration_sec"
    event_type_column = "event_type"
    name_column = "description"

    _default_unit = TimeUnit.seconds
    coordinate_type = NumberType.float

    # Promote these source columns to typed fields.
    column_specs = {
        "image_filename": str,
        "graphical_element_id": str,
    }


typed = ThoresenTypedLoader()
typed.load(THORESEN / "thoresen_test.tsv")

That is the entire idea: columns are a source artefact; fields are a TimeToAlign! artefact. column_specs is the bridge. A bare type is the gentlest entry — the in-depth CSV/TSV how-to covers the full resolution chain (composite columns, semantic pitch/id fields, and the Step-2 field_specs promotion stage) for richer formats.




The Thoresen data has a rect_coords_json column containing pixel coordinates as JSON:
{"x": 10, "y": 90, "width": 148, "height": 55}
Use Field("column", "nested_field") to point a coordinate attribute straight at a nested value. TimeToAlign! parses the JSON automatically. ComputedField lets you derive a coordinate from a small formula over those nested values:

from timetoalign.loader import Field  # noqa: E402


class ThoresenGraphicalLoader(TsvLoader):
    """Loader using PIXEL coordinates from a nested JSON column."""

    # Nested fields are addressed directly; JSON is parsed automatically.
    start_column = Field("rect_coords_json", "x")
    end_column = ComputedField(
        "end", formula="rect_coords_json.x + rect_coords_json.width"
    )

    _default_unit = TimeUnit.pixels
    coordinate_type = NumberType.float
    default_event_type = "Rectangle"


graphical = ThoresenGraphicalLoader()
graphical.load(THORESEN / "thoresen_test.tsv")

{
    "unit": str(graphical.unit),
    "coordinate_range": graphical.events.coordinate_range(),
}

title: How to Load Tabular Data
text:
TsvLoader is the generic starting point for a TSV whose columns you control. Declare the coordinate columns and promote the values you want as typed fields. For a standard ms3 score export, use the score Ms3Loader instead; it understands its notes, measures, chords, and harmonies facets.
The file gives each note’s length twice: duration_qb in quarters, written as a decimal (a twelfth as 0.08333333333333333), and duration in whole notes, written as an exact ratio (1/48). On an exact (Fraction) axis the loader completes each end as start + duration exactly, and for a note starting at 529/12 the sum with that decimal’s binary value needs a numerator wider than the 64 bits an exact value is stored in, so a duration_column = "duration_qb" is refused rather than guessed back into a ratio. Complete the ends from the exact duration column instead, with a ComputedField as below, or declare coordinate_type = NumberType.float for a file that gives its durations only as decimals.

from fractions import Fraction  # noqa: E402

import pyarrow as pa  # noqa: E402

from timetoalign.core import NumberType, RedundantNumberField, TimeUnit  # noqa: E402
from timetoalign.loader import ComputedField  # noqa: E402
from timetoalign.loader.tabular import TsvLoader  # noqa: E402


def end_in_quarters(table: pa.Table) -> pa.Array:
    """A note's end in quarters: its start plus four times its whole-note duration."""
    starts = table["quarterbeats"].to_pylist()
    wholes = table["duration"].to_pylist()
    # Written as "n/d" text, which the loader reads exactly.
    return pa.array(
        [
            None if s is None else str(Fraction(s) + 4 * Fraction(w))
            for s, w in zip(starts, wholes)
        ]
    )


class BeethovenNotesLoader(TsvLoader):
    """Generic TSV configuration for the coordinate and pitch columns used here."""

    start_column = "quarterbeats"
    end_column = ComputedField("end", expr=end_in_quarters)
    _default_unit = TimeUnit.quarters
    coordinate_type = NumberType.fraction
    # The whole-note column keeps its exact values under its own name, so it
    # is not read as the events' duration, which is in quarters.
    column_specs = {
        "duration": RedundantNumberField(name="duration_whole"),
        "midi": int,
        "staff": int,
        "voice": int,
    }


loader = BeethovenNotesLoader()
loader.load(BEETHOVEN / "WoO71.notes.tsv")

f"{len(loader.events):,} notes loaded"

'4,753 notes loaded'

from timetoalign.loader.tabular import TsvLoader  # noqa: E402


class ThoresenLoader(TsvLoader):
    """Minimal loader — maps the core event fields."""

    id_column = "event_id"
    start_column = "start_time_sec"
    duration_column = "duration_sec"
    event_type_column = "event_type"
    name_column = "description"

    _default_unit = TimeUnit.seconds
    coordinate_type = NumberType.float


thoresen = ThoresenLoader()
thoresen.load(THORESEN / "thoresen_test.tsv")
thoresen.events.to_dataframe()

title: How to Load Tabular Data
text:
The Thoresen data has a rect_coords_json column containing pixel coordinates as JSON:
{"x": 10, "y": 90, "width": 148, "height": 55}
Use Field("column", "nested_field") to point a coordinate attribute straight at a nested value. TimeToAlign! parses the JSON automatically. ComputedField lets you derive a coordinate from a small formula over those nested values:

from timetoalign.loader import Field  # noqa: E402


class ThoresenGraphicalLoader(TsvLoader):
    """Loader using PIXEL coordinates from a nested JSON column."""

    # Nested fields are addressed directly; JSON is parsed automatically.
    start_column = Field("rect_coords_json", "x")
    end_column = ComputedField(
        "end", formula="rect_coords_json.x + rect_coords_json.width"
    )

    _default_unit = TimeUnit.pixels
    coordinate_type = NumberType.float
    default_event_type = "Rectangle"


graphical = ThoresenGraphicalLoader()
graphical.load(THORESEN / "thoresen_test.tsv")

{
    "unit": str(graphical.unit),
    "coordinate_range": graphical.events.coordinate_range(),
}

When your data carries events from multiple sources (images, pages, tracks), pass group_by to create_timeline() to split the events into one child timeline per unique value. The Thoresen data has events from five different image files:

title: How to Load Tabular Data
text:
Goal
How




Load an ms3 score TSV
Ms3Loader() + loader.load(path)


Map your own columns
Subclass TsvLoader / CsvLoader, set start_column etc.


Promote a column to a typed field
Name it in column_specs ({"col": int})


Reach a nested JSON value
Field("column", "nested") as a coordinate attribute


Derive a coordinate
ComputedField("end", formula="...")


Split into child timelines
create_timeline(loader, group_by="column")



from timetoalign.loader.tabular import TsvLoader

class MyLoader(TsvLoader):
    start_column = "onset"
    duration_column = "dur"
    column_specs = {"pitch": int, "velocity": int}

Key Takeaway: Tabular loaders map CSV/TSV columns to TimeToAlign! events declaratively. Unnamed columns ride along as property columns; column_specs promotes the ones you want as typed fields; Field reaches nested JSON. For the full column-to-field mechanism — composite columns, semantic field types, and Step-2 promotion — continue to the in-depth CSV/TSV how-to.

title: How to Load an Audio-to-Score Alignment Corpus and Compare Performances
text:
A Performance Precision specimen bundles one symbolic score with several recorded performances of it, plus the audio-to-score alignments that connect them. This guide loads such a specimen in a single call and arrives at the question the corpus was built to answer: how do different pianists shape the same piece in time?
The specimen here is Chopin’s Nocturne in E♭ major, Op. 9 No. 2 — a .solo score, a Verovio timemap giving each measure’s position in quarter notes, and an Alignments/ directory holding three alignment files (note, bar, beat) for each of seven recordings. By the end we will read, for one shared score position, the seven different moments at which each pianist played it.
The arc:

Load the whole specimen in one call.
Inspect the measure structure recovered from the timemap.
Read the score Timeline (in quarters) and see how a measure+offset label resolves.
Read the per-performer Timelines (in seconds).
Inspect the MatchClaims, tagged by granularity.
Compare the performers’ timing through the AlignmentBundle.




from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from fractions import Fraction

import pandas as pd

from timetoalign.core import EnharmonicPitch
from timetoalign.loader.alignment import PerformancePrecisionLoader
from timetoalign.loader.tabular.solo import SoloLoader
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

SPECIMEN_DIR = ensure_data("performance_precision")
SOLO_FILE = SPECIMEN_DIR / "Chopin Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2.solo"




PerformancePrecisionLoader ingests the whole directory — the .solo score, the Verovio timemap, and every per-performer alignment file — through the standard two-phase loader pattern. from_file() is the one-line form.

loader = PerformancePrecisionLoader.from_file(SPECIMEN_DIR)
loader






Sources
3 file(s): Chopin Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2.solo, Chopin Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2.json, Alignments


Events
0


Try
create_timeline(), create_timelines(), create_bundle()





Seven recordings, and a few thousand MatchClaims linking the score to them. Everything below reads from this single loaded object.




The Verovio timemap records each measure’s absolute position in quarter notes. The loader walks it into a MetricMap — a ConversionMap from a quarter position to its measure count — and exposes it directly:

metric_map = loader.metric_map
metric_map

MetricMap(n_measures=38, total_length=425/2)


Thirty-eight measures spanning 212.5 quarters. The companion .meter file is deliberately left unread: it encodes only meter changes (four rows across the whole piece), so it cannot by itself bound the final measure. The timemap’s terminal position supplies that bound, which is why it is preferred here.
The paired MetricalPositionMap is a CombinationMap carrying both directions of the measure↔︎quarter relationship. quarters_at(mc, beat) goes from a metrical position to a quarter coordinate; mn_at(quarters) returns the measure-number label at a quarter position:

metrical_position_map = loader.metrical_position_map

{
    "downbeat of MC 2 (quarters)": metrical_position_map.quarters_at(2),
    "downbeat of MC 3 (quarters)": metrical_position_map.quarters_at(3),
    "measure label at quarter 0.0": metrical_position_map.mn_at(0.0),
    "measure label at quarter 7.0": metrical_position_map.mn_at(7.0),
}

{'downbeat of MC 2 (quarters)': Fraction(1, 2),
 'downbeat of MC 3 (quarters)': Fraction(13, 2),
 'measure label at quarter 0.0': '1',
 'measure label at quarter 7.0': '3'}






The score is a logical Timeline measured in quarters. It holds every note of the .solo score, each placed at its absolute quarter position. The Projections the alignment’s note claims stand on are not here yet: they are added when the bundle is created (§5). The loader asks for it by its role, "score"; its stored ID is the role followed by a minted one, score:clt_…, seeded from the specimen’s files.

score_tl = loader.create_timeline(uid="score")
score_tl

ContinuousLogicalTimeline[score:clt_380f83wpy32ig] (2494 events, 1 cmaps)
                      0 _______________________________ 212.5 quarters




Both the .solo score and the alignment files write score positions as "<measure>+<offset>", where the offset is given in whole notes. The resolver is one line of arithmetic — measure_start + offset × 4 (the × 4 converts whole notes to quarters) — with one wrinkle: measure 0 is the anacrusis (the pickup), whose offsets are measured back from a virtual full-bar downbeat preceding the first sounding note. The very first note of the piece, labelled 0+11/8, therefore lands exactly on quarter 0:

first_three = score_tl.get_events().table.slice(0, 3).to_pandas()
first_three[["id", "start"]]

A TimeStamp is the primary way to query the score timeline at a coordinate — here the downbeat of the first full measure, half a quarter in:

score_tl.get_timestamp(Fraction(1, 2))

TimeStamp

cmap



Try: ts.get_coordinate_for(<tl_id>), ts.get_unit(<unit>), ts.get_conversion_for(<key>)





The score timeline carries pitch as the raw MIDI pitch integer that the .solo file recorded — faithful to the source, which notes no accidental spelling. When a typed pitch field is wanted, it lives on a freshly composed SoloLoader reading the same .solo file. There the field materialises as EnharmonicPitch scalars, and the canonical glyphs ♯/♭ render in their labels:

solo = SoloLoader.from_file(SOLO_FILE)
pitch_field = solo.events.get_field(EnharmonicPitch)
{"first five pitches": [pitch_field[i] for i in range(5)]}

{'first five pitches': [EP(A♯/B♭4),
  EP(A♯/B♭4),
  EP(D♯/E♭2),
  EP(G5),
  EP(D♯/E♭2)]}


Because .solo records only the MIDI pitch number, an enharmonic pair such as G♯3 and A♭3 both surface as the same number — the field reports what was represented, not what could be inferred.





Each recording is a physical Timeline measured in seconds, one Note per aligned note onset, and it gains no Projection with the bundle (§5). Each is named by its performer key, by which the loader also finds it; its stored ID is minted, perf:cpt_…. The Ashkenazy recording is "Chopin_Ashkenazy":

performer_keys = [tl.name for tl in loader.create_timelines() if tl is not score_tl]
performer_keys

['Chopin_Ashkenazy',
 'Chopin_Barenboim',
 'Chopin_Freire',
 'Chopin_Horowitz',
 'Chopin_Pollini',
 'Chopin_Rachmaninoff',
 'Chopin_Rubinstein']



ashkenazy = loader.create_timeline(uid="Chopin_Ashkenazy")
ashkenazy

ContinuousPhysicalTimeline[perf:cpt_09wbt9uiqwvz1] (480 events)
                      0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 209.1 seconds


A score position is in quarters; a performance position is in seconds. The alignment is what relates the two, and that is carried by the MatchClaims.




The AlignmentBundle assembles the loaded data: the score in its own group, each performance standalone, and every alignment row as a cross-group MatchClaim.

bundle = loader.create_bundle()
bundle

AlignmentBundle[bundle_3g5rm783z3jw7]

  TimelineGroup[group_1nxld73ojhzgn] (1 timelines)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ContinuousLogicalTimeline[score:clt_380f83wpy32ig] (5933 events, 1 cmaps)  │
  │                       0 ___________________________________ 212.5 quarters │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Standalone timelines (7):
    Chopin_As...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 209.1 seconds (480 ev)
    Chopin_Ba...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 231.9 seconds (480 ev)
    Chopin_Fr...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 216.2 seconds (480 ev)
    ... (1 more)
    Chopin_Po...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 208.7 seconds (480 ev)
    Chopin_Ra...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 256.9 seconds (480 ev)
    Chopin_Ru...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 227.1 seconds (480 ev)

  MatchClaims: 6769


A MatchClaim joins two events. An alignment row names its score position by a measure+offset label, which may stand for several notes of a chord, so on a note row the score side is a Projection: an event added to the score timeline at the label’s position when create_bundle() states the claims, naming the performer’s Note it stands for (projection_of). The score shown in §3 held Notes only and holds these Projections from here on. An unmatched note row is a NOMATCH stated from its score position, so its score side is a Projection of no event, one per position. A bar or beat row has no note on either side: both sides are the sentinel CHUNK, whose coordinates the claim’s anchor states, and no Projection is added for them, so the recordings hold none:

{
    "score Notes": len(score_tl.get_events(event_type="Note")),
    "score Projections": len(score_tl.get_events(event_type="Projection")),
    "Ashkenazy Projections": len(ashkenazy.get_events(event_type="Projection")),
}

{'score Notes': 2494, 'score Projections': 3439, 'Ashkenazy Projections': 0}


Each recording was aligned at three granularities — note, bar, and beat — and the loader records which one produced each claim in its Provenance: the claim’s provenance.note names the granularity after the tool. Counting the claims for one performer shows the shape of a single recording’s alignment. A NOMATCH claim names the score event left unmatched and the sentinel opposite it; it holds no coordinate, so it prints as its two timelines and the [NOMATCH] badge:

    quarters = float(metrical_position_map.quarters_at(mc))
    onset_stamp = bundle.get_matchstamp_at(quarters, score_tl.id)
    row = {"score (quarters)": quarters}
    for key in performer_keys:
        perf_id = loader.create_timeline(uid=key).id
        coord = onset_stamp.coordinates.get(perf_id)
        row[key.replace("Chopin_", "")] = (
            round(float(coord), 3) if coord is not None else None
        )
    rows.append(row)

Each column is one pianist’s arrival times in seconds; each row is a shared score position. The gaps between successive rows within a column are the inter-downbeat durations — read down a column and the performer’s local tempo is visible, read across a row and the performers’ differing placements of the same beat stand side by side. The same procedure at the beat or note granularity yields a finer-grained timing profile, all from the one AlignmentBundle.

title: How to Load an Audio-to-Score Alignment Corpus and Compare Performances
text:
The Verovio timemap records each measure’s absolute position in quarter notes. The loader walks it into a MetricMap — a ConversionMap from a quarter position to its measure count — and exposes it directly:

metric_map = loader.metric_map
metric_map

MetricMap(n_measures=38, total_length=425/2)


Thirty-eight measures spanning 212.5 quarters. The companion .meter file is deliberately left unread: it encodes only meter changes (four rows across the whole piece), so it cannot by itself bound the final measure. The timemap’s terminal position supplies that bound, which is why it is preferred here.
The paired MetricalPositionMap is a CombinationMap carrying both directions of the measure↔︎quarter relationship. quarters_at(mc, beat) goes from a metrical position to a quarter coordinate; mn_at(quarters) returns the measure-number label at a quarter position:

metrical_position_map = loader.metrical_position_map

{
    "downbeat of MC 2 (quarters)": metrical_position_map.quarters_at(2),
    "downbeat of MC 3 (quarters)": metrical_position_map.quarters_at(3),
    "measure label at quarter 0.0": metrical_position_map.mn_at(0.0),
    "measure label at quarter 7.0": metrical_position_map.mn_at(7.0),
}

{'downbeat of MC 2 (quarters)': Fraction(1, 2),
 'downbeat of MC 3 (quarters)': Fraction(13, 2),
 'measure label at quarter 0.0': '1',
 'measure label at quarter 7.0': '3'}

title: How to Load an Audio-to-Score Alignment Corpus and Compare Performances
text:
The score is a logical Timeline measured in quarters. It holds every note of the .solo score, each placed at its absolute quarter position. The Projections the alignment’s note claims stand on are not here yet: they are added when the bundle is created (§5). The loader asks for it by its role, "score"; its stored ID is the role followed by a minted one, score:clt_…, seeded from the specimen’s files.

score_tl = loader.create_timeline(uid="score")
score_tl

ContinuousLogicalTimeline[score:clt_380f83wpy32ig] (2494 events, 1 cmaps)
                      0 _______________________________ 212.5 quarters




Both the .solo score and the alignment files write score positions as "<measure>+<offset>", where the offset is given in whole notes. The resolver is one line of arithmetic — measure_start + offset × 4 (the × 4 converts whole notes to quarters) — with one wrinkle: measure 0 is the anacrusis (the pickup), whose offsets are measured back from a virtual full-bar downbeat preceding the first sounding note. The very first note of the piece, labelled 0+11/8, therefore lands exactly on quarter 0:

first_three = score_tl.get_events().table.slice(0, 3).to_pandas()
first_three[["id", "start"]]

The score timeline carries pitch as the raw MIDI pitch integer that the .solo file recorded — faithful to the source, which notes no accidental spelling. When a typed pitch field is wanted, it lives on a freshly composed SoloLoader reading the same .solo file. There the field materialises as EnharmonicPitch scalars, and the canonical glyphs ♯/♭ render in their labels:

solo = SoloLoader.from_file(SOLO_FILE)
pitch_field = solo.events.get_field(EnharmonicPitch)
{"first five pitches": [pitch_field[i] for i in range(5)]}

{'first five pitches': [EP(A♯/B♭4),
  EP(A♯/B♭4),
  EP(D♯/E♭2),
  EP(G5),
  EP(D♯/E♭2)]}


Because .solo records only the MIDI pitch number, an enharmonic pair such as G♯3 and A♭3 both surface as the same number — the field reports what was represented, not what could be inferred.

title: How to Load an Audio-to-Score Alignment Corpus and Compare Performances
text:
Each recording is a physical Timeline measured in seconds, one Note per aligned note onset, and it gains no Projection with the bundle (§5). Each is named by its performer key, by which the loader also finds it; its stored ID is minted, perf:cpt_…. The Ashkenazy recording is "Chopin_Ashkenazy":

performer_keys = [tl.name for tl in loader.create_timelines() if tl is not score_tl]
performer_keys

['Chopin_Ashkenazy',
 'Chopin_Barenboim',
 'Chopin_Freire',
 'Chopin_Horowitz',
 'Chopin_Pollini',
 'Chopin_Rachmaninoff',
 'Chopin_Rubinstein']



ashkenazy = loader.create_timeline(uid="Chopin_Ashkenazy")
ashkenazy

ContinuousPhysicalTimeline[perf:cpt_09wbt9uiqwvz1] (480 events)

A score position is in quarters; a performance position is in seconds. The alignment is what relates the two, and that is carried by the MatchClaims.

title: How to Load an Audio-to-Score Alignment Corpus and Compare Performances
text:
The AlignmentBundle assembles the loaded data: the score in its own group, each performance standalone, and every alignment row as a cross-group MatchClaim.

bundle = loader.create_bundle()
bundle

AlignmentBundle[bundle_3g5rm783z3jw7]

  TimelineGroup[group_1nxld73ojhzgn] (1 timelines)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ContinuousLogicalTimeline[score:clt_380f83wpy32ig] (5933 events, 1 cmaps)  │
  │                       0 ___________________________________ 212.5 quarters │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Standalone timelines (7):
    Chopin_As...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 209.1 seconds (480 ev)
    Chopin_Ba...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 231.9 seconds (480 ev)
    Chopin_Fr...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 216.2 seconds (480 ev)
    ... (1 more)
    Chopin_Po...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 208.7 seconds (480 ev)
    Chopin_Ra...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 256.9 seconds (480 ev)
    Chopin_Ru...     0 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 227.1 seconds (480 ev)

  MatchClaims: 6769


A MatchClaim joins two events. An alignment row names its score position by a measure+offset label, which may stand for several notes of a chord, so on a note row the score side is a Projection: an event added to the score timeline at the label’s position when create_bundle() states the claims, naming the performer’s Note it stands for (projection_of). The score shown in §3 held Notes only and holds these Projections from here on. An unmatched note row is a NOMATCH stated from its score position, so its score side is a Projection of no event, one per position. A bar or beat row has no note on either side: both sides are the sentinel CHUNK, whose coordinates the claim’s anchor states, and no Projection is added for them, so the recordings hold none:

{
    "score Notes": len(score_tl.get_events(event_type="Note")),
    "score Projections": len(score_tl.get_events(event_type="Projection")),
    "Ashkenazy Projections": len(ashkenazy.get_events(event_type="Projection")),
}

{'score Notes': 2494, 'score Projections': 3439, 'Ashkenazy Projections': 0}


Each recording was aligned at three granularities — note, bar, and beat — and the loader records which one produced each claim in its Provenance: the claim’s provenance.note names the granularity after the tool. Counting the claims for one performer shows the shape of a single recording’s alignment. A NOMATCH claim names the score event left unmatched and the sentinel opposite it; it holds no coordinate, so it prints as its two timelines and the [NOMATCH] badge:

bundle.get_match_claims()

title: How to Load an Audio-to-Score Alignment Corpus and Compare Performances
text:
The corpus exists to compare how performers shape the same music in time. The AlignmentBundle answers this directly: given one score coordinate, get_matchstamp_at returns the corresponding coordinate on every connected timeline. A MatchStamp at the first full downbeat is therefore one score quarter mapped to seven performed seconds:

stamp = bundle.get_matchstamp_at(downbeat, score_tl.id)

Reading that across a sequence of downbeats gives each performer’s arrival time at each measure — the raw material of a tempo comparison. We take the first several measure downbeats, ask the bundle for each performer’s onset there, and tabulate the seconds against the score quarters:

downbeat_mcs = range(2, 10)
rows = []
for mc in downbeat_mcs:
    quarters = float(metrical_position_map.quarters_at(mc))
    onset_stamp = bundle.get_matchstamp_at(quarters, score_tl.id)
    row = {"score (quarters)": quarters}
    for key in performer_keys:
        perf_id = loader.create_timeline(uid=key).id
        coord = onset_stamp.coordinates.get(perf_id)
        row[key.replace("Chopin_", "")] = (
            round(float(coord), 3) if coord is not None else None
        )
    rows.append(row)

tempo_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("score (quarters)")

Each column is one pianist’s arrival times in seconds; each row is a shared score position. title: How to Load Anything
text:
This notebook demonstrates the unified Loader API in the TimeToAlign! library. Each section exercises a loader following the same pattern:

Loading: loader.load(*paths) or Loader.from_file(path)
Inspection: loader, loader.store, loader.store.<type_property>
Timeline creation: create_timeline(), create_timelines()
Event access: get_events(), get_event(id), get_events_at(coord)
Timestamps: get_timestamp_at(coord), get_timestamp_for(id), get_timestamps_for(ids), get_timestamp_table()
Groups (where applicable): create_group(), group methods
Bundles (where applicable): create_bundle(), create_match_claims()

Retrieval names follow one grid, so the same four questions read the same way on every object below. The suffix says what you are asking with: _at takes a position, _for takes a key such as an event ID. The plural of the noun takes many of them and gives back a list. The bare name (get_timestamp(...)) is a convenience dispatcher that picks the precise method from what you passed it. Tabulating is the same query with get_timestamp_table(...), which returns a PyArrow table by default and a pandas frame with format="dataframe".



import warnings

from timetoalign import Provenance
from timetoalign.testdata import DATA_DIR, ensure_data
from timetoalign.timelines import Timeline

# How the example MatchClaims below were made
EXAMPLE_PROVENANCE = Provenance(method="manual", note="notebook example")

ensure_data("score", "midi", "vienna_1x22", "supra", "tabular", "thoresen")

SCORE_DIR = DATA_DIR / "score"
MIDI_DIR = DATA_DIR / "midi"
VIENNA_DIR = DATA_DIR / "vienna_1x22"

Every loader section below needs an event key to demonstrate the _for getters and a short list of keys to demonstrate their plurals. Deriving those is the same two lines each time, so they live here once.

def first_id(timeline: Timeline) -> str:
    """Return the ID of the timeline's first event."""
    return next(iter(timeline.get_events()))["id"]


def first_ids(timeline: Timeline, n: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    """Return the IDs of the timeline's first ``n`` events."""
    return [evt["id"] for evt in list(timeline.get_events())[:n]]

Batch retrieval has two flavours. Coordinate-batch — “resolve THESE coordinates” — resolves a handful of query coordinates on one timeline into one full cross-section each. The whole-alignment table below instead tabulates the entire alignment. Users hold coordinates, not MatchClaim objects, so the coordinate-batch form is the recommended entry point.
A match file aligns notes, so every claim it yields is an interval claim pairing a note’s score span with its performed span. A score position can lie in several such spans at once — the notes of a chord played slightly spread, or a note that ends where the next begins — and each claim then contributes its own performance candidate. The stamp lists them side by side and never merges them; the performance belongs to the stamp’s coordinates only where all candidates agree.

def first_id(timeline: Timeline) -> str:
    """Return the ID of the timeline's first event."""
    return next(iter(timeline.get_events()))["id"]


def first_ids(timeline: Timeline, n: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    """Return the IDs of the timeline's first ``n`` events."""
    return [evt["id"] for evt in list(timeline.get_events())[:n]]

title: How to Load Anything
text:
Parses MusicXML and MEI files using the music21 library. music21 gives a measure without timed content no length, so a source holding such measures (the MEI skeleton of this piece, whose measures are empty) states no measure positions through it and the load raises ValueError. The piece’s MusicXML times every measure.

Batch retrieval has two flavours. Coordinate-batch — “resolve THESE coordinates” — resolves a handful of query coordinates on one timeline into one full cross-section each. The whole-alignment table below instead tabulates the entire alignment. Users hold coordinates, not MatchClaim objects, so the coordinate-batch form is the recommended entry point.
A match file aligns notes, so every claim it yields is an interval claim pairing a note’s score span with its performed span. A score position can lie in several such spans at once — the notes of a chord played slightly spread, or a note that ends where the next begins — and each claim then contributes its own performance candidate. The stamp lists them side by side and never merges them; the performance belongs to the stamp’s coordinates only where all candidates agree.

The Timeline and TimelineGroup rows are the same four names because retrieval is one grid: _at for a position, _for for a key, the plural for many of them, and get_*_table() for the tabular form of the same query. The bundle row is that grid again, spelled matchstamp because a row there crosses timelines rather than staying inside one.

title: How to Load an IEEE 1599 Document
text:
IEEE 1599 is a multi-layer XML standard for encoding a single musical work once and relating every representation of it — the score, engraved page images, audio recordings, analytical annotations — back to a common axis. That axis is the <spine>: a flat, ordered list of abstract events in virtual time units (VTU), unit-less by design. Every other layer states where in its own coordinate space one of those spine events falls, via an event_ref. The spine is the hub; the layers refer to it; event_ref is the correspondence — exactly the shape of an alignment.
Ieee1599Loader reads one such document into a single multimodal AlignmentBundle: the spine as one Timeline in ticks, the logically-organised-symbols (LOS) layer of notes, rests and lyrics on another, one graphical timeline per engraved edition, one physical timeline per audio track, and the whole set of correspondences as one columnar MatchClaimField. The document’s own analytical layer — a segmentation of the spine resolving to places of a Petri net — is carried too, not as timing but as an external reference.
We load an existing document; nothing here runs an aligner. The correspondences are the document’s own event_ref cross-references; the loader’s job is to read them faithfully.
The work is Erik Satie’s Gymnopédie No. 1.
The arc:

Load the document in one call and read its title.
The spine, in ticks — a cumulative virtual-time axis — and the LOS layer of notes and rests sitting at spine coordinates.
The graphical editions as nested SegmentLines of pages and accolades, in pixels, and the audio tracks, in seconds.
The correspondences, reached through the uniform MatchClaimField API, and the cross-section they describe over spine coordinates.
The structural layer: a Petri-net analysis carried as external references on the spine.




from __future__ import annotations

import pyarrow.compute as pc

from timetoalign import IntervalToConstantMap
from timetoalign.alignment.claims import MatchClaim
from timetoalign.loader.alignment.ieee1599 import Ieee1599Loader
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

base = ensure_data("ieee1599")
document_path = base / "SatiePetriNets" / "ieee1599" / "gymnopedie_01.xml"




Ieee1599Loader parses the whole document — spine, LOS, every graphical edition, every audio track, and the structural analysis — into curated tables, then assembles them into timelines and a claim field. from_file() is the one-line form of the standard two-step loader pattern: parse, then build.

loader = Ieee1599Loader.from_file(document_path)

Every LOS event — a Note, a Rest, or a lyric Syllable — sits at the VTU coordinate of the spine event its event_ref names; that reference is its temporal position; the LOS layer carries no timing of its own. It is a second DiscreteLogicalTimeline, sharing the spine’s unit and length but its own event set — 557 LOS events against 382 spine events, since a chord’s several noteheads and a measure’s clefs and key signatures do not correspond one-to-one.

Notated durations are kept as the verbatim num/den pair rather than a reduced fraction, so a duration notated 1/4 never silently becomes something else; the exact value is Fraction(duration_num, duration_den). Each <graphic_instance_group> — one engraved edition of the score — is its own nested SegmentLine, in unit pixels. An edition is printed on pages, and a page is one image file with its own pixel origin, so the edition’s segments are its pages and a page’s segments are the accolades engraved on it. Within a page, x coordinates zig-zag along the spine: when a new system begins beyond half of that page’s x-span, the reset starts a new accolade. How




The spine, a cumulative VTU axis

title: How to Load an IEEE 1599 Document
text:
from __future__ import annotations

import pyarrow.compute as pc

from timetoalign import IntervalToConstantMap
from timetoalign.alignment.claims import MatchClaim
from timetoalign.loader.alignment.ieee1599 import Ieee1599Loader
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

title: How to Load an IEEE 1599 Document
text:
Ieee1599Loader parses the whole document — spine, LOS, every graphical edition, every audio track, and the structural analysis — into curated tables, then assembles them into timelines and a claim field. from_file() is the one-line form of the standard two-step loader pattern: parse, then build.

loader = Ieee1599Loader.from_file(document_path)

text:
The spine’s timing attribute is a relative integer delta against the previous <event>; the loader accumulates it into an absolute coordinate, so the stored value is the running sum — the cumulative VTU. Events notated as simultaneous carry timing="0" and land on the same coordinate. The spine is a DiscreteLogicalTimeline in ticks:

spine = bundle.get_timeline(loader.spine_uid)

Every LOS event — a Note, a Rest, or a lyric Syllable — sits at the VTU coordinate of the spine event its event_ref names; that reference is its temporal position; the LOS layer carries no timing of its own. It is a second DiscreteLogicalTimeline, sharing the spine’s unit and length but its own event set — 557 LOS events against 382 spine events, since a chord’s several noteheads and a measure’s clefs and key signatures do not correspond one-to-one.

los = bundle.get_timeline(loader.los_uid)
los

DiscreteLogicalTimeline[los:dlt_1jakoeq0r1wr9] (557 events)
                       0 ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, 236544 ticks


Notated durations are kept as the verbatim num/den pair rather than a reduced fraction, so a duration notated 1/4 never silently becomes something else; the exact value is Fraction(duration_num, duration_den). The opening melodic notes — each a quarter note (duration_num=1, duration_den=4) — carry their pitch as a step, octave and accidental, e.g. the first is F♯6:

notes = los.get_events(event_type="Note").to_dataframe()
notes.head(5)

title: How to Load an IEEE 1599 Document
text:
Each <graphic_instance_group> — one engraved edition of the score — is its own nested SegmentLine, in unit pixels. An edition is printed on pages, and a page is one image file with its own pixel origin, so the edition’s segments are its pages and a page’s segments are the accolades engraved on it. Within a page, x coordinates zig-zag along the spine: when a new system begins beyond half of that page’s x-span, the reset starts a new accolade. Both gymnopédie editions have four pages carrying 4 + 5 + 5 + 4 accolades.

for uid in loader.edition_uids:
    edition = bundle.get_timeline(uid)
    print(f"{edition.id}: {edition.name!r}, {edition.length}")
