The edition’s segments are its pages; each page’s segments are its accolades. iter_segments() yields both levels in spine order, together with each child’s offset in its parent’s coordinates. A page carries its <graphic_instance> attributes — the image file_name above all — in meta["page"]:

print(f"{edition.class_name}: {edition.n_segments} pages")
for _, page_offset, page in edition.iter_segments():
    print(f"{page.name} at x={page_offset.value}: {page.meta['page']['file_name']}")
    for _, offset, accolade in page.iter_segments():
        print(f"    {accolade.name} at x={offset.value}, length={accolade.length}")

An IntervalToConstantMap on the edition resolves any edition-wide x coordinate to the page-image file_name that contains it, without descending the hierarchy. The first graphical event provides one such coordinate:

page_image_map = next(
    cmap
    for cmap in edition._conversion_maps.values()
    if isinstance(cmap, IntervalToConstantMap)
)
first_graphical_event = graphical_events.iloc[0]
page_image_map(first_graphical_event["start"])

text:
Every LOS, graphical and audio event contributes one synchronous MatchClaim joining it to the spine event it references; both sides are events, each at its own timeline’s coordinate. All three layers go into one field — the alignment they express is one alignment, hub-and-spoke around the spine — reached through the uniform field API:

field = loader.get_field(MatchClaim)

{
    "field type": type(field).__name__,
    "claims": len(field),
}

{'field type': 'MatchClaimField', 'claims': 2085}

What the bundle expresses
How




The spine, a cumulative VTU axis
spine:dlt_… (loader.spine_uid), DiscreteLogicalTimeline, ticks


Notes, rests, lyrics at spine coordinates
los:dlt_… (loader.los_uid), verbatim duration_num/duration_den


Engraved editions, page-image boxes
one nested SegmentLine per edition:


4 page segments carrying 18 accolades, an IntervalToConstantMap to page images, pixels



Audio recordings
one ContinuousPhysicalTimeline per track, seconds


Every reference to the spine
one columnar MatchClaimField via loader.get_field(MatchClaim)


The cross-section over spine coordinates
bundle.get_matchstamp_table(from_graph=True)


The Petri-net analysis
spine.external_references — segment → place, resolved without opening any .pnml



One IEEE 1599 document — one spine, several layers referring to it, one analytical annotation layer — loaded into a single AlignmentBundle in which every representation of the work stays reachable from the axis the document itself defines.

title: How to Transfer Annotations Between Graphical Analyses
text:
This notebook demonstrates how to project graphical annotations from one image-based analytical diagram onto another using the TimeToAlign! library.
The use case comes from Lasse Thoresen’s spectromorphological analyses of Objets Obscurs by Manuella Blackburn. Two published editions of the same analysis exist:

DGT2 (2010): five separate images (strips), each covering roughly 30 seconds of music.
DGT1 (2009): a single image with five horizontally stacked systems.

Eleven annotated sound-object rectangles are placed on DGT2. The goal is to project them onto DGT1 via a shared physical timeline (seconds), creating cross-domain MatchClaims that record the correspondence. DGT1 has no events of its own, so each claim’s DGT1 side is a Projection: an event standing on DGT1 for the DGT2 rectangle it projects.



Building a SegmentLine by concatenation (DGT2: total length unknown in advance)
Building a plain DiscreteGraphicalTimeline with children (DGT1: known layout)
Attaching ScalarMap and ConstantMap to timeline segments
Adding interval events to child timelines
Querying TimeIntervalStamp via get_timestamp_for()
Projecting events onto another timeline with AlignmentBundle.create_match_claims()
Querying MatchStamp from both a single claim and an AlignmentBundle
Transferring y-coordinates via per-segment LinearMap





import json

import pandas as pd

from timetoalign import (
    AlignmentBundle,
    ConstantMap,
    Coordinate,
    DiscreteGraphicalTimeline,
    LinearMap,
    Provenance,
    ScalarMap,
    TimeUnit,
)
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data  # noqa: E402
from timetoalign.timelines import SegmentLine

DATA_DIR = ensure_data("thoresen")




The file thoresen_test.tsv contains 11 annotated sound-object rectangles, each with pixel coordinates on one of the five DGT2 images and a start time and duration in seconds (from manual alignment with the audio).

# Segment bounds: (x0, x1, y_axis) for each image
DGT2_BOUNDS = [
    (8, 874, 15),  # page1_1
    (7, 874, 18),  # page1_2
    (7, 874, 19),  # page1_3
    (8, 872, 15),  # page1_4
    (9, 873, 20),  # page2_1
]
DGT2_LENGTHS = [x1 - x0 for x0, x1, _ in DGT2_BOUNDS]

DGT2_IMAGE_FILES = [
    "thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_1.jpeg",
    "thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_2.jpeg",
    "thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_3.jpeg",
    "thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page1_4.jpeg",
    "thoresen_2010_form-building-patterns_p90-91_page2_1.jpeg",
]

# Audio spans 150 seconds total (5 segments x 30 seconds each)
AUDIO_DURATION = 150.0
SECONDS_PER_SEGMENT = AUDIO_DURATION / 5  # 30.0

# Build a lookup from image filename to segment index
IMAGE_TO_SEGMENT = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(DGT2_IMAGE_FILES)}





dgt2 = SegmentLine[DiscreteGraphicalTimeline](
    length=0,
    unit="pixels",
    uid="dgt_2",
    name="Thoresen 2010",
)

dgt2_segments = []
for i, (seg_len, filename) in enumerate(zip(DGT2_LENGTHS, DGT2_IMAGE_FILES)):
    seg = DiscreteGraphicalTimeline(
        length=seg_len,
        unit="pixels",
        uid=f"dgt2_seg{i+1}",
        name=f"seg_{i+1}",
    )

    # Attach ScalarMap: pixels -> seconds
    px_to_sec = ScalarMap(
        scalar=SECONDS_PER_SEGMENT / seg_len,
        source_unit="pixels",
        target_unit="seconds",
        name=f"px_to_sec_{i+1}",
    )
    seg.add_conversion_map(px_to_sec)

    # Attach ConstantMap: every coordinate carries the source filename
    fname_map = ConstantMap(value=filename, name="filename")
    seg.add_conversion_map(fname_map)

    dgt2.append_segment(seg, name=f"seg_{i+1}")
    dgt2_segments.append(seg)

print(f"DGT2 total length: {dgt2.length} (expected: {sum(DGT2_LENGTHS)})")
print(f"Number of segments: {dgt2.n_segments}")

DGT2 total length: 4328 pixels (expected: 4328)
Number of segments: 5





Each event is placed on the correct DGT2 segment using the image_filename column from the TSV. Coordinates are converted to local segment pixels (subtracting the segment’s x0 boundary).

for _, row in events_df.iterrows():
    seg_idx = IMAGE_TO_SEGMENT[row["image_filename"]]
    x0 = DGT2_BOUNDS[seg_idx][0]

    # Local coordinates within the segment
    local_start = row["x"] - x0
    local_end = local_start + row["width"]

    dgt2_segments[seg_idx].add_events(
        [
            {
                "id": row["graphical_element_id"],
                "event_type": "sound_object",
                "start": float(local_start),
                "end": float(local_end),
            }
        ]
    )

print("Events added to DGT2 segments")
for i, seg in enumerate(dgt2_segments):
    n = seg.n_events
    if n > 0:
        print(f"  seg_{i+1}: {n} events")

  seg_2: 2 events

Event H (rect_h2) is the specimen highlighted in the manuscript. It sits on segment 2 (page1_2.jpeg) at raw pixel x=385, width=139.

Local x: 385 - 7 = 378 to 378 + 139 = 517
Global x: 866 + 378 = 1244 to 866 + 517 = 1383
Expected seconds: ~43.1 to ~47.9 (pixel-derived)
TSV ground truth: 43.5 s, duration 4.5 s


stamp_h = dgt2.get_timestamp_for("rect_h2")
print(stamp_h)

TimeIntervalStamp [1244, 1383) pixels
  dgt_2  1244  1383 pixels
  dgt2_seg2  378  517 pixels



# Extract the key values for validation
h_start_global = stamp_h.start.axis
h_end_global = stamp_h.end.axis
print(f"Event H global pixels: [{h_start_global}, {h_end_global})")
print("  Expected: [1244, 1383)")

Event H global pixels: [1244 pixels @dgt_2, 1383 pixels @dgt_2)
  Expected: [1244, 1383)



# Helper: convert a global DGT2 pixel coordinate to seconds.
# The ScalarMap on each segment converts local pixels to the *local* seconds
# within a 30-second window.  We need to know the segment index and offset
# to compute the absolute time.
def dgt2_global_px_to_sec(global_px: float) -> float:
    """Convert a global DGT2 pixel coordinate to absolute seconds."""
    offset = 0
    for i, seg_len in enumerate(DGT2_LENGTHS):
        if global_px < offset + seg_len:
            local_px = global_px - offset
            local_sec = local_px * (SECONDS_PER_SEGMENT / seg_len)
            return i * SECONDS_PER_SEGMENT + local_sec
        offset += seg_len
    # Edge: coordinate at the very end
    return AUDIO_DURATION


h_start_sec = dgt2_global_px_to_sec(h_start_global.value)
h_end_sec = dgt2_global_px_to_sec(h_end_global.value)
print(f"Event H seconds (pixel-derived): [{h_start_sec:.2f}, {h_end_sec:.2f})")
print("  TSV ground truth: [43.5, 48.0)")

The pixel-derived seconds differ slightly from the TSV values because the linear mapping assumes uniform time-per-pixel across each segment, whereas the TSV values come from a separate manual alignment. The difference is small enough to demonstrate the coordinate-transfer workflow.

DGT1_SEGMENT_LENGTH = 967  # x1 - x0 = 969 - 2
DGT1_TOTAL_WIDTH = DGT1_SEGMENT_LENGTH * 5  # 4835

dgt1 = DiscreteGraphicalTimeline(
    length=DGT1_TOTAL_WIDTH,
    unit="pixels",
    uid="dgt_1",
    name="Thoresen 2009",
)

# Attach a single ScalarMap on the parent: pixels -> seconds
dgt1_px_to_sec = ScalarMap(
    scalar=AUDIO_DURATION / DGT1_TOTAL_WIDTH,
    source_unit="pixels",
    target_unit="seconds",
    name="px_to_sec",
)
dgt1.add_conversion_map(dgt1_px_to_sec)

# Create 5 children (systems)
dgt1_children = []
for i in range(5):
    child = dgt1.create_child(
        length=DGT1_SEGMENT_LENGTH,
        offset=i * DGT1_SEGMENT_LENGTH,
        uid=f"dgt1_sys{i+1}",
        name=f"sys_{i+1}",
    )
    dgt1_children.append(child)

print(f"DGT1 total length: {dgt1.length}")
print(f"Number of children: {len(dgt1_children)}")

Number of children: 5





Both timelines are added directly to the bundle as standalone timelines (no explicit TimelineGroup wrapping needed – the bundle creates implicit singleton groups).

bundle = AlignmentBundle(name="Thoresen Annotation Transfer")
bundle.add_timeline(dgt2)
bundle.add_timeline(dgt1)
print(bundle)

    Thoresen ...     0 ∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶ 4328 pixels
    Thoresen ...     0 ∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶ 4835 pixels

  MatchClaims: 0





For each event on DGT2, we: 1. Get its TimeIntervalStamp to extract global pixel coordinates and seconds. 2. State the DGT1 side as a position in seconds: DGT1’s ScalarMap places it on DGT1’s pixel axis. 3. Let bundle.create_match_claims() add a Projection of the DGT2 event at that position on DGT1 and make the MatchClaim between the two events.

# Collect all event IDs from the TSV
event_ids = events_df["graphical_element_id"].tolist()

event_pairs = []
projection_data = []

for event_id in event_ids:
    # Get the TimeIntervalStamp from DGT2
    stamp = dgt2.get_timestamp_for(event_id)

    # Extract global DGT2 coordinates (on the SegmentLine axis)
    dgt2_start = stamp.start.axis
    dgt2_end = stamp.end.axis

    # Convert global pixels to seconds via the segment-aware helper
    sec_start = dgt2_global_px_to_sec(dgt2_start.value)
    sec_end = dgt2_global_px_to_sec(dgt2_end.value)

    # The DGT1 side: a span in seconds, which DGT1's ScalarMap places on its
    # pixel axis when the Projection is added
    dgt1_side = {
        "start": Coordinate(sec_start, TimeUnit.seconds),
        "end": Coordinate(sec_end, TimeUnit.seconds),
    }
    event_pairs.append((event_id, dgt2.id, dgt1_side, dgt1.id))

    # Track data for the summary table
    projection_data.append(
        {
            "event_id": event_id,
            "dgt2_start_px": dgt2_start,
            "dgt2_end_px": dgt2_end,
            "seconds_start": round(sec_start, 2),
            "seconds_end": round(sec_end, 2),
        }
    )

claims = bundle.create_match_claims(
    event_pairs,
    provenance=Provenance(
        method="manual",
        note="Thoresen analysis: projection via the shared physical timeline",
    ),
)

# The DGT1 pixels each claim holds, for the summary table
for row, claim in zip(projection_data, claims):
    row["dgt1_start_px"] = claim.start_anchor.coordinate_b.value
    row["dgt1_end_px"] = claim.end_anchor.coordinate_b.value

This notebook demonstrated the full annotation-transfer workflow:

DGT2 was built as a SegmentLine by concatenation, with ScalarMap (pixels to seconds) and ConstantMap (source filename) on each segment.
DGT1 was built as a plain DiscreteGraphicalTimeline with five children and a single ScalarMap on the parent.
11 MatchClaims were created by projecting DGT2 events through seconds onto DGT1 with bundle.create_match_claims(), which added one Projection per rectangle on DGT1.
MatchStamps confirmed the coordinate correspondence from both the claim and bundle perspectives.
Y-coordinates were transferred via per-segment LinearMap, mapping each segment’s event space to the corresponding DGT1 system.

The two construction patterns – SegmentLine concatenation (DGT2) vs. plain timeline with children (DGT1) – illustrate how TimeToAlign! supports both “accumulate as you go” and “known layout” approaches.

# Helper: convert a global DGT2 pixel coordinate to seconds.
# The ScalarMap on each segment converts local pixels to the *local* seconds
# within a 30-second window.  We need to know the segment index and offset
# to compute the absolute time.
def dgt2_global_px_to_sec(global_px: float) -> float:
    """Convert a global DGT2 pixel coordinate to absolute seconds."""
    offset = 0
    for i, seg_len in enumerate(DGT2_LENGTHS):
        if global_px < offset + seg_len:
            local_px = global_px - offset
            local_sec = local_px * (SECONDS_PER_SEGMENT / seg_len)
            return i * SECONDS_PER_SEGMENT + local_sec
        offset += seg_len
    # Edge: coordinate at the very end
    return AUDIO_DURATION

text:
For each event on DGT2, we: 1. Get its TimeIntervalStamp to extract global pixel coordinates and seconds. 2. State the DGT1 side as a position in seconds: DGT1’s ScalarMap places it on DGT1’s pixel axis. 3. Let bundle.create_match_claims() add a Projection of the DGT2 event at that position on DGT1 and make the MatchClaim between the two events.

# Collect all event IDs from the TSV
event_ids = events_df["graphical_element_id"].tolist()

event_pairs = []
projection_data = []

for event_id in event_ids:
    # Get the TimeIntervalStamp from DGT2
    stamp = dgt2.get_timestamp_for(event_id)

    # Extract global DGT2 coordinates (on the SegmentLine axis)
    dgt2_start = stamp.start.axis
    dgt2_end = stamp.end.axis

    # Convert global pixels to seconds via the segment-aware helper
    sec_start = dgt2_global_px_to_sec(dgt2_start.value)
    sec_end = dgt2_global_px_to_sec(dgt2_end.value)

    # The DGT1 side: a span in seconds, which DGT1's ScalarMap places on its
    # pixel axis when the Projection is added
    dgt1_side = {

            "dgt2_end_px": dgt2_end,
            "seconds_start": round(sec_start, 2),
            "seconds_end": round(sec_end, 2),
        }
    )

    event_pairs,

)

DGT1_Y_RANGES = [(18, 165), (205, 353), (396, 544), (588, 736), (785, 933)]
DGT2_Y_RANGES = [(15, 148), (18, 150), (19, 152), (15, 147), (20, 152)]




Each segment has a LinearMap that maps [dgt2_y0, dgt2_y1] to [dgt1_y0, dgt1_y1]. The linear mapping is:
\[y_{\text{DGT1}} = y_{0}^{\text{DGT1}} + \frac{y - y_{0}^{\text{DGT2}}}{h^{\text{DGT2}}} \cdot h^{\text{DGT1}}\]

y_maps = []
for i, ((d2_y0, d2_y1), (d1_y0, d1_y1)) in enumerate(zip(DGT2_Y_RANGES, DGT1_Y_RANGES)):
    d2_height = d2_y1 - d2_y0
    d1_height = d1_y1 - d1_y0
    scalar = d1_height / d2_height
    offset = d1_y0 - scalar * d2_y0

    lmap = LinearMap(
        scalar=scalar,
        offset=offset,
        name=f"y_transfer_seg{i+1}",
    )
    y_maps.append(lmap)
    print(
        f"Segment {i+1}: DGT2 [{d2_y0}, {d2_y1}] -> DGT1 [{d1_y0}, {d1_y1}], "
        f"scalar={scalar:.4f}, offset={offset:.2f}"
    )

title: How to Transfer Annotations Between Graphical Analyses
text:
This notebook demonstrated the full annotation-transfer workflow:

DGT2 was built as a SegmentLine by concatenation, with ScalarMap (pixels to seconds) and ConstantMap (source filename) on each segment.
DGT1 was built as a plain DiscreteGraphicalTimeline with five children and a single ScalarMap on the parent.
11 MatchClaims were created by projecting DGT2 events through seconds onto DGT1 with bundle.create_match_claims(), which added one Projection per rectangle on DGT1.
MatchStamps confirmed the coordinate correspondence from both the claim and bundle perspectives.
Y-coordinates were transferred via per-segment LinearMap, mapping each segment’s event space to the corresponding DGT1 system.

The two construction patterns – SegmentLine concatenation (DGT2) vs. plain timeline with children (DGT1) – illustrate how TimeToAlign! supports both “accumulate as you go” and “known layout” approaches.

title: How to Construct Timelines Manually
How to Align an Engraved Score with a Recording and a Drawn Time Axis
text:
Three files often travel together when a score is studied against a performance:

the engraved score, here an MEI file, read through Verovio by VerovioLoader;
a note alignment between that score and a recording, in the MAPS format that the TROMPA project’s trompa-align writes, read by MapsLoader as MatchClaims;
a drawing of the score shifted to the recording’s time, with a time axis below it, as ScoreWarp writes it into an SVG, read by ScoreWarpLoader.

Each file states its time in its own unit: quarters for the score, seconds for the recording, CSS pixels for the drawing. This guide loads all three and answers one question across them: which score position lies under a point of the drawing?
The score comes from the library’s test corpus. The alignment and the drawing are illustrative: this guide writes both itself, a few rows and a few ticks, with invented times. They have the shape the two tools write, so the same calls read the real files.
The arc:

Load the score: exact quarters, notes by xml:id, Verovio’s own seconds.
Write a MAPS file, state it as MatchClaims, and ask a bundle for a MatchStamp between two aligned notes.
Write a ScoreWarp SVG, read its time axis, and take a point of the drawing to seconds and on to the score.
Calibrate a drawn axis by hand with create_calibrated_child.
Save the bundle as a package and read it back.



VerovioLoader needs the verovio extra: install the library with pip install "timetoalign[verovio]". The files this guide writes go to a temporary directory. Three helpers keep the cells short: notes_at lists the score’s notes in a span of quarters, ids_at names the notes starting at one position, and claims_table shows a list of claims one row each, a NOMATCH claim at the start of the one event it names.

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import tempfile
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

from timetoalign import AlignmentBundle, MapsLoader, ScoreWarpLoader, VerovioLoader
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data
from timetoalign.timelines import (
    ContinuousGraphicalTimeline,
    ContinuousPhysicalTimeline,
)

SCORE_PATH = (
    ensure_data("score")
    / "flow_control"
    / "out_of_the_flow_experience-polyrhythm_only.mei"
)
FILES = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())

NOTE_COLUMNS = ["id", "start", "end", "mc", "staff", "midi"]


def notes_at(timeline, start, stop) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The notes of *timeline* starting in ``[start, stop)`` quarters."""
    notes = timeline.get_events(include_children=True, event_type="Note").to_dataframe()
    span = notes[(notes["start"] >= start) & (notes["start"] < stop)]
    return span[NOTE_COLUMNS].reset_index(drop=True)


def ids_at(timeline, position) -> list[str]:
    """The ``xml:id`` of every note of *timeline* starting at *position*."""
    return list(notes_at(timeline, position, position + Fraction(1, 1000))["id"])


def claims_table(claims, *timelines) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per claim: its type, the events it names, and both sides.

    A synchronous claim gives the two coordinates of its anchor. A NOMATCH
    claim holds no coordinate: it names one event and the sentinel. MAPS
    states that event on timeline A and the sentinel on timeline B, so its
    ``at`` is the event's start, read from the event on timeline A among
    *timelines*; its ``there`` is empty, and its ``event there`` is the
    sentinel as the MatchClaim table writes it, ``NOMATCH_SENTINEL``.
    """
    by_id = {timeline.id: timeline for timeline in timelines}
    rows = []
    for claim in claims:
        if claim.is_synchronous:
            here, there = (
                claim.start_anchor.coordinate_a,
                claim.start_anchor.coordinate_b,
            )
        else:
            here = by_id[claim.timeline_a_id].get_coordinate_for(
                claim.event_a_id, format="coordinate"
            )
            there = None
        rows.append(
            {
                "claim_type": claim.claim_type.value,
                "event": claim.event_a_id,
                "from": claim.timeline_a_id,
                "at": str(here),
                "to": claim.timeline_b_id,
                "there": "" if there is None else str(there),
                "event there": claim.event_b_id,
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)




VerovioLoader reads any format Verovio reads (MEI, MusicXML, Humdrum, …) and takes the score’s time from Verovio’s timemap, which states every onset as an exact fraction of a quarter. The test score sets tuplets against plain sixteenths: seven eighths in the time of three, each 3/14 of a quarter long, and five sixteenths in the time of three, each 3/20. Its positions are therefore multiples of 3/14 and of 3/20 of a quarter, such as 3/20, 3/14 and 3/10 in the first quarter: exact fractions keep them apart.
create_timeline() builds the logical timeline in quarters. A movement (<mdiv>) of the file that is named, by its @label, becomes a child timeline holding that movement’s events. This score’s one <mdiv> has no label, so the score is a single timeline holding every event.

The inserted note, which the score lacks, is added to the recording as a Projection of no event under its MAPS id, and becomes a NOMATCH claim from the recording.

ScoreWarp engraves the score with Verovio, shifts every note to its time in the recording, and appends a time axis to the SVG: a <g class="timeAxis"> holding a horizontal line.horizontalAxis, a vertical line per tick, a number under every labelled tick and one title, such as Time (s), naming the unit. The helper below writes such an axis, from 0 to 4 seconds at 100 pixels per second, starting 50 pixels from the left edge.

def scorewarp_svg(path: Path, *, left: float, per_second: float, seconds: int) -> Path:
    """Write an SVG holding a ScoreWarp-shaped time axis, ticks every half second."""
    right = left + per_second * seconds
    parts = [
        f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="{right + 20}" height="120" '
        f'viewBox="0 0 {right + 20} 120" overflow="visible">',
        '<g class="timeAxis">',
        f'<line class="horizontalAxis" x1="{left}" x2="{right}" y1="100" y2="100"/>',
        '<text x="2" y="96">Time (s)</text>',
    ]
    for half in range(2 * seconds + 1):
        x = left + per_second * half / 2
        parts.append(
            f'<line x1="{x}" x2="{x}" y1="100" y2="{106 if half % 2 == 0 else 103}"/>'
        )
    for second in range(seconds + 1):
        parts.append(f'<text x="{left + per_second * second}" y="116">{second}</text>')
    parts.append("</g></svg>")
    path.write_text("\n".join(parts), encoding="utf-8")
    return path

The drawing joins the bundle like the other two timelines. to_file() writes the bundle as a package: a TimeToShare manifest holding the timelines, their children and conversion maps and the score’s measures, and beside it the MatchClaim table and the recording’s Projections, as its registry rows and the pre-parsed Projection table; the manifest names the registry and the MatchClaim table in its resources. A manifest names no event: the claims name the score’s notes by their xml:id, which the MEI file holds. The file opens with the manifest’s inline JSON-LD @context; the cell below lists the directory, where the MAPS file and the SVG are this guide’s own, and prints the manifest from timelines on.

print(sorted(path.name for path in FILES.iterdir()))

title: How to Align an Engraved Score with a Recording and a Drawn Time Axis
text:
VerovioLoader needs the verovio extra: install the library with pip install "timetoalign[verovio]". The files this guide writes go to a temporary directory. Three helpers keep the cells short: notes_at lists the score’s notes in a span of quarters, ids_at names the notes starting at one position, and claims_table shows a list of claims one row each, a NOMATCH claim at the start of the one event it names.

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import tempfile
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

from timetoalign import AlignmentBundle, MapsLoader, ScoreWarpLoader, VerovioLoader
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data
from timetoalign.timelines import (
    ContinuousGraphicalTimeline,
    ContinuousPhysicalTimeline,
)

SCORE_PATH = (
    ensure_data("score")
    / "flow_control"
    / "out_of_the_flow_experience-polyrhythm_only.mei"
)
FILES = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())

NOTE_COLUMNS = ["id", "start", "end", "mc", "staff", "midi"]


def notes_at(timeline, start, stop) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The notes of *timeline* starting in ``[start, stop)`` quarters."""
    notes = timeline.get_events(include_children=True, event_type="Note").to_dataframe()
    span = notes[(notes["start"] >= start) & (notes["start"] < stop)]
    return span[NOTE_COLUMNS].reset_index(drop=True)


def ids_at(timeline, position) -> list[str]:
    """The ``xml:id`` of every note of *timeline* starting at *position*."""
    return list(notes_at(timeline, position, position + Fraction(1, 1000))["id"])


def claims_table(claims, *timelines) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One row per claim: its type, the events it names, and both sides.

    A synchronous claim gives the two coordinates of its anchor. A NOMATCH
    claim holds no coordinate: it names one event and the sentinel. MAPS
    states that event on timeline A and the sentinel on timeline B, so its
    ``at`` is the event's start, read from the event on timeline A among
    *timelines*; its ``there`` is empty, and its ``event there`` is the
    sentinel as the MatchClaim table writes it, ``NOMATCH_SENTINEL``.
    """
    by_id = {timeline.id: timeline for timeline in timelines}
    rows = []
    for claim in claims:
        if claim.is_synchronous:
            here, there = (
                claim.start_anchor.coordinate_a,
                claim.start_anchor.coordinate_b,
            )
        else:
            here = by_id[claim.timeline_a_id].get_coordinate_for(
                claim.event_a_id, format="coordinate"
            )
            there = None
        rows.append(
            {
                "claim_type": claim.claim_type.value,
                "event": claim.event_a_id,
                "from": claim.timeline_a_id,
                "at": str(here),
                "to": claim.timeline_b_id,
                "there": "" if there is None else str(there),
                "event there": claim.event_b_id,
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

VerovioLoader reads any format Verovio reads (MEI, MusicXML, Humdrum, …) and takes the score’s time from Verovio’s timemap, which states every onset as an exact fraction of a quarter. The test score sets tuplets against plain sixteenths: seven eighths in the time of three, each 3/14 of a quarter long, and five sixteenths in the time of three, each 3/20. Its positions are therefore multiples of 3/14 and of 3/20 of a quarter, such as 3/20, 3/14 and 3/10 in the first quarter: exact fractions keep them apart.
create_timeline() builds the logical timeline in quarters. A movement (<mdiv>) of the file that is named, by its @label, becomes a child timeline holding that movement’s events. This score’s one <mdiv> has no label, so the score is a single timeline holding every event.

text:
A MAPS file is a JSON list of rows. Each row pairs the score notes heard together, named by xml:id, with one time of the recording in seconds, obs_mean_onset; obs_num numbers the rows from 1. trompa-align writes two more kinds of rows: a score note that was not played, at onset -1, and a played note the score does not have, under an id beginning trompa-align_inserted_.
The file below aligns the notes on the sixteenth-note grid of the first measures, one unplayed note and one inserted note. Its times are invented.

onsets = {
    Fraction(0): 0.5,
    Fraction(1, 4): 0.88,
    Fraction(1, 2): 1.27,
    Fraction(3, 4): 1.69,
    Fraction(1): 2.08,
    Fraction(3, 2): 2.9,
}
rows = [{"obs_mean_onset": -1, "xml_id": ids_at(score, Fraction(3, 20))}]
rows += [
    {"obs_mean_onset": seconds, "xml_id": ids_at(score, quarter)}
    for quarter, seconds in onsets.items()
]
rows.insert(5, {"obs_mean_onset": 1.85, "xml_id": "trompa-align_inserted_Cs5"})
for number, row in enumerate(rows, start=1):
    row["obs_num"] = number

maps_path = FILES / "alignment.json"
maps_path.write_text(json.dumps(rows, indent=1), encoding="utf-8")
maps = MapsLoader.from_file(maps_path)

create_match_claims(score, performance) states every listed id as a claim of its own. A MatchClaim joins two events, and the recording has no events of its own: for a note at a time of the recording, a Projection of that note is added to the recording at that time, and the claim is an event_match between the score note and the Projection. The unplayed note becomes a NOMATCH claim from the score. The inserted note, which the score lacks, is added to the recording as a Projection of no event under its MAPS id, and becomes a NOMATCH claim from the recording.
The recording is a timeline in seconds; any physical timeline works, and one in samples reaches seconds through its C-Map.

title: How to Align an Engraved Score with a Recording and a Drawn Time Axis
text:
ScoreWarp engraves the score with Verovio, shifts every note to its time in the recording, and appends a time axis to the SVG: a <g class="timeAxis"> holding a horizontal line.horizontalAxis, a vertical line per tick, a number under every labelled tick and one title, such as Time (s), naming the unit. The helper below writes such an axis, from 0 to 4 seconds at 100 pixels per second, starting 50 pixels from the left edge.

def scorewarp_svg(path: Path, *, left: float, per_second: float, seconds: int) -> Path:
    """Write an SVG holding a ScoreWarp-shaped time axis, ticks every half second."""
    right = left + per_second * seconds
    parts = [
        f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="{right + 20}" height="120" '
        f'viewBox="0 0 {right + 20} 120" overflow="visible">',
        '<g class="timeAxis">',
        f'<line class="horizontalAxis" x1="{left}" x2="{right}" y1="100" y2="100"/>',
        '<text x="2" y="96">Time (s)</text>',
    ]
    for half in range(2 * seconds + 1):
        x = left + per_second * half / 2
        parts.append(
            f'<line x1="{x}" x2="{x}" y1="100" y2="{106 if half % 2 == 0 else 103}"/>'
        )
    for second in range(seconds + 1):
        parts.append(f'<text x="{left + per_second * second}" y="116">{second}</text>')
    parts.append("</g></svg>")
    path.write_text("\n".join(parts), encoding="utf-8")
    return path


svg_path = scorewarp_svg(FILES / "warped.svg", left=50.0, per_second=100.0, seconds=4)

text:
ScoreWarpLoader reads the axis it finds in CSS pixels as drawn; an axis in another drawing, or one placed through a transform, is calibrated by hand with Timeline.create_calibrated_child. It takes the child’s length and offset and a list of (position, value) pairs, such as the labelled ticks of an axis, and fits the conversion map through them.
Here the drawing is in user_units, the coordinate system of an SVG viewBox, whose size in inches only the document knows. The axis runs from 120 to 1920 user units, labelled every second:

page = ContinuousGraphicalTimeline(length=2000, unit="user_units", name="Page")

)

Below, the tick at 720 is mislabelled 1.5 seconds: the line from (120, 0) to (1920, 3) reaches 1.5 only at 1020, so that pair is refused before the child is created, and the page keeps only the axis made above:

        1800, 120, [(120, 0), (720, 1.5), (1320, 2), (1920, 3)], value_unit="seconds"
    )

title: How to Align an Engraved Score with a Recording and a Drawn Time Axis
text:
The drawing joins the bundle like the other two timelines. to_file() writes the bundle as a package: a TimeToShare manifest holding the timelines, their children and conversion maps and the score’s measures, and beside it the MatchClaim table and the recording’s Projections, as its registry rows and the pre-parsed Projection table; the manifest names the registry and the MatchClaim table in its resources. A manifest names no event: the claims name the score’s notes by their xml:id, which the MEI file holds. The file opens with the manifest’s inline JSON-LD @context; the cell below lists the directory, where the MAPS file and the SVG are this guide’s own, and prints the manifest from timelines on.

bundle.add_timeline(drawing)
bundle_path = bundle.to_file(FILES / "out_of_the_flow.yaml")
text = bundle_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
start = text.index("timelines:")
print(sorted(path.name for path in FILES.iterdir()))
print("\n".join(text[start:][:24]))

['alignment.json', 'extractions.parquet', 'match_claims.parquet', 'out_of_the_flow.yaml', 'projections.parquet', 'registry.parquet', 'warped.svg']
timelines:
  -
    children:
      -
        conversion_maps:
          -
            id: "#cmap_00dw2bvv9zhtm"
            scalar: 0.01
            source_unit: css_pixels
            target_unit: seconds
            type: LinearMap
        id: "#cgt_1wmo13tawdnbo"
        length: 400.0
        locked: true
        name: "Time (s)"
        offset: 50.0
        unit: css_pixels
    id: "#cgt_2p9zca1mjm161"
    length: 470.0
    meta:
      svg_height: "120"
      svg_width: "470.0"
    name: warped
    unit: css_pixels


from_file() reads the package back, the claims and the recording’s Projections with it, and the bundle answers as before: the drawing’s point at x = 258 is still 2.08 seconds, and the septuplet note still warps to the same time.

read = AlignmentBundle.from_file(bundle_path)
read.get_timeline(drawing.id).get_timestamp_at(258), read.get_matchstamp_at(
    Fraction(3, 7), score.id
)

title: How to Align a Piano Roll (SUPRA)
text:
This tutorial applies everything we’ve learned to a real-world case study: aligning a scanned piano roll image with MIDI files, audio, and score annotations from the Stanford University Piano Roll Archive (SUPRA).
Learning Objectives: - Create a graphical timeline from ATON analysis data - Add C-Maps for physical unit conversion (pixels to inches/cm) - Use the child timeline API for hierarchical relationships - Load MIDI, audio, and score data with specialized loaders - Build a TimelineGroup connecting all representations - Transfer coordinates across the entire alignment chain using Timestamps
Prerequisites: - Notebook 04 (Timelines, hierarchies) - Notebook 05 (Timestamps) - Notebook 07 (Alignment Basics, TimelineGroup)
Data Source: - Roll: WM 990 (Welte-Mignon red roll, T-100) - Piece: Richard Wagner - Meistersinger von Nurnberg: Vorspiel (Prelude) - Performer: Myrtle Elvyn, piano (December 6, 1905) - SUPRA URL: https://supra.stanford.edu/ - DRUID: fd660zf8362


Per the ZERO TOLERANCE policy, all values use exact counts from the SUPRA analysis:



Parameter
Value
Description




IMAGE_WIDTH
4,096
Image width in pixels


IMAGE_HEIGHT
299,400
Image height in pixels


LENGTH_DPI
300.25
Scan resolution (pixels per inch)


PHYSICAL_LENGTH
997.17
Roll length in inches (25.33 m)


FIRST_HOLE
15,343
Pixel row of first musical hole


LAST_HOLE
293,119
Pixel row of last musical hole


MUSICAL_LENGTH
277,776
Pixels from first to last hole


MUSICAL_HOLES
30,092
Individual hole punches (raw MIDI events)


RAW_MIDI_NOTES
30,092
Raw MIDI note count (1 per hole)


EXP_MIDI_NOTES
6,380
Expressive MIDI note count (merged)


SCORE_NOTES
5,577
Notes in DCML score


SCORE_MEASURES
222
Measures in DCML score


SCORE_LENGTH
888
Total quarterbeats








from timetoalign import Coordinate, IdCoordinate, Ms3Loader, TimelineGroup, TimeUnit
from timetoalign.loader.graphical.aton import ATONLoader
from timetoalign.loader.midi import PerformanceMidiLoader
from timetoalign.loader.physical import AudioLoader
from timetoalign.maps import ScalarMap
from timetoalign.testdata import ensure_data

DATA_DIR = ensure_data("supra")

ATON_FILE = DATA_DIR / "image" / "fd660zf8362_analysis.txt"
MIDI_RAW_PATH = DATA_DIR / "midi" / "fd660zf8362_raw.mid"
MIDI_EXP_PATH = DATA_DIR / "midi" / "fd660zf8362_exp.mid"
MP3_PATH = DATA_DIR / "midi" / "fd660zf8362.mp3"
DCML_DIR = DATA_DIR / "dcml"

{"Data directory": str(DATA_DIR), "ATON file": ATON_FILE.name}

{'Data directory': '/home/laser/git/tta/timetoalign/tests/data/supra',
 'ATON file': 'fd660zf8362_analysis.txt'}






The ATON (Artistic Text-based Object Notation) file contains hole punch data from the Stanford SUPRA project’s piano roll analysis. The loader creates a timeline with all hole events already populated at their absolute pixel coordinates.
Note: We use the from_file() constructor for one-line instantiation.

aton_loader = ATONLoader.from_file(ATON_FILE)

assert aton_loader.musical_holes == 30092
assert aton_loader.musical_notes == 8718
assert aton_loader.first_hole.value == 15343
assert aton_loader.last_hole.value == 293119
assert aton_loader.musical_length.value == 277776
assert aton_loader.image_dimensions["height"] == 299400

{
    "Image height": f"{aton_loader.image_dimensions['height']:,} pixels",
    "Musical holes": f"{aton_loader.musical_holes:,}",
    "First hole": aton_loader.first_hole,
    "Last hole": aton_loader.last_hole,
    "Musical length": aton_loader.musical_length,
    "Verification": "PASSED",
}

{'Image height': '299,400 pixels',
 'Musical holes': '30,092',
 'First hole': Coordinate(15343, pixels),
 'Last hole': Coordinate(293119, pixels),
 'Musical length': Coordinate(277776, pixels),
 'Verification': 'PASSED'}


The loader’s create_timeline() method creates a timeline spanning the full image with holes at absolute coordinates.

dgt1 = aton_loader.create_timeline(uid="dgt_1", name="Piano Roll Image (WM 990)")
dgt1

DiscreteGraphicalTimeline[dgt_1] (30092 events)
                       0 ∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶ 299400 pixels






The piano roll was scanned at 300.25 DPI (dots per inch). We attach ConversionMaps to convert pixel coordinates to physical units.
Important: We specify name= for human-readable column headers in timestamp tables. Without it, columns would show as “map:ScalarMap_1”.
Calculation: 299,400 pixels / 300.25 DPI = 997.17 inches = 25.33 meters

LENGTH_DPI = 300.25

# Note: name= provides readable column headers (defaults to "source_to_target")
dgt1.add_conversion_map(
    ScalarMap(
        scalar=1 / LENGTH_DPI,
        source_unit="pixels",
        target_unit="inches",
        name="pixels_to_inches",  # Human-readable name for timestamp columns
    )
)

dgt1.add_conversion_map(
    ScalarMap(
        scalar=2.54 / LENGTH_DPI,
        source_unit="pixels",
        target_unit="cm",
        name="pixels_to_cm",  # Human-readable name for timestamp columns
    )
)

The convert_to method returns proper Coordinate objects with units.

image_length_inches = dgt1.convert_to(dgt1.length, "inches")
image_length_cm = dgt1.convert_to(dgt1.length, "cm")

{
    "Image length": dgt1.length,
    "Image length (inches)": image_length_inches,
    "Image length (cm)": image_length_cm,
    "Image length (meters)": f"{image_length_cm.value / 100:.2f} meters",
}

{'Image length': Coordinate(299400, pixels),
 'Image length (inches)': Coordinate(997.1690258118235, inches),
 'Image length (cm)': Coordinate(2532.8093255620315, centimeters),
 'Image length (meters)': '25.33 meters'}






The musical content doesn’t span the entire image - holes start at pixel 15,343. We create a child timeline to provide a relative coordinate view where the first hole = 0 pixels.
Key insight: The child has no events of its own. It’s purely a coordinate transformation. When we get timestamps, we see event coordinates in BOTH the parent (absolute) and child (relative) coordinate systems - for free!

dgt_holes = dgt1.create_child(
    length=aton_loader.musical_length,
    offset=aton_loader.first_hole,
    uid="dgt_holes",
    name="Musical Holes Region",
)
dgt1

DiscreteGraphicalTimeline[dgt_1] (30092 events, 1 children, 2 cmaps)
                       0 ∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶ 299400 pixels
  └─ Musical H...  15343  ∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶∶  293119






With the parent-child hierarchy established, we can generate timestamps that show coordinates in both the parent (full image) and child (holes region) coordinate systems simultaneously.
Note: get_timestamp_table(format="dataframe") gives column names with units appended (e.g., “pixels_to_inches (inches)”) and one scalar per cell in each axis’s declared number type. This is the recommended way to get timestamp data for display.

timestamps_df = dgt1.get_timestamp_table(format="dataframe")

{"Total timestamps": len(timestamps_df), "Columns": list(timestamps_df.columns)}

{'Total timestamps': 20680,
 'Columns': ['dgt_1 (pixels)',
  'dgt_holes (pixels)',
  'pixels_to_inches (inches)',
  'pixels_to_cm (centimeters)']}


Why ~20,680 timestamps?
The timestamp table has one row per unique event coordinate in the hierarchy: - Parent timeline (dgt_1) contains 30,092 hole events at absolute pixel coordinates - But many holes share the same pixel row (multiple notes at one time position) - After de-duplication: ~20,676 unique coordinates plus 4 boundary coordinates
Each row shows the coordinate in all coordinate systems simultaneously, and every column is named for the timeline or C-Map it belongs to: - dgt_1 (pixels): The root (parent) coordinate in pixels - dgt_holes (pixels): Relative coordinate in child timeline (first hole = 0, NaN if outside) - C-Map columns: Physical units with names like “pixels_to_inches (inches)”
There is no separate axis column. The coordinate the query was made on is already the dgt_1 column, so a second column repeating it under a generic name carried no information the row did not already hold.

In this tutorial, we demonstrated a complete alignment workflow:

Image Timeline (DGT1): Created from ATON analysis with holes as events
Physical C-Maps: Attached with human-readable names (name=)
Child Timeline (dgt_holes): Modeled the musical region as a child
Timestamps: Showed cross-section views through the hierarchy
External Data: Loaded MIDI, audio, and score with harmonies + chords
TimelineGroup: Connected all timelines (no root - all peers)
Coordinate Transfer via Timestamps: The RIGHT way to transfer coordinates!






Pattern
Usage




One-line loading
ATONLoader.from_file(path)


Direct timeline creation
loader.create_timeline(uid=...)


Named C-Maps
ScalarMap(..., name="pixels_to_inches")


Coordinate transfer
group.get_timestamp_at(coord, timeline_id)


Timeline display
Just timeline (no print() needed)

title: How to Align a Piano Roll (SUPRA)
text:
The piano roll was scanned at 300.25 DPI (dots per inch). We attach ConversionMaps to convert pixel coordinates to physical units.
Important: We specify name= for human-readable column headers in timestamp tables. Without it, columns would show as “map:ScalarMap_1”.
Calculation: 299,400 pixels / 300.25 DPI = 997.17 inches = 25.33 meters

LENGTH_DPI = 300.25

# Note: name= provides readable column headers (defaults to "source_to_target")
dgt1.add_conversion_map(
    ScalarMap(
        scalar=1 / LENGTH_DPI,
        source_unit="pixels",
        target_unit="inches",
        name="pixels_to_inches",  # Human-readable name for timestamp columns
    )
)

dgt1.add_conversion_map(
    ScalarMap(
        scalar=2.54 / LENGTH_DPI,
        source_unit="pixels",
        target_unit="cm",
        name="pixels_to_cm",  # Human-readable name for timestamp columns
    )
)

The convert_to method returns proper Coordinate objects with units.

image_length_inches = dgt1.convert_to(dgt1.length, "inches")
image_length_cm = dgt1.convert_to(dgt1.length, "cm")

{
    "Image length": dgt1.length,
    "Image length (inches)": image_length_inches,
    "Image length (cm)": image_length_cm,
    "Image length (meters)": f"{image_length_cm.value / 100:.2f} meters",
}

title: How to Align a Piano Roll (SUPRA)
text:
The musical content doesn’t span the entire image - holes start at pixel 15,343. We create a child timeline to provide a relative coordinate view where the first hole = 0 pixels.
Key insight: The child has no events of its own. It’s purely a coordinate transformation. When we get timestamps, we see event coordinates in BOTH the parent (absolute) and child (relative) coordinate systems - for free!

dgt_holes = dgt1.create_child(
    length=aton_loader.musical_length,
    offset=aton_loader.first_hole,
    uid="dgt_holes",
    name="Musical Holes Region",
)

text:
With the parent-child hierarchy established, we can generate timestamps that show coordinates in both the parent (full image) and child (holes region) coordinate systems simultaneously.
Note: get_timestamp_table(format="dataframe") gives column names with units appended (e.g., “pixels_to_inches (inches)”) and one scalar per cell in each axis’s declared number type. This is the recommended way to get timestamp data for display.

timestamps_df = dgt1.get_timestamp_table(format="dataframe")

{"Total timestamps": len(timestamps_df), "Columns": list(timestamps_df.columns)}

{'Total timestamps': 20680,
 'Columns': ['dgt_1 (pixels)',
  'dgt_holes (pixels)',
  'pixels_to_inches (inches)',
  'pixels_to_cm (centimeters)']}


Why ~20,680 timestamps?
The timestamp table has one row per unique event coordinate in the hierarchy: - Parent timeline (dgt_1) contains 30,092 hole events at absolute pixel coordinates - But many holes share the same pixel row (multiple notes at one time position) - After de-duplication: ~20,676 unique coordinates plus 4 boundary coordinates
Each row shows the coordinate in all coordinate systems simultaneously, and every column is named for the timeline or C-Map it belongs to: - dgt_1 (pixels): The root (parent) coordinate in pixels - dgt_holes (pixels): Relative coordinate in child timeline (first hole = 0, NaN if outside) - C-Map columns: Physical units with names like “pixels_to_inches (inches)”
There is no separate axis column. The coordinate the query was made on is already the dgt_1 column, so a second column repeating it under a generic name carried no information the row did not already hold.

title: How to Align a Piano Roll (SUPRA)
text:
Now we bring everything together in a TimelineGroup. This establishes commensurability between all timelines, enabling coordinate transfer.
Important: A TimelineGroup does NOT have a root timeline - all timelines are peers. We create it from a list of timelines.
Alignment structure:
dgt_holes (pixels)
    |
    +-- dlt1_raw (MIDI ticks)
    |
    +-- dlt2_exp (MIDI ticks)
    |
    +-- dpt1_audio (samples)
    |
    +-- clt1_score (quarterbeats)

group = TimelineGroup(
    id="supra_alignment",
    name="SUPRA Piano Roll Alignment",
    timelines=[dgt_holes, dlt1_raw, dlt2_exp, dpt1_audio, clt1_score],
)

text:
The right way to transfer coordinates is through timestamps! Instead of asking for one target coordinate at a time with get_coordinate_at(), we use get_timestamp_at(), which returns a full cross-section through all timelines in a single call.


Let’s take the first occurrence of a I chord (C major) and find its position in every timeline.

# Find the first I chord (tonic) harmony
i_chords = score_loader.store.annotations.filter(text="I")
if len(i_chords) > 0:
    first_i = i_chords.to_dataframe().iloc[0]
    i_chord_qb = float(first_i["start"])
    i_chord_label = first_i["text"]
    i_chord_mc = first_i["mc"]
else:
    # Fallback if no I chord
    first_harmony = score_loader.store.annotations.to_dataframe().iloc[0]
    i_chord_qb = float(first_harmony["start"])
    i_chord_label = first_harmony["text"]
    i_chord_mc = first_harmony["mc"]

{

    "Position (quarterbeats)": i_chord_qb,
    "Measure": i_chord_mc,
}

title: How to Load an Audio-to-Audio Alignment (Listen Here!)
text:
Listen Here! aligns several recordings of one work to each other and exports the result as a single JSON file. Each recording is warped onto a shared, equidistant reference grid: per recording, the file stores a times array whose i-th entry is that recording’s clock-time (in seconds) at reference-grid column i. Because every recording is sampled against the same grid, the arrays are parallel and equal length — together they form a dense alignment matrix of shape (recordings × grid columns). This guide loads such an export into a single audio-to-audio AlignmentBundle with ListenHereLoader.
This is a different shape of data from the score↔︎performance loaders. There, each file relates one score to one performance, and a MatchGraph only emerges once several such bundles are combined. A Listen Here! file instead encodes the alignment of all recordings against one another directly — one file already carries the whole graph. The natural reading is a complete pairwise topology: at every grid column, every unordered pair of recordings is related by a synchronous instant MatchClaim. The file states positions on a grid and no events (no note, no beat), so each side of such a claim is the sentinel CHUNK: a position on a timeline that holds no event for it, stated by the claim’s anchor.
We load an existing alignment; nothing here runs an aligner. The warp was computed once, offline, and written to disk; the loader reads it faithfully.
The arc:

Load the export in one call and read the reference recording.
Reach the columnar MatchClaimField through the uniform get_field API, and inspect a single claim.
Build the AlignmentBundle.
The headline: place a point on one recording and read it on all the others.
A note on scale — why the claims live in columns, not a million objects.



The example data is a real Listen Here! alignment export of six recordings of the whole of Beethoven’s Eroica Variations, Op. 35 — six readings of the entire work warped onto one reference grid. The file is large (about 14 MB of parallel onset arrays), so it is read directly from its place on disk rather than fetched through the test-data helper. The cell below walks up from the notebook to the directory that holds the export.

from __future__ import annotations

import os
from pathlib import Path

from timetoalign.alignment.claims import MatchClaim
from timetoalign.loader.alignment import ListenHereLoader

# Locate the local Listen Here! alignment export by walking up the directory
# tree until an ancestor contains it. This reads a local export file directly;
# it is not a packaged test corpus.
_EXPORT_REL = Path("beethoven_eroica_variations_op35/variation_14/mdw/alignment.json")
_search_roots = [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents]
if "__file__" in globals():
    _search_roots += list(Path(__file__).resolve().parents)
_alignment_json = next(
    candidate for base in _search_roots if (candidate := base / _EXPORT_REL).exists()
)




ListenHereLoader parses the single alignment JSON file: it reads each recording’s times array, checks that they all index the same reference grid (equal length), and assembles the complete pairwise claim set. from_file() is the one-line form of the standard two-phase loader pattern.

loader = ListenHereLoader.from_file(_alignment_json)
loader

The loader names the reference recording — the recording whose clock defines the grid origin. Reading the reference matters because it is the anchor against which every other recording was warped; it is, however, just another recording in the bundle, not a privileged hub. Every recording is related to every other directly, so the bundle can be read from any of them.

Six recordings, reported as sorted stems:

The alignment is reached through the uniform field API: loader.get_field(MatchClaim) returns a MatchClaimField — a columnar, PyArrow-backed store that holds the entire set of pairwise MatchClaims as Arrow columns and materialises individual MatchClaim objects only on demand. Its length is the complete topology: for R recordings and N grid columns, every unordered pair at every column, i.e. C(R, 2) × N claims. Six recordings give C(6, 2) = 15 pairs, and this 25-minute work is sampled at 76 376 grid columns — so the field holds well over a million claims:

field = loader.get_field(MatchClaim)

{
    "field type": type(field).__name__,
    "claims": len(field),
    "C(6,2) pairs": 15,
    "grid columns": len(field) // 15,
}

 'claims': 1145640,
 'C(6,2) pairs': 15,
 'grid columns': 76376}


The field is held columnar precisely so that this many claims need not be a million Python objects. Indexing it materialises one MatchClaim on demand — an ordinary pairwise claim joining two recordings at one grid column, CHUNK on both sides (the card names CHUNK as each side’s event): its anchor holds the two positions in seconds, exactly the numbers the file states, and no event stands behind either. It carries the shared provenance the export recorded (Listen Here!’s chroma-feature DTW). We look at a single claim to see the shape; we do not iterate or materialise the whole field.

Try: claim.get_matchstamp()






create_bundle() assembles the AlignmentBundle: one seconds Timeline per recording, each in its own group, and the complete pairwise claim set tying every recording to every other. The file gives seconds, so each recording is a continuous seconds timeline with the number type float, its length the duration the file stores, and every grid time stays the number the file wrote. The loader reads no recording, so it states no sample rate and adds no samples axis. The timelines hold no events, since the file names none. All the alignment lives in the bundle’s one MatchClaim table, which the bundle keeps columnar rather than exploding into a million claim objects.

bundle = loader.create_bundle()

{

}

Here is the promise that makes audio-to-audio alignment compelling: place a point on one recording, and it is instantly placed on all the others. get_matchstamp_at takes a coordinate on any one recording’s timeline and returns the corresponding coordinate on every recording connected to it.
The query coordinate must land on an exact grid column carried by the field, so we take a real one from the data rather than inventing a value: a claim from roughly the middle of the work, read off the reference recording’s clock. Each recording’s group is named by its stem, and its timeline’s ID is minted, so the reference timeline is found through its group.

reference_group = next(
    group
    for group in bundle.groups.values()
    if group.name == os.path.splitext(loader.reference)[0]
)
reference_uid = reference_group.timeline_ids[0]

reference_claims = field.connecting(reference_uid)
mid_claim = reference_claims[len(reference_claims) // 2]
query_coord = mid_claim.start_anchor.get_coordinate_for(reference_uid)

Read across that MatchStamp: the same musical instant the reference reaches at this second falls at a different time in each of the other five recordings — a quicker reading reaches it earlier, a steadier one later. Each reading is one of the file’s own times values. One coordinate, placed once, located in all six recordings in a single query:

    "timelines in the stamp": stamp.n_timelines,
    "seconds per recording": {
        bundle.get_timeline(tl_id).name: stamp.get_coordinate_for(tl_id, format="float")

  'mdw Hyo Eun PARK': 742.4865538184648,

Because the topology is complete, the same query works from any recording as the anchor, not only the reference — every pair is directly related, so no recording is a required hub.




This single file holds more than a million pairwise claims: six recordings give C(6, 2) = 15 pairs, and a 25-minute work sampled at 50 Hz runs to tens of thousands of grid columns. A whole-work export with more recordings would be larger still.
This is exactly why the claims live in a MatchClaimField rather than as a million individual MatchClaim objects. The field stores the whole set as Arrow columns, one per property of a claim (the two timeline ids as strings, each coordinate as a struct of value, numerator, denominator, unit and number type), and the loader builds it vectorised — never constructing a Python claim per row. A MatchClaim is materialised only when a single row is indexed. get_matchstamp_at likewise filters the columns vectorised and materialises only the handful of claims at the queried coordinate. The columnar store is what lets one AlignmentBundle hold a whole-work, every-pair audio-to-audio graph without strain.










What the bundle expresses
How




One recording per group
cpt_… seconds timeline (float), recording-length, no events


The whole pairwise alignment
a columnar MatchClaimField via get_field(MatchClaim)


One claim, materialised
field[i] → a synchronous instant MatchClaim, CHUNK on both sides


The reference recording
loader.reference — the grid origin, but just another recording


A point placed everywhere
bundle.get_matchstamp_at(coord, timeline_id) → every recording at once



A single file encodes an entire audio-to-audio MatchGraph — every recording of one work warped onto a shared reference grid, every pair directly related. ListenHereLoader reads it into one AlignmentBundle in which a coordinate placed on any one recording resolves, in a single query, across all the others; and the dense claim set that makes that possible is held in columns, not a million objects.

The field is held columnar precisely so that this many claims need not be a million Python objects. Indexing it materialises one MatchClaim on demand — an ordinary pairwise claim joining two recordings at one grid column, CHUNK on both sides (the card names CHUNK as each side’s event): its anchor holds the two positions in seconds, exactly the numbers the file states, and no event stands behind either. It carries the shared provenance the export recorded (Listen Here!’s chroma-feature DTW). We look at a single claim to see the shape; we do not iterate or materialise the whole field.

title: How to Load an Audio-to-Audio Alignment (Listen Here!)
text:
create_bundle() assembles the AlignmentBundle: one seconds Timeline per recording, each in its own group, and the complete pairwise claim set tying every recording to every other. The file gives seconds, so each recording is a continuous seconds timeline with the number type float, its length the duration the file stores, and every grid time stays the number the file wrote. The loader reads no recording, so it states no sample rate and adds no samples axis. The timelines hold no events, since the file names none. All the alignment lives in the bundle’s one MatchClaim table, which the bundle keeps columnar rather than exploding into a million claim objects.

bundle = loader.create_bundle()

{

{'timelines': 6, 'groups': 6}

title: How to Load an Audio-to-Audio Alignment (Listen Here!)
text:
Here is the promise that makes audio-to-audio alignment compelling: place a point on one recording, and it is instantly placed on all the others. get_matchstamp_at takes a coordinate on any one recording’s timeline and returns the corresponding coordinate on every recording connected to it.
The query coordinate must land on an exact grid column carried by the field, so we take a real one from the data rather than inventing a value: a claim from roughly the middle of the work, read off the reference recording’s clock. Each recording’s group is named by its stem, and its timeline’s ID is minted, so the reference timeline is found through its group.

reference_group = next(
    group
    for group in bundle.groups.values()
    if group.name == os.path.splitext(loader.reference)[0]
)
reference_uid = reference_group.timeline_ids[0]

reference_claims = field.connecting(reference_uid)
mid_claim = reference_claims[len(reference_claims) // 2]
query_coord = mid_claim.start_anchor.get_coordinate_for(reference_uid)

query_coord

IdCoordinate(763.76, seconds, 'cpt_17736i4qztp3p')


That instant — about twelve and a half minutes into the reference reading — resolves to a MatchStamp spanning all six recordings at once:

stamp = bundle.get_matchstamp_at(query_coord, reference_uid)

Read across that MatchStamp: the same musical instant the reference reaches at this second falls at a different time in each of the other five recordings — a quicker reading reaches it earlier, a steadier one later. Each reading is one of the file’s own times values. One coordinate, placed once, located in all six recordings in a single query:

title: How to Load an Audio-to-Audio Alignment (Listen Here!)
text:
This single file holds more than a million pairwise claims: six recordings give C(6, 2) = 15 pairs, and a 25-minute work sampled at 50 Hz runs to tens of thousands of grid columns. A whole-work export with more recordings would be larger still.
This is exactly why the claims live in a MatchClaimField rather than as a million individual MatchClaim objects. The field stores the whole set as Arrow columns, one per property of a claim (the two timeline ids as strings, each coordinate as a struct of value, numerator, denominator, unit and number type), and the loader builds it vectorised — never constructing a Python claim per row. A MatchClaim is materialised only when a single row is indexed. get_matchstamp_at likewise filters the columns vectorised and materialises only the handful of claims at the queried coordinate. The columnar store is what lets one AlignmentBundle hold a whole-work, every-pair audio-to-audio graph without strain.

What the bundle expresses
How




One recording per group

The whole pairwise alignment
a columnar MatchClaimField via get_field(MatchClaim)


One claim, materialised
field[i] → a synchronous instant MatchClaim, CHUNK on both sides


The reference recording
loader.reference — the grid origin, but just another recording


A point placed everywhere
bundle.get_matchstamp_at(coord, timeline_id) → every recording at once



A single file encodes an entire audio-to-audio MatchGraph — every recording of one work warped onto a shared reference grid, every pair directly related. ListenHereLoader reads it into one AlignmentBundle in which a coordinate placed on any one recording resolves, in a single query, across all the others; and the dense claim set that makes that possible is held in columns, not a million objects.

title: How to Describe What a Bundle and Its Timelines Stand For
text:
A TimeToShare manifest holds two planes. Its temporal structure states how coordinates relate: timelines, their nesting, maps, regions and flow control. Its statements state what the elements stand for and how those things relate to others, and never nest, order or align anything.
Three kinds of element are subjects of statements: the bundle, which is the manifest itself and names the work it is about; every timeline, at any depth, for the manifestation it is the axis of (an edition, an encoding, a recording file, a video); and every region, for the stretch of that manifestation it marks. A statement is a pair of a property and a value, both identifiers in published vocabularies where they name things; the property type reads “is a”. Works and expressions are never elements: they appear as values, the work under the bundle’s schema:about.
A manifest carrying statements is YAML-LD: its inline @context declares the prefixes its compact IRIs use, so it reads as linked data without fetching anything. The catalogue that comes with the TimeToShare package knows the vocabularies, the identifier systems and the verbs that state one relation in each of them.
This guide describes the LayerIt example: an MEI encoding of the first six bars of Debussy’s Clair de lune, a concert video of Maria João Pires and a WAV file cut from its sound. It states what each timeline is, who performs, who said so and who believes it, offers candidates, describes a region, writes the manifest, and imports the description of an MEI header and of a MeLODy repository. The format is specified in TimeToShare’s description of a manifest.


Install the library with pip install timetoalign; the MeLODy import also needs rdflib, pip install "timetoalign[rdf]". No data is downloaded: the MEI header and the MeLODy repository are written below into a temporary directory. The identifiers are those of public catalogues; the editor who states the pairs and the days are invented.
show prints the pairs of a subject, or of a value node inside it, and the provenance entry of each pair that has one, marked stated or candidate; a value node’s own entries are shown when show is given that node. show_manifest prints a manifest as canonical YAML, leaving the format’s own terms out of @context so that only the prefixes remain.

import json
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from timetoshare import FORMAT_CONTEXT, dumps, to_file_id

import timetoalign as tta
from timetoalign.loader import MeiHeadLoader, MelodyLoader

EDITOR = "https://example.org/people/editor"
REVIEWER = "https://example.org/people/reviewer"
DAY = "2026-11-18"
FOLDER = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())


def text(value):
    """Write a JSON value on one line."""
    return json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False)


def show(holder, node=()):
    """Print the pairs of a holder or of one of its value nodes, then their entries.

    A value node's own entries are left out of its pair; ``node=`` shows them.
    """
    for property, value in holder.get_pairs(node=node):
        if isinstance(value, dict):
            value = {key: item for key, item in value.items() if key != "provenance"}
        print(f"{property}: {text(value)}")
    candidates = holder.get_candidates(node=node)
    for entry in holder.get_provenance(node=node):
        kind = "candidate" if entry in candidates else "stated"
        rest = {
            key: value
            for key, value in entry.items()
            if key not in ("property", "value")
        }
        print(f"[{kind}] {entry['property']}: {text(entry['value'])}")
        print(f"    {text(rest)}")


def show_manifest(manifest):
    """Print a manifest as canonical YAML, its context reduced to the prefixes."""
    prefixes = {
        key: value
        for key, value in manifest["@context"].items()
        if key not in FORMAT_CONTEXT
    }
    print(dumps({**manifest, "@context": prefixes}), end="")

The bundle holds the three timelines: the encoding clt_6 in quarters, 27 of them for six bars of 9/8; the video cpt_1 in seconds, of unknown length, with a child cpt_2 for the part the example uses; and the WAV file dpt_1 in samples.

bundle = tta.AlignmentBundle(
    id="layerit", name="LayerIt, Clair de lune mm. 1–6 (Pires)"
)
score = tta.ContinuousLogicalTimeline(
    length=27, uid="clt_6", name="Clair de lune, mm. 1–6 (MEI)"
)
video = tta.ContinuousPhysicalTimeline(
    length=None, uid="cpt_1", name="Maria João Pires live at Jardin Musical"
)
video.create_child(length=33.353016, uid="cpt_2")
wav = tta.DiscretePhysicalTimeline(
    length=1470868, uid="dpt_1", name="ClairDeLune_MariaJoaoPires_untilM6.wav"
)
for timeline in (score, video, wav):
    bundle.add_timeline(timeline)
bundle.timeline_ids

['clt_6', 'cpt_1', 'dpt_1']





add_statement() states one pair on a timeline or a bundle, in place. The bundle is about the work, named here by its Wikidata item; the value is a node, a thing with an id and a label cached for display. The video’s timeline is a video: type takes a class, and the catalogue’s verb is_a states the same in Wikidata’s vocabulary, as an instance of (wdt:P31) the item for a video, wd:Q98069877. add_verb() takes the verb, the system and the value, and states the pairs the catalogue’s pattern for them gives.

bundle.add_statement("schema:about", {"id": "wd:Q29117946", "label": "Clair de lune"})
video.add_statement("type", "schema:VideoObject")
video.add_verb("is_a", "wikidata", "wd:Q98069877")
video.statements

{'type': ['schema:VideoObject'], 'wdt:P31': [{'id': 'wd:Q98069877'}]}





The pianist is named in two systems: by a Wikidata item through Wikidata’s property “performer” (wdt:P175), and by a VIAF identifier through the MARC relator “performer” (rel:prf), the fallback for a system without a property of its own. Each pair holds a node of its own.

video.add_verb("performed_by", "wikidata", "wd:Q235650", label="Maria João Pires")
video.add_verb("performed_by", "fallback", "viaf:113931950")
[(rectangle.verb, rectangle.things) for rectangle in video.get_rectangles()]

[('is_a',
  ('http://schema.org/VideoObject',
   'http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q98069877')),
 ('performed_by', ('http://viaf.org/viaf/113931950',)),
 ('performed_by', ('http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q235650',))]


get_rectangles() gathers the pairs the catalogue reads as one verb about one thing. So far the two performers are two things. A value node is a subject too: node= addresses it by its path, the property and the index, and schema:sameAs on the Wikidata node ties the two. The pairs then form one rectangle, labelled by the node’s label.

video.add_statement("schema:sameAs", {"id": "viaf:113931950"}, node=("wdt:P175", 0))
[
    (rectangle.verb, rectangle.label, rectangle.things)
    for rectangle in video.get_rectangles()
]

[('is_a',
  None,
  ('http://schema.org/VideoObject',
   'http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q98069877')),
 ('performed_by',
  'Maria João Pires',
  ('http://viaf.org/viaf/113931950',
   'http://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q235650'))]





A pair without a provenance entry is stated by the manifest’s publisher. provenance= gives the pair an entry naming who stated it, when, how and why; the keys are those the file writes. actor= records the person stating the pair as believing it, with the belief "true" and the day. A loader or a service records how a pair was made and holds no belief. get_provenance() answers the entries.

video.add_statement(
    "schema:sameAs",
    {"id": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ch2mrPm1JnM"},
    provenance={
        "stated_by": [EDITOR],
        "date": DAY,
        "method": "manual",
        "note": "pasted URL",
    },
    actor=EDITOR,
    date=DAY,
)
video.get_provenance()

[{'property': 'schema:sameAs',
  'value': {'id': 'https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ch2mrPm1JnM'},
  'stated_by': ['https://example.org/people/editor'],
  'date': '2026-11-18',
  'method': 'manual',
  'note': 'pasted URL',
  'beliefs': [{'actor': 'https://example.org/people/editor',
    'belief': 'true',
    'date': '2026-11-18'}]}]





A candidate is a pair held only as its entry: the subject does not state it, and it waits for someone to. add_candidate() offers one. The WAV file was cut from the video’s sound, which is an inference. A value naming an element of the manifest is the node of its reference, # followed by its ID, which to_file_id() builds.

source = {"id": to_file_id(video.id)}
wav.add_candidate(
    "dcterms:source",
    source,
    stated_by=EDITOR,
    method="inferred",
    date=DAY,
    note="assumed ripped from the video's sound and cut",
)
show(wav)

[candidate] dcterms:source: {"id": "#cpt_1"}
    {"stated_by": ["https://example.org/people/editor"], "date": "2026-11-18", "method": "inferred", "note": "assumed ripped from the video's sound and cut"}


Stating the candidate with add_statement() makes it a pair of the subject; its entry keeps every key and records the person stating it as believing it.

wav.add_statement("dcterms:source", source, actor=EDITOR, date="2026-11-19")
show(wav)

dcterms:source: {"id": "#cpt_1"}
[stated] dcterms:source: {"id": "#cpt_1"}
    {"stated_by": ["https://example.org/people/editor"], "date": "2026-11-18", "method": "inferred", "note": "assumed ripped from the video's sound and cut", "beliefs": [{"actor": "https://example.org/people/editor", "belief": "true", "date": "2026-11-19"}]}


Any actor may record a belief in any pair with add_belief(): "true", "false" or "unlikely", at most one per actor, a later one replacing the earlier. A belief never changes what is stated: a reviewer who believes the source "false" leaves the pair in place, and nothing derives a truth value from the beliefs. The belief filter reads them for one actor, the believer, keeping the states listed in beliefs= ("true", "undecided" where the believer holds no belief, "unlikely", "false"); by default every state but "false".

wav.add_belief(
    "dcterms:source", source, actor=REVIEWER, belief="false", date="2026-11-20"
)
(
    wav.statements,
    len(wav.get_provenance(believer=REVIEWER)),
    len(wav.get_provenance(believer=EDITOR, beliefs=["true"])),
)

({'dcterms:source': [{'id': '#cpt_1'}]}, 0, 1)


A candidate an actor believes "false" was examined and refused; it is kept, so that it is not offered to that actor again. A lookup in the GND offers its entry “Clair de lune” as the work the encoding is an example of; it is Debussy’s song on Verlaine’s poem, not the piano piece. The entry keeps how the candidate was found beside the belief. get_candidates() answers every candidate, and with believer= those the believer does not believe "false".

score.add_statement("type", "melod:Manifestation")
score.add_candidate(
    "schema:exampleOfWork",
    {"id": "gnd:1156628156"},
    stated_by=EDITOR,
    method="reconciled",
    service="https://lobid.org/gnd/search",
    date=DAY,
)
score.add_belief(
    "schema:exampleOfWork",
    {"id": "gnd:1156628156"},
    actor=EDITOR,
    belief="false",
    date=DAY,
    note="GND 'Clair de lune' is Debussy's song L 32 on Verlaine, not the piano piece",
)
show(score)
len(score.get_candidates()), score.get_candidates(believer=EDITOR)

type: "melod:Manifestation"
[candidate] schema:exampleOfWork: {"id": "gnd:1156628156"}
    {"stated_by": ["https://example.org/people/editor"], "date": "2026-11-18", "method": "reconciled", "service": "https://lobid.org/gnd/search", "beliefs": [{"actor": "https://example.org/people/editor", "belief": "false", "date": "2026-11-18", "note": "GND 'Clair de lune' is Debussy's song L 32 on Verlaine, not the piano piece"}]}


(1, [])


Candidates and beliefs take a node path as statements do. The encoding is an edition of the work (wdt:P629), and the GND entry for the piano piece is offered as the same work, inside that node.

score.add_statement("wdt:P629", {"id": "wd:Q29117946", "label": "Clair de lune"})
score.add_candidate(
    "schema:sameAs",
    {"id": "gnd:300042558"},
    node=("wdt:P629", 0),
    stated_by=EDITOR,
    method="reconciled",
    service="https://lobid.org/gnd/search",
    match="exact",
    date=DAY,
)
show(score, node=("wdt:P629", 0))

[candidate] schema:sameAs: {"id": "gnd:300042558"}
    {"stated_by": ["https://example.org/people/editor"], "date": "2026-11-18", "method": "reconciled", "service": "https://lobid.org/gnd/search", "match": "exact"}





A region stands for the stretch of its timeline’s manifestation it marks. Regions are frozen: with_statement() returns a copy holding the pair, and replace_region() stores it in the place of the region with its ID. The region’s siblings without_statement(), with_candidate(), with_belief(), with_verb() and with_prefix() mirror the timeline’s remove_statement(), add_candidate(), add_belief(), add_verb() and add_prefix().

opening = score.create_region(0, 9, id="opening", name="mm. 1–2")
score.replace_region(
    opening.with_statement("rdfs:comment", "the opening, before the melody enters")
)
opening.statements, score.get_region("opening").statements

({}, {'rdfs:comment': ['the opening, before the melody enters']})





to_dict() writes each element’s statements and provenance where the element stands, and an @context holding the format’s terms and the prefixes the statements use, no others. Every prefix used here is the catalogue’s; a prefix it lacks is declared on the element with add_prefix(), and a pair using an undeclared one is refused.

manifest = bundle.to_dict()
show_manifest(manifest)

              id: "viaf:113931950"
      "wdt:P31":
        -
          id: "wd:Q98069877"
    unit: seconds
  -
    id: "#dpt_1"
    length: 1470868
    name: ClairDeLune_MariaJoaoPires_untilM6.wav
    provenance:
      -
        beliefs:
          -
            actor: "https://example.org/people/editor"
            belief: "true"
            date: "2026-11-19"
          -
            actor: "https://example.org/people/reviewer"
            belief: "false"
            date: "2026-11-20"

        method: inferred
        note: "assumed ripped from the video's sound and cut"
        property: "dcterms:source"
        stated_by: ["https://example.org/people/editor"]
